#3544. Star Trek's Gates McFadden And John De Lancie React To Death Of Patrick Stewart

It's never easy saying goodbye to heroes we grew up adoring, but some deaths take even longer than others to process. The loss of "Star Trek" and "X-Men" legend Patrick Stewart still doesn't feel quite real yet, even as it feels like we've spent every day since celebrating all of his greatest and most memorable moments on the screen. When it comes to the tight-knit bonds formed between members of the "Trek" family, well, they've proven that it really is a family. Some relationships have experienced more friction than others, such as the widely-publicized rift between William Shatner and the late Walter Koenig, but others have gone through the fire and emerged stronger than ever.

That sense of history through the decades is probably why two celebrations of Stewart's life hit harder than the rest. In a pair of separate posts, "Star Trek: The Next Generation" co-stars Gates McFadden and John de Lancie both memorialized their longtime friend and screen partner. Cast as Beverly Crusher and the enigmatic cosmic being Q, respectively, McFadden and de Lancie represent two of Jean-Luc Picard's most popular and well-established character dynamics throughout their collective run on "Trek." Both shared countless memories together with Stewart on- and off-screen, and, fittingly enough, both received satisfying send-offs alongside their captain on "Star Trek: Picard."

For those prone to bursting into tears over such heartbreaking tributes, be warned that this will likely unleash the waterworks.

Jean-Luc Picard meant so much to so many, and Patrick Stewart's portrayal of the venerated captain represented something deeper and more meaningful than a simple "Trek" character. And while fans all over the world have attempted to verbalize just how important he was, the woman behind Dr. Beverly Crusher has now captured it as eloquently as only she can.

Gates McFadden was one of the many Hollywood icons who initially reacted to Stewart's passing. But in a guest article in Variety, she's penned a full-length eulogy for her friend's well-lived life. However, though it's well worth reading in full, one particular passage draws a direct link between the integrity of Stewart's performance as Picard and our desperate need for genuine leadership in real life (a particularly poignant message on the U.S.' Election Day):

"One thing is for certain: Patrick's reach across the continents was massive. After word of his death surfaced, the internet, not surprisingly, was filled with thousands of tributes of admiration and overflowing love for the Yorkshire man. He touched so many people in so many ways. Not only was he the captain of the Enterprise crew, he seems to have been everyone's captain because of how he walked in the world.

What a breath of fresh air to have a leader who cared about the ethics of what he said! The result was eloquence. Seriousness. Intellect. The character of Jean-Luc Picard, which Patrick played brilliantly, was the antithesis of many of our leaders today."

McFadden sums up Stewart's life and his tragic loss thusly: "Jean-Luc Picard embodied that ideal. Patrick's death means the loss of Picard, which for some hurts even more than the loss of Patrick Stewart. Jean-Luc gave us hope."

Where Dr. Beverly Crusher brought both a platonic and romantic dimension to her relationship with Jean-Luc Picard, Q represents a very different extreme of emotions. Picard's longtime frenemy spent many an episode of "The Next Generation" annoying our good captain to no end, oftentimes outwitting our hero and proving himself an equal match in intellect or philosophy. But their two diametrically opposite perspectives on humanity added so much to their adventures over the years and, ultimately, reached a tearjerking crescendo in the Season 2 finale of "Star Trek: Picard" as they say an emotional goodbye to one another.

Actor John de Lancie struck that exact same tone in a Facebook post over the weekend. It's not easy to encapsulate such a complicated, prickly, but oh-so-entertaining dynamic between two such worthy opponents, but the Q scene-stealer certainly found a way. In a much shorter (though no less sincere) remembrance, he stated:

"For forty years, Q has been a thorn in Jean-Luc Picard's side. And what a pleasure it has been to be that thorn.

Patrick Stewart was a wonderful actor. He brought intelligence and depth to every role he played. It was a privilege to have worked with him.

The universe is a little smaller and a little less bright today with his passing.

We couldn't have said it any better than that. Most Trekkies would put the Q and Picard rivalry up there among the best in the entire franchise — a testament to Stewart and de Lancie's easy chemistry and witty repartee. It's devastating to know we'll never see that on-screen again, yet reassuring to know it'll always stand the test of time.

Disney has always been known for its animated blockbusters, but Frozen (which is streaming with a Disney+ subscription) became a full-blown sensation upon its release in 2013. Its sequel Frozen II crushed at the box office, and two more sequels were quickly announced. Although the studios' Head of Animation recently revealed a big change coming to the next two installments of the franchisee

The first Frozen III footage debuted at D23 over the summer, so anticipation for the threequel is steadily building. While we'll have to wait another year until it arrives in November of 2027, Disney's Jared Bush spoke to Collider about how the studio is approaching the next two movies. He revealed that they're putting a full emphasis on the third movie, rather than trying to put out 3 and 4 in quick succession. In his words:

Looking at Frozen 3 and what a Frozen 4 could look like, I know early on it was, 'We're going to put them right together, and they're going to be out in the world. It's going to happen quick.' That's not what we're doing, for a lot of reasons.

Rather than trying to produce a third and fourth Frozen movie as a cash grab (although they're sure to rake in the bucks), it sounds like the powers that be at Disney are putting story first. This is sure to be a relief for fans who might be worried about the property's legacy being soiled by the next two installments.

Fans are excited for Anna and Kristoff's wedding in the threequel, and to reportedly see Olaf get a love interest. Although we shouldn't expect Frozen III to do a bunch of set up for the developing fourth movie. As Bush went on to say:

To me, an important one is we want to make sure that Frozen 3 is the best movie it can possibly be, so that when you get to the end of the movie, do you feel like you've watched a complete story? That it feels like something that feels fulfilling. That doesn't always mean that everything is buttoned up, but it does mean that you have to be building to something that feels worthy of the end of a franchise that's that important to people.

Honestly, I love this strategy. Rather than getting too big picture about the Frozen franchise as a whole, it sounds like the next two installments will tell independent, fully formed stories. So we shouldn't expect any MCU-esque credits scene that help to set up the fourth movie once Frozen III hits theaters next year.

Sometimes thinking too far ahead can frustrate moviegoers when it comes to franchise films. For instance, Halloween Kills got some backlash upon its release for keeping Jamie Lee Curtis' Laurie Strode in the background and set up her role in the threequel. Luckily the third Frozen movie won't be doing that, and will instead tell its own complete narrative.

All will be revealed when Frozen III hits theaters November 24th, 2027. Since its not on the 2026 movie release list, we'll have to practice patience until footage get its wide release.

#3541. Johnny Depp Has One Condition To Return For Pirates Of The Caribbean 6

Will Captain Jack Sparrow suit up for one last ride? At the very least, Johnny Depp isn't ruling it out, but the actor has a condition to return for "Pirates of the Caribbean 6." Depp is in the midst of mounting a Hollywood comeback following his fall from grace several years ago, thanks to his highly publicized legal feud with his ex-wife Amber Heard. The Depp/Heard case was even explored in a two-part Discovery+ documentary. Now, though? He's back and may (emphasis on "may") yet return to his most famous role.

During a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight for his Hollywood comeback movie "Ebenezer," the actor was asked about reprising his role as Jack Sparrow in the next "Pirates of the Caribbean" film, which has been in the works at Disney for some time. Here's what he had to say about it:

"If things are exactly where they need to be with regard to how they are going to top off the 'Pirates' franchise ...The only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.

"I will go to work with [producer] [Jerry] Bruckheimer tomorrow for anything," Depp added. "Doesn't matter ...If it's Jerry, I trust him. We have a deep friendship."

All of the "Pirates of the Caribbean" movies have been hits at the box office, with much of that attributed to Depp's work as Jack Sparrow. In light of everything that's happened in recent years, it's also easy to forget that he was nominated for an Oscar for his work on "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl." So, it's not hard to grasp why bringing him back might seem appealing. But Disney needs to decide if the inevitable circus that will create would be worth it.

Johnny Depp hasn't been in a big blockbuster in nearly a decade. He dropped out of the "Fantastic Beasts" franchise after a court case verdict related to the tabloid The Sun running a story where it referred to him as a "wife beater." Since then, he's taken on roles in smaller movies like "Jeanne du Barry."

Depp lost his suit against The Sun, but the actor and Amber Heard later settled a defamation case in 2022. And while that sort of paved the way for his attempted comeback, the optics surrounding Depp are still pretty lousy. Unfortunately, in Hollywood, money speaks louder than anything else. That is to say, should "Ebenezer" become a hit (suggesting the general public has an appetite for a Johnny Depp comeback), we'll be all the more likely to see Jack Sparrow again.

Setting aside the Depp of it all, Disney ultimately needs to decide how they want to handle this franchise's future. "Pirates of the Caribbean" remains the studio's only theme park ride turned hit film property, but getting a sixth movie made has proved difficult. At one point, it looked like "Pirates of the Caribbean 6" was going to set sail with Margot Robbie in the lead, but that has yet to happen.

At another point, it was suggested that the next "Pirates of the Caribbean" movie would be a total reboot. Multiple scripts have been developed, yet nothing has stuck. Basically, this movie is going to happen at some point, with or without Depp. So, Disney needs to decide what, exactly, it wants to do here. We'll see how it all shakes out.

"Pirates of the Caribbean 6" doesn't currently have a release date, but stay tuned.

#3540. iOS 27.2 adds two FaceTime features, including a personal favorite

iOS 27.2 adds new features to Messages, Podcasts, Photos, and more—including some easy-to-miss upgrades to FaceTime. Here’s what’s new.

Dual Capture was added to FaceTime in iOS 27 and quickly became one of my favorite features. Rather than having to choose between showing your face or the rear camera view, Dual Capture lets you show both at once.

iOS 27.2 expands Dual Capture to work on all video calls, even with groups. Previously the feature was limited to one-on-one calls.

If you have an iPhone 17 or newer, all you have to do on a video call is hit the ‘Flip’ button, and by default both the front and back camera will be activated.

It’s a huge upgrade to the FaceTime experience, and especially great if, like in my case, you have young kids running around and want to let grandparents see them and you at the same time.

The only drawback: everyone in the call needs to have iOS 27, iPadOS 27, or macOS 27 installed.

iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime more accessible by adding support for third-party sign language interpreters and live captioning.

Inside the three-dot icon, you’ll find a ‘Sign Language’ button that lets you pick an installed VRS (Video Relay Service) app for direct access to an interpreter. The app will appear as a participant tile in the call with a “Waiting for Interpreter” status, then your interpreter’s name will display after they join.

For third-party live captioning, Apple has a step-by-step support document here that outlines the process. You can also optionally stick with the existing built-in Live Captions feature to have your iPhone add automatic captions. It’s available from Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ FaceTime ⇾ Live Captions.

If you have an iPhone Duo, iOS 27.2 also introduced a new Edge Light feature that works across multiple video calling apps, including FaceTime.

Edge Light works just like on the Mac, adding a ring of light around the iPhone Duo display to better illuminate your face on calls. It’s a built-in alternative to using a physical ring light.

To enable the feature, open Control Center while on a FaceTime call then hit ‘FaceTime Controls’ and tap ‘Edge Light.’ Once enabled, you can adjust settings like the intensity and color temperature.

Have you tried any of iOS 27.2’s new FaceTime features? Let us know in the comments.

#3539. Why the Holidays Are Actually the Best Time of Year to Start Working Out

If you have even the tiniest inkling that you might want to get in shape in the new year—or anytime really—don’t wait until January. This isn't a "winter arc" self-improvement pitch; it's just facts. The best time to start a gym habit is before the holiday season. Heck, in December, you’ll even have the place mostly to yourself.

Sure, technically “right now” is always the best time to start exercising, but the holiday season is special. If you wait until January, gyms will be packed. The first two weeks of the year, everybody thinks they’re at the start of an amazing new fitness habit...and by February, most of them have forgotten all about it. Don’t make life harder for yourself by starting during the big rush. Classes will fill up, you’ll have to fight people for the squat rack, and it will be hard to have any real fun. So start now.

In October and November, gyms and classes are at more or less their normal capacities. This is a good time to feel out the vibe of a new place. But it gets better: Once December rolls around, the fair-weather gymgoers will be off shopping for gifts after work and attending holiday parties on the weekends. They won’t feel like getting out of their warm beds in the morning, either. When you arrive, the squat rack will be free. You’ll have your choice of treadmills. The gym will be your oyster.

If you start now, you'll have about two months to get up to speed before the rush starts in January. And that is a perfect little time frame to set a small goal and keep it. Vow to hit the gym three times a week, and you’ll be able to get in 24 workouts before Christmas, even if you take a few days off for festivities. You can get a lot stronger in 24 workouts. Or run, if that's the fitness journey you're most excited about. If you start a couch-to-5k running plan now, you’ll be routinely running 30 minutes at a stretch by the time we get to January.

Yes, the holiday season can be busy and stressful, but remember that working out tends to help our brains manage stress. Mark workouts on your calendar, and keep those appointments with yourself.

Don’t worry about missing out on deals. Any gym or studio that offers a January special probably offers sales year-round anyway. And ultimately, if you get into the habit of actually using the gym, you're getting a lot more value for your money than somebody who joins in January and quickly stops showing up.

#3537. Daniel Craig's Early-Career Miniseries Is A Masterpiece Every British TV Fan Has To Watch

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When I saw a 24-year-old Daniel Craig play the sadistic South African Police Sergeant Jaapie Botha in John G. Avildsen's 1940s Apartheid drama "The Power of One," I can't say that I had him pegged for the next James Bond, but I did know that he was a remarkably hissable villain. The film quickly faded from memory, but every time Craig turned up in a movie during the 1990s, I'd remember how effective he was as Botha, and wonder why he wasn't getting meatier roles.

What I didn't know at the time was that he'd given a tour de force performance in the 1996 BBC drama serial "Our Friends in the North." The nine-part series spans 31 years in the lives of four friends from Newcastle upon Tyne, and boosted the careers of Craig, Mark Strong, Christopher Eccleston and Gina McKee. But no one demonstrated greater range than Craig, whose character, Geordie, flees an abusive, alcoholic father to pursue an unpromising life in low-level crime.

British television wasn't immediately accessible in the United States in 1996 (unless it was a pop cultural sensation like "The Office" or "Little Britain"), so I didn't find out about "Our Friends in the North" until a decade later, directly after Daniel Craig had rejuvenated the James Bond franchise in "Casino Royale." I can understand why it didn't leap over the pond. The historical references are specific and steeped in British politics, which, to American viewers, makes it somewhat daunting. But Peter Flannery's writing and the dynamite acting ensemble will hook you just as sharply as David Simon plunged you into the Baltimore social stratum with "The Wire."

Unfortunately, "Our Friends in the North" isn't readily available in the United States on streaming, but if you've got a region-free Blu-ray player you can purchase it for $33.00 on Amazon, and it's worth it. I grew up watching British crime movies like "The Long Good Friday," "Mona Lisa," and "The Krays," and Flannery's writing doesn't suffer fools. But his dialogue is so crisp and layered and immaculately performed that you feel compelled to understand it. You're thrust into a society that, from the corrupt parliament down to the alcoholic, homeless dregs, is foreign yet familiar.

Craig's Geordie faces the most dire swings of fortune. He's not a bad person, but, like so many people who choose a criminal lifestyle and succumb to substance abuse, he makes so many compromises that there's eventually no way out. It's a harrowing journey and I wish I could tell you it ends well for Geordie, but "Our Friends in the North" is not out to comfort.

#3536. I Tested ChatGPT's New 'Slides' Tool, and Here's How It Compares to Gemini

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

ChatGPT's capabilities continue to expand apace, and the latest feature is a fully capable slideshow creator. Announced a few weeks ago, ChatGPT Slides lets you create PowerPoint-style decks from inside your conversations, and it's now appearing for those on the Pro tier and above (meaning right now, you need to spend at least $100 a month to get it).

If you're on the free ChatGPT plan or the $20-a-month Plus tier, you can still get ChatGPT to generate downloadable PowerPoint files from the content of your conversations. However, they'll be more basic than those made in the full version of ChatGPT Slides, and there are no collaboration or native edit options.

ChatGPT Slides is part of OpenAI's push to give users a complete office suite inside the ChatGPT apps. Pages (the word processor) is already available for Pro tiers and above, while a spreadsheet app is on the way—the idea being that you will soon be able to get all your work done without any help from Google or Microsoft.

While Chatgpt Slides is only available on pricey plans right now, it's likely to come to lower subscription tiers in the future. But for now, how does the tool compare to what's available in the free and Plus tiers, not to mention what you can do with Gemini inside Google Slides? I've taken a detailed look.

When it comes to testing out AI tools, it helps to focus on something you're already knowledgeable about so you can spot any mistakes. To test this, I decided to see what ChatGPT could hoover up from the web about the new iPhone Duo. If you're on the free or Plus plans, you can start a conversation, then ask for a slideshow or PowerPoint about it.

Plus accounts also have access to a specific Presentations add-on, available via the + (plus) menu in the prompt box, though I get the impression this feature is in a state of flux since ChatGPT Slides arrived. In any case, you can begin asking about the iPhone Duo specs and early online reactions, and then say "build me a slideshow on the key features and reviews so far".

What I got back on the $20 Plus account was a fairly competent slideshow on Apple's foldable, with accurate information as far as I could see, and a simple series of layouts. It looked like something you might whip up from a template if you were in a rush and didn't have time to properly align all the bullet points or be very selective about which details you included and which you left out. One neat touch is that ChatGPT was able to drop in an official photo of the iPhone Duo at the start of the slideshow, but I had to specifically ask for one.

You can go back and make specific edits to the slideshow, but you have to describe them in the general prompt box—you can't select individual slide elements and make more precise changes. Still, if all you want to do is occasionally convert your ChatGPT conversations into a rough and ready slideshow, there's no real need to upgrade from the free or Plus accounts for now.

Switching to a Pro account, I gave a similar task to ChatGPT Slides hoping for something more comprehensive. To begin with, Slides gets its own dedicated area in the app, so you can start up a blank presentation from scratch—there are some basic image and text features, but the idea is to use prompts to build your slide deck. It's like a really basic Google Slides, with a prompt box.

Creating a slideshow this way feels rather tedious: Typing out what you want to say and then waiting for ChatGPT to do it isn't as intuitive as just throwing in some graphics and text yourself, as you might do in PowerPoint. It also seems to be a bit buggy, at least during the time I spent testing it, with some requests not properly completing.

Starting a standard conversation with ChatGPT and then turning all the information into a deck is much more useful from my perspective. My iPhone Duo slideshow was longer, laid out better, and more informative than the one I created on the Plus plan—there were even charts of battery life and official photos this time.

However, whether I used the free, Plus, or Pro tools, my presentations didn't come across as particularly well thought through. They don't really flow smoothly, either across individual slides or the slideshow as a whole—it feels very much like an algorithm, rather than a person, has decided what information to include and where on the slides to stick it.

Whether you create presentations in chats or through the ChatGPT Slides space, you're able to click on individual elements and do some basic manual resizing and repositioning. You can also request edits via prompts: "Drop in an image of a cat", "make this pop more", "center all of this information", or whatever it is.

ChatGPT Slides does offer collaborative tools, which I wasn't able to test, and I can see that being useful for teams heavily invested in ChatGPT's ecosystem. I can also imagine ChatGPT Slides coming in handy when you've got a lot of information you need to quickly dump into a slideshow that looks vaguely presentable.

In general though, I think I'd much rather stick to the traditional way of making slideshows for now. These old methods are more precise and more manageable, and give you full control over what's shown and where—even if they do take a bit longer. What's more, modern-day presentation tools come with so many templates and other layout aids that it's not difficult to put together something that's easy on the eyes while including all of the information you think is most critical.

Google is, of course, also all the way in on AI (and then some), and if you pay for Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) or above, you can have Gemini pop up right inside Google Slides to give you some assistance with your presentation-making. To compare the tools, I gave it the same task as I did ChatGPT, asking for a slide deck on the new iPhone Duo.

Gemini actually asked some questions along the way: about wht visual style to use, the audience to aim the slideshow at, and the details to highlight. Though it's always possible to put this sort of information manually into a prompt, this would be a helpful additional to ChatGPT Slides.

What Gemini and Google Slides produced was impressive in terms of the layout and overall vibe of the presentation: It felt much more like a human being had put together the slide deck compared to what ChatGPT had produced, in terms of the information chosen, the way the slides were laid out, and the color picks.

However, Google's result had its faults too: The presentation got the facts on the maximum brightness of the iPhone Duo screen wrong, and produced an "iPhone Duo" graphic that looked like two iPhones from around 2021 stuck together. ChatGPT Slides at least managed to pull official imagery from the Apple website.

You can't attach individual edit prompts to specific parts of your presentation in Google Slides as you can in ChatGPT Slides—you have to mention them in the general prompt box. That said, Google Slides is obviously a much more mature and established slideshow tool compared to the OpenAI equivalent, in terms of its features and layout options (it has been around for a decade, after all).

Given that extra software structure and the lower cost of entry, Gemini and Google Slides is the better option for AI-assisted slideshow making at the moment—though I wouldn't bet against OpenAI catching up. For now, ChatGPT Slides is something that's good to have available if you're already paying a lot for ChatGPT every month, but not a feature that makes it worth your while to swap your AI allegiance.

#3535. ‘Knives Out’ director launches iPhone camera app that shoots like his movies

Hollywood director Rian Johnson (Star Wars: The Last Jedi) announced a new iPhone camera app that uses the same image processing techniques as his ‘Knives Out‘ films. Here are the details.

Over the past few years, there has been no shortage of discussions about the iPhone’s image processing, and, particularly, its often heavy-handed approach to post-processing.

And while things seem to have gotten better more recently, Apple’s approach to computational photography has helped fuel the development of third-party camera apps that offer more control over how photos are processed, chief among them Halide’s Mark III – Pro Camera app and Process Zero feature.

This week, Hollywood director Rian Johnson introduced Chromagraph Camera, an iPhone app he commissioned from cinematographer Steve Yedlin that promises to bring the same image processing used in the ‘Knives Out‘ films to the iPhone.

Chromagraph Camera is available for $12.99 with no in-app purchases. It already supports the iPhone Duo, though at least one review suggests its adapted interface could use some fine-tuning.

Here’s how the Chromagraph Camera is described on the App Store:

Chromagraph starts from raw image data and builds the image its own way: not a filter laid over the usual look processing, but a different process from the start.

SHOOT FIRST, SEE THE LOOK AFTERAs with a film camera, you frame through the viewfinder and see the finished look only after the image is processed. Take the picture, then open the gallery to see it with the Chromagraph look applied.

ADJUST WITHOUT LOSING THE LOOKIntuitive yet powerful tools for color, tone, and texture give you real control while keeping every image true to the look that’s the core of the app.

A GALLERY THAT KEEPS THE ORIGINALSStore full-quality raw files and view them in the app with the look applied live, along with any adjustments you make. Export smaller files to share with friends or save to your photo library, or turn on auto-export in Preferences to send every photo to your library right away as a JPEG or HEIC with the look applied.

NOT A FILTERA filter sits on top of the processing your phone has already done. Chromagraph skips that processing and uses its own methods for the curated look preferred by director Rian Johnson and cinematographer Steve Yedlin.

On X, Johnson explained that he originally asked Yedlin and color science developer Eric Cameron to create the app for his personal use, before they decided to make it available to everyone.

He added that, despite having tried plenty of third-party camera apps, he wanted a more streamlined solution that combined custom image processing with editing tools for color, exposure, grain, and halation.

To check out Chromagraph Camera, which is currently the top paid app in the App Store’s Photo & Video category, follow this link.

#3534. New Godzilla LEGO Set Builds A Big, Thick King Of The Monsters

Godzilla has been back in a big way since returning to theaters in 2016. Not only has Legendary's Monsterverse given the atomic kaiju plenty of screentime in the decade since then, but Japan also gave us one of the best Godzilla movies ever with "Godzilla Minus One," soon to be followed by "Godzilla Minus Zero." Ever since debuting in 1954, Godzilla just keep stomping through cities, and now he's entered the world of LEGO.

LEGO has announced the first official Godzilla building brick set, inspired by the kaiju's appearance in Legendary's Monsterverse movies. Clocking in at 5,363 pieces with a height of 27.5 inches, including the monster's heat ray blasting from its mouth. That will make it quite monstrous among the modular buildings out there, even LEGO's Marvel Avengers Tower.

All those LEGO pieces combine to form the massive monster, right down to the glowing spines on his back and his tail that's ready for to be whipped around as a weapon. Let's take a closer look below.

The official Godzilla LEGO set is the latest to come from the LEGO Ideas program, where master builders and fans can submit their own designs to be voted on and potentially considered for production by LEGO. Creator Matthew Esposito is behind the design, and it was perfected with the help of LEGO model designers Jim Clayton and Markus Rollbühler and creative design lead Jordan Scott.

This is the largest creature ever designed by LEGO, and the designers weren't even sure they'd be able to make it 50cm tall. But they ended up with a Godzilla LEGO set that stands at 70cm, making him a true titan in LEGO form.

While Godzilla probably looks coolest with blue blast out of his mouth, that element can be removed, and you can just have Godzilla's tongue sitting in there instead, roaring into the sky.

The Godzilla LEGO set is coming for Black Friday on November 27, and it will cost $449.99 on the LEGO website. If we're lucky, maybe there will be a King Kong LEGO set that will arrive sometime in the future, so all those LEGO cityscapes out there can see some serious kaiju action.

This weekend Bill Hader is the voice of the animated The Cat In The Hat movie on the 2026 release schedule. But did you know that over a decade ago he totally dressed up as the beloved Dr. Seuss character for a Saturday Night Live sketch? When we chatted with the SNL alum, I had to ask about the memories of playing the role IRL.

Of course, Mike Myers famously took the live-action approach for the 2003 book-to-screen adaptation. In our interview, Hader seems to counts himself lucky to have just lent the voice to the character after spending a day in the literal paws of the character way back when. In his words:

I’m very happy to do it animated because that suit was very hot. And the makeup took a long time. It was the second music number, and then another pre-tape thing that I wasn't in just so they could put all the makeup on me. It was the last sketch of the night, so we did it really fast. So yeah, it was really hot and I had all that stuff on my face. I don't know how Mike Myers did it.

Myers' own process took two and a half hours and was very hot to act in a yak-hair suit all day. Jim Carrey had it even worse as The Grinch. He had to go through such a grueling process a specialist in torture was hired to help him withstand the eight-hour get ready time. In our interview above, you can see Quinta Brunson school Hader on what happened and watch his real-time reaction.

Instead of going through all that makeup time for months, it was just for one night. He played the character on October 11, 2014 in an episode he hosted in the season right after his exit from the show following an eight-year run. You can check out the sketch below:

It’s such a funny spin on the classic children’s book. When two sibling children are bored on a rainy day, they conjure up The Cat in the Hat, but something unexpected happens: he’s already acquainted with their mom, Linda. Playtime with the whimsical figure turns into an awkward reunion between The Cat and Linda. The best line has to be when Linda says: “He’s reliable. I don’t have to say a rhyme to make him come home.” ‘

And then, Linda’s husband ends up being Thing 2, who goes by Jona-Thing now. He comes home disappointed to see The Cat In The Hat with his wife and kids. The sketch hilariously ends with The Cat In The Hat saying “But oh, the places she let me go!” as he leaves them, which is obviously a NSFW reference to another Dr. Seuss book.

When CinemaBlend also spoke to the movie’s writer/directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni, we had to ask if the SNL sketch was involved at all with casting Hader. Here’s what Rivinoja told us:

It was completely random, of course, but we might wanna do a sequel with that character and with Linda. We're very excited about Linda.

Hader’s animated version of The Cat in the Hat is much different than SNL because it isn’t a parody like his first run as the character was. It’s a more family-friendly retelling of the picture book with an expanded story about where The Cat comes from, and involves an imaginative plot line that’s perfect for the medium of animation. It hits theaters this Friday, November 6.

#3532. This New Garmin Feature Is Draining Battery Life, but There's a Quick Fix

Garmin users are taking to the company's support forums with a common grievance: The newly introduced "OK Garmin" hands-free voice feature appears to be eating through battery life. The feature arrived through Garmin’s September software updates, bringing hands-free voice activation to the Fenix 8, Forerunner 570 and 970, Venu 4, and several other models. Here's how to make sure Garmin's new updates aren't slashing your watch's battery life.

Last month's updates for select watches also brought all-day fall detection, a set of new Quick Workouts and Garmin Run Coach plans, as well as that "OK Garmin" hands-free voice command feature. It's exactly what it sounds like: Instead of pressing a button, users can simply say “OK Garmin” to activate voice commands. However, it looks like "OK Garmin" in particular is what causes some watch's projected runtimes to drastically drop, allegedly by roughly 35% to 50% in some cases.

Garmin does acknowledge that enabling these settings shortens battery life, though it doesn't say by how much. The tradeoff makes sense, since the watch has to listen constantly for its wake phrase. Even so, giving up several days of runtime is a steep price for a feature that many people may seldom use. Luckily, the fix is simple: Turning off "OK Garmin" should restore your battery life estimates right away.

If your watch has been draining faster since the update, go to Settings > System > Voice and disable "OK Garmin." If needed, you can also switch off the Phone Assistant wake word from the same area. The good news is that turning this feature off won't even take voice commands away—you can still trigger them manually using the watch's physical controls.

Keep in mind that these numbers are battery estimates rather than independently tested, real-world runtimes. Some of the battery complaints that surfaced after the update may also stem from unrelated issues. Still, trading away as much as half your battery life just to avoid pressing a button is a difficult bargain to defend.

#3531. The Wendy’s JRPG Is a Searing Anti-Capitalist Screed About Humans Making Real Art

'Wendy's should not have a game that's this good'

The resistance against the AI art apocalypse is being televised in a marketing campaign about burgers.

Over the past year, Wendy’s — yes, the same Wendy’s known for its square burgers, thick milkshakes, and unlikely stewardship of a mid-tier donut chain — has made waves through a series of unconventional creative partnerships. Amid slumps in sales and attention, Wendy’s has turned to popular artistic mediums, like music and video games, to try and reverse course.

The buzziest Wendy’s-affiliated project was the post-hardcore EP Songs to Listen to in a Wendy’s Parking Lot, which featured six tracks written by musicians from bands with legit emo cred, like Anberlin, Blessthefall, Silverstein, and Winona Fighter. Look, I am as sorry as you are to hand anything to Big Corporate, but all six tracks are straight bangers. (Just listen to “She Said She Didn’t Want Fries” and try to tell me you didn’t have that on repeat in a Wendy’s parking lot in 2008.) On the heels of that album release is the classic JRPG riff WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones. Like Songs to Listen to, it boasts a similar unmistakable authenticity.

“Wendy’s should not have a game that’s this good,” Stephane Cotichini, founder and game director at 81Monkeys, the studio behind WendyQuest, told Polygon in a video call. (For the record, 81Monkeys was not named after the viral 2025 news story about meth dealers attempting to smuggle 81 monkeys across the Thailand-Cambodia border. Pure coincidence. “Somebody forwarded me the article the day it broke and I was, like, ‘Seriously? How?!’” Cotichini said. “Of all the numbers of monkeys, it had to be our number?”)

WendyQuest started as many projects in the indie gaming world do: funding. Or, rather, a lack thereof.

For the past several years, 81Monkeys has been working on an ambitious, systems-heavy pixel art RPG called World of Anterra. Though World of Anterra was successfully funded through Kickstarter in 2022, the scope and ambition of the game continued to swell, and the team found itself rapidly running out of runway. But as any indie or even mid-sized game developer will tell you, funding in the games industry has all but evaporated since the early 2020s gold rush. Things were looking “dire,” according to Cotichini, who said he had post-Kickstarter funding conversations with 60 prospects that went nowhere. Then an email landed in his inbox through the studio’s website form.

“Normally, I would have ignored the email, but because he said they're fans of the game, I was like, ‘Oh, I'll hear them out.’ So I get on a call and I find out it was Wendy's. And when I found out what the game was, I instantly knew we were the right team,” Cotichini said.

Within a week, 81Monkeys signed the deal for WendyQuest, allowing the studio to continue working on World of Anterra. 81Monkeys split its team 50/50 to work on both games.

The Wendy’s people apparently had the general picture and the overarching creative vision for WendyQuest, but the team at 81Monkeys still had its work cut out for it in turning it into a viable video game. They revised the battle system away from purely turn-based combat to a more active one. This echoes one of the studio’s core principles: Nostalgia has to feel contemporary, otherwise it’s just going to feel dated. Cotichini also acknowledged that while the original script had strong ideas (the Wendy’s marketing team is known for its witty social media posts), it didn’t quite click for a video game, where the writing isn’t just about telling a narrative but also about making a world feel real and lived-in.

Ultimately, writers at 81Monkeys rewrote “99%” of the script, according to Cotichini. Everything still had to fly by corporate for brand-safety reasons, but there are some unmistakable nods to the competition: The logo for WendyQuest’s villain, Dr. Mechborg, is a giant golden “M.” “Sure, sure, serving billions is great,” MechBorg says in his introductory villain proselytizing that’s mandatory for most every JRPG. “But it’s time I make billions.” He then directs his army to “cut corners.”

I’ve played a little bit of WendyQuest, and to quote the kids, it slaps. Beyond its immediate 16-bit-era vibes, the combat system is the main draw. The system is built around a gauge that rapidly fills up at the bottom of the screen. You have to press the attack button as close to full as possible; tap too early and you’ll deal less damage or miss your attack, but if you get it right, you’ll deal maximum damage. It’s a nice touch that keeps WendyQuest from feeling like yet another Final Fantasy clone. The game is pretty funny, too; its jokes-per-minute ratio is on par with TV shows like Veep or 30 Rock. Cotichini is right: Wendy’s should not have a game that’s this good.

“Initially, they weren't gonna credit us,” Cotichini said. “I mean, that's the nature of this type of agreement, right? We're just a silent partner, we'll make this game, and then they launch it.”

But he pushed back. In late 2023, when the project initially began development, AI was out in the wild, though not yet the industry-demolishing force it is today. AI grows more unpopular every year, but gaming audiences in particular react with visceral repudiation; even a trailer that features AI-generated assets can prompt a major company to reverse on a dime and issue a public apology.

“You want people to know that it was 100% human-made by an actual indie studio,” Cotichini said.

That ethos is reflected in a line of bolded text front and center on the Steam pages for both WendyQuest and World of Anterra: “100% human made.”

“Part of why World of Anterra is as good as it is, and I know the world hasn't played it yet, neither have you, but it's because of the time it took to bring it to life. It's because of the struggle it took. All of that comes across in the product that ends up being created, and I think that's essential. So the more AI is used to make a game, the worse the game becomes,” Cotichini said. “Because the more you speed up that process, the less opportunity you have to improve it.”

Earlier in World of Anterra’s development, 81Monkeys dabbled with AI for project management and efficiency, but found that despite promises peddled by the likes of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the tools actually increased costs and decreased productivity. They also found that generative AI offered solutions for problems that already had solutions. Cotichini floated the idea of using AI to help speed up the creation of NPCs, for instance. “They were, like, ‘Why don’t we just make a script to do that?’”

For WendyQuest, according to Cotichini, the marketing team at Wendy’s actively pushed 81Monkeys to steer clear of AI tools and workflows.

No one could claim that WendyQuest is as in-depth as, say, Final Fantasy Resonance or other big-budget RPGs capitalizing on the nostalgia trend du jour. But there’s a real richness — and more importantly, a real authenticity — to its design. This is why Songs to Listen to in a Wendy’s Parking Lot ended up resonating so much with retired scene kids. These were real songs written by legit artists who we actually listened to in Wendy’s parking lots 20 years ago. In an era where McDonald’s is using AI to create nightmare fever dream ads and implement dynamic pricing algorithms, Wendy’s investing instead in the arts stands out.

“I think that creative work in general has gotten watered down over the last couple decades,” Cotichini said. “And the reason is because it became more influenced and controlled by business interest and less by the creative. Now, I actually see a swing the other way.”

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

That might sound like an oxymoron coming from the mouth of the guy who’s making a game for a company with a $2.2 billion market cap. But really, why should it? Is the Wendy’s logo being on this thing any different than Sony’s or Microsoft’s or, hell, even Nintendo’s? (None of gaming’s three biggest companies started out as video game publishers.) Yes, it’s marketing, and yes, it is transparently transactional. But the games industry is facing down its fifth year of a dry spell for traditional funding models. That’s not changing any time soon. If a Fortune 500 company was debating how to allocate 0.5% of its 2027 marketing budget, would you rather it be spent on a month of YouTube preroll or on a year of overhead for a budding independent studio?

“The industry's really suffering right now. Things have never looked more dire,” Cotichini said. “This is the thing that I hope will come of WendyQuest. Wendy’s spends some millions of dollars in marketing every year. WendyQuest costs a fraction of that. So many brands out there do the same thing. My hope is that when people see WendyQuest — and that, actually, if a studio cares about a branded game, it can be a really good game — that more brands seek partnerships like we made with Wendy's. I think that could become an alternate funding source for so many really talented indies in the industry.”

Bruce Straley isn't all too fond of generative AI art

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Nuanced situation -- like, yes it's silly for this to exist, but I'd rather that a indie studio be able to stick around by getting funding like this than all of them be put out of work

#3530. 5 Best Movies Like The Love Hypothesis

There was never any doubt that Lili Reinhart's rom-com "The Love Hypothesis" would become a big hit for Prime Video. Streaming platforms have struck gold by taking romance books and turning them into comforting crowd-pleasers for the small screen. Sometimes this results in films as vapid as "My Fault: London," but often it results in charming movies that take allow us to indulge romantic fantasies via two hot people falling in love.

That's exactly what we got when "The Love Hypothesis" transformed from "Star Wars" fan fiction, of all things, into a novel and then a streaming movie. Ali Hazelwood's book about a biology PhD student who pretends to date her professor, only for the two to fall deeply in love became a hit, and was promptly given a film adaptation in which Reinhart plays the student, Olive Smith, while British actor Tom Bateman plays the ornery professor, Dr. Adam Carlsen.

There were two main tropes to both the book and the film: mismatched lovers who cross a boundary to be together, and the good old fake relationship that becomes very real. Of course, this is far from the first time these tropes have been used in romance movies, which is why it's actually quite easy to recommend films just like "The Love Hypothesis." While there are plenty of golden-age romance movies that used these plot devices (1941's "Come Live with Me" saw James Stewart and Hedy Lamarr fake a marriage only to fall head over heels), we're betting that fans of Reinhart's movie will want more modern examples. With that in mind, here's a list of the best movies like "The Love Hypothesis."

"My Oxford Year" may have a controversial ending but it's got everything you could want from a modern-day streaming flick based on a book. Melodrama and fairytale romance combine in this Netflix movie, which stars Sofia Carson (who's fast becoming the streamer's go-to romantic drama leading lady) as American exchange student Anna De La Vega. Before descending into a life of corporate drudgery, Anna decides to study Victorian poetry at the University of Oxford for a year. Wouldn't you know it, once there she meets an unreasonably charming and handsome English DPhil student and tutor named Jamie Davenport (Corey Mylchreest).

"My Oxford Year" shares much in common with "The Love Hypothesis." Not only are both based on books (though the former actually began as a screenplay before it was adapted into a novel), they both feature a student/teacher relationship that gets off to a rough start only to flourish into a modern-day fairytale. Both also feature strapping English leading men (though Bateman plays an American in "The Love Hypothesis") who start out as jerks only to reveal a tender side as things progress.

It is worth noting that there's a tragic element to "My Oxford Year," so if you're looking for something that wraps up as neatly as "The Love Hypothesis," this might not be the ideal watch. But otherwise fans of Lily Reinhart's movie should fall madly in love with Carson's alternative.

These streaming movies are all well and good but there has to be at least one undisputed classic on this list. There's no better example of the fake relationship trope than this 1990 romantic comedy in which we got to see prime-era Richard Gere and Julia Roberts fall for one another. The movie did what "The Love Hypothesis" and its fellow streaming-age rom-coms did decades before Netflix was even a thing, bringing together impossibly beautiful stars via a fake relationship that blossoms into the real thing.

If you don't know the plot of what might just be Julia Roberts' best movie, I'm not sure what to tell ya. He's a corporate raider, she's a sex worker he asks for directions. So begins a love affair that sees Gere's Edward Lewis paying Roberts' Vivian Ward to spend a week with him and act as his girlfriend. Needless to say, this confected relationship becomes a real one. Ward melts Lewis' cold corporate heart and Lewis draws out the real Ward from behind a wall of dissociation built up over her time spent as a sex worker.

If you're somehow yet to see the film, and are worried the tale of a millionaire corporate raider falling for a sex worker might not have the wholesome charm of "The Love Hypothesis," don't worry. There's a reason Roger Ebert called the film "the sweetest and most openhearted love fable since 'The Princess Bride.'" "Pretty Woman" is as romantic a comedy as they come. But beyond that, it somehow manages to feel grounded thanks to its multi dimensional characters, without compromising the fairytale romance aspect.

Sofia Carson will soon have a monopoly on streaming romance movies. Her 2025 romantic drama "The Life List" dominated Netflix just prior to the similarly successful release of "My Oxford Year." But before either of these movies, Carson made her Netflix romance debut with the 2022 film "Purple Hearts." Guess what — the whole thing was based on a book, Tess Wakefield's 2017 novel of the same name.

In "Purple Hearts" we get a modern day version of James Stewart's "Come Live with Me." This Carson-led love story sees the former Disney Channel star play diabetic waitress and musician Cassie Salazar, who's working herself ragged just to afford insulin. Her salvation arrives in the form of hunky Marine Luke Morrow (Nicholas Galitzine), who agrees to marry Cassie so she can gain health coverage and he can benefit from a pay bump. You can see where this is going.

Much like with "The Love Hypothesis," this is a story about a couple who agree to act as though they're together only to develop real feelings along the way. There's plenty of BookTok-style melodrama on display here, too, which should please anyone who enjoyed the tension of the third act fall-out in "The Love Hypothesis."

It's the film that made Glen Powell a star and proved Sydney Sweeney could make popular stuff outside of "Euphoria." If your favorite thing about "The Love Hypothesis" was watching two attractive people make out, then "Anyone But You" should be right up your alley. In fact, "Anyone But You" is arguably the apotheosis of the modern day two-hot-actors-fall-in-love rom-com. But there's a stronger connection between this film and "The Love Hypothesis."

Lily Reinhart's Olive Smith and Tom Bateman's Dr. Adam Carlsen agreed to fake a relationship for mutually beneficial reasons, and the same happens with Sweeney's Beatrice Messina and Powell's Ben. The duo pretend to be a couple so that Bea's parents will stop trying to repair her relationship with her ex, and Ben can make his own ex jealous. We all knew where it was going from the very beginning but that didn't make it any less enjoyable to watch.

Unlike with "The Love Hypothesis," the guy in this romantic comedy isn't a complete jerk. Full of himself, maybe, but not an anti-social hermit like Bateman's "Dr. Evil." Still, he and Sweeney's law student don't exactly get along, especially after their first meeting ended on awkward terms. That, alongside the fake relationship trope, gives Powell and Sweeney's couple a similar dynamic to that of Olive and Adam in "The Love Hypothesis." So if you somehow missed the unlikely box office smash that was "Anyone But You" back in 2024, now's the time to remedy that.

In 2018, "To All the Boys I've Loved Before" became the new gold standard for teen rom-coms. It also happens to be a nice little companion to "The Love Hypothesis." Based on a book? Check. Fake relationship trope? Check. Academic setting? Sort of check. Rather than college, this tale of teen love, adapted from Jenny Han's YA novel, plays out in high school, where Lara Jean Covey (Lana Condor) writes secret letters to her crushes. Of course, she never intends for any of them to read her missives, but guess what — that's exactly what happens.

Lara Jean's biggest crush is Josh Sanderson (Israel Broussard), and when she sees him approaching with his letter in hand, she kisses another one of the letter recipients, Peter Kavinsky (Noah Centineo) in an attempt to throw Josh off. Soon, Peter and Lara Jean are fake dating. This allows the former to distract from the embarrassment of Josh receiving a letter, and the latter to make his ex-girlfriend Gen (Emilija Baranac) jealous. But you know how this goes. Real romance develops, melodrama ensues, feelings get hurt.

"To All the Boys I've Loved Before" is, however, more than your standard BookTook phenomenon turned Netflix romance movie. The film is surprisingly well shot, retains a heartfelt sensibility throughout, and isn't afraid to embrace its classic fake relationship rom-com influences. It's a touching little high school melodrama that's well worth a watch for anyone who even remotely enjoyed "The Love Hypothesis."

#3527. How To Watch Other Mommy At Home

This has been a great year for horror, from the monumental successes of "Backrooms" and "Obsession," to more high profile favorites like "The End of Oak Street" and "Resident Evil." We've seen independent productions make waves, established filmmakers making their comebacks, and much more. There have also been plenty of lackluster horror movies with just enough interesting ideas to strike a chord with audiences.

Case in point, "Other Mommy," a pretty okay horror film that features Jessica Chastain doing her best Pennywise. That's it, that's the whole movie. Adapting Josh Malerman's novel "Incidents Around the House," Rob Savage helms a stylish horror film that is carried entirely by Jessica Chastain's unhinged performance and a fair amount of violence and spooky stuff.

In spite of less than stellar reviews, "Other Mommy" was a hit with audiences. The movie rose above its abysmal Rotten Tomatoes and CinemaScore evaluation, audiences showed up to theaters, and "Other Mommy" became a box office hit. It's a testament to the marketing department and the trailers for the movie, which hooked audiences on the premise of Savage's film long before the reviews dropped.

Now that Halloween has passed, it's slim pickings for horror at the box office. The good news is that all the horror films released before Halloween are going to start being released on home video soon. Universal Pictures Home Entertainment has announced that "Other Mommy" will release on digital platforms November 10, 2026 with a Blu-ray release expected later, on December 29, 2026.

One of the more intriguing and also confounding aspects of "Other Mommy" is its titular character, whose strange powers seem like Pennywise, Freddy Krueger, and a whole bunch of nightmares combined. It makes her a bit convoluted, sure, but also one of the most exciting horror villains in a while.

It remains to be seen if "Other Mommy" will warrant a sequel, or if Jessica Chastain would return to deliver more horrors. In the meantime, however, you can watch more than what was in theaters, because "Other Mommy" is bringing deleted scenes and other bonus features when it hits home video.

Jessica Chastain stars in a terrifying trip into the darkening world of a young girl, Bela, who forms a relationship with a disturbing entity in her home who looks uncannily like her own mother. 'Other Mommy' proves to be more than a mere figment of the girl's imagination as she becomes a sinister, manipulative presence determined to tear apart Bela's family.

The following bonus content is available when you purchase "Other Mommy" at participating retailers.

EFFECTING FEAR: An exploration of the ways special effects complemented each other to amplify the relentless tension, suspense, and fear driving the story.

A FAMILY IN PIECES: A behind-the-scenes look at the fractured family at the heart of the film and the standout performances that bring them to life.

BREAKING RULES WITH OTHER MOMMY: Cast and filmmakers discuss subverting horror tropes through Bela's perspective and disrupting the expected cadence of the genre.

#3525. Apple confirms iOS 27.3 beta is coming next week with Apple Intelligence in China

Apple today took the unusual step of confirming when its next iOS developer beta is expected to arrive, as part of an announcement detailing the upcoming launch of Apple Intelligence in China. Here are the details.

In mid-July, Reuters reported that, following a lengthy back-and-forth with Chinese regulators and multiple delays, Apple Intelligence had finally cleared a major regulatory hurdle ahead of its long-awaited launch in the country.

Then, a couple of weeks ago, Bloomberg reported that Apple was planning to launch Apple Intelligence in China in December as part of iOS 27.3, although without Siri AI and other newer features.

The following day, China’s state-backed media outlet The Paper reported that Tim Cook had confirmed regulatory approval for the platform, with a test version expected before the end of October.

Then, just last Monday, Apple released iOS 27.2 and its counterparts, expanding Siri AI support to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. On the same day, the company announced that four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, would be supported by the end of the year.

However, while that announcement confirmed additional language support for Siri AI, it offered no updates on the rollout of Apple Intelligence in China, where Siri AI itself will remain unavailable for the time being.

While Apple typically releases the first beta of its next software update shortly after the previous version becomes available, iOS 27.3 has yet to materialize.

Now, as spotted by MacRumors, a press release published on Apple’s Chinese Newsroom website confirms that testing of Apple Intelligence in China will begin on November 4, as part of the next iOS developer beta.

Importantly, Apple has only confirmed November 4 as the start of Apple Intelligence testing in China, not necessarily the release date of iOS 27.3 beta 1 itself.

In the press release, Apple confirms that users in China will get an improved Siri experience, including Type to Siri and the ability to access Alibaba’s Qwen for certain requests, but not Siri AI itself.

The Qwen integration will also extend to Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence. According to Apple, users will be able to ask questions about photos and documents, including PDFs and presentations, as well as generate original content from scratch through Writing Tools. Users will be able to access Qwen by signing into their accounts or using Sign in with Apple.

Other features included in the initial rollout are Live Translation in Messages, FaceTime, and Phone, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up in Photos, natural-language photo searches, priority notifications, notification summaries, and Smart Reply, among others.

Apple also noted that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained.

The features will be available on the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max, iPhone 16 and later, iPhone Air, and iPhone Duo, with both Siri and the device language required to be set to either English or Simplified Chinese.

The company also confirmed that the features will become publicly available in December, with the official release of iOS 27.3.

#3524. The Garmin Cirqa Finally Got a Much-Needed Feature

This week Garmin's screenless Cirqa smart band received a firmware update that fixes one of its most obvious gaps: the lack of alerts from your phone. With Version 4.20, you can now set up your smart band to buzz your wrist for texts, calls, and other smart notifications from your phone. The addition is listed on Garmin's forums as "Support vibration for smart notifications/incoming calls." Reaction has been upbeat, too—users on the Garmin subreddit have been glad to see the feature arrive.

Amusingly, Garmin's own FAQ still states that the Cirqa does not vibrate for text messages, phone calls, or other smartphone notifications. Clearly that page is now out of date, so Garmin will want to correct it. Since Garmin doesn't yet have step-by-step instructions, I tested the text-message vibrations myself. Here's how you can set up your Cirqa smart band to vibrate for calls and texts, in addition to a number of other promising updates to check out.

To receive these alerts, your band must be running firmware 4.20 or later. Here is how to get everything configured.

Update the firmware. Open your Garmin Connect app and sync your Cirqa, so the app can check for and install version 4.20 or newer.

Grant the necessary phone permissions. In your phone's settings, make sure Garmin Connect has permission to access SMS, Contacts, and Phone.

Configure notifications in Garmin Connect. Back in Garmin Connect, tap the Menu (or More) tab. Select Garmin Devices, then choose your Cirqa Smart Band. Go to Notifications & Alerts (or Smart Notifications) and turn on text and call alerts.

Troubleshooting tip: If alerts aren't coming through, check that Do Not Disturb, Sleep Mode, and any aggressive Battery Saver settings are turned off on both your phone and the band.

For most a lot of Cirqa fans, the phone alerts are the headline, but the 4.20 update carries a solid list of other improvements and bug fixes:

Trail Run: Run/Walk detection is now available for Trail Run activities.

Timestamp fix: Resolved a problem where an activity's recorded time didn't match the time on your phone.

Distance calibration: You can now calibrate distance for Treadmill Run, Indoor Rowing, and Indoor Cycling before saving the activity on the device.

Duration alerts: Duration time alerts for speaking out now accumulate.

Stress alerts: Stress alerts are now blocked while Auto Activity Detection is recording.

Bedtime reminders: Fixed an issue where the bedtime approaching notification sometimes failed to trigger.

Live Activity: Heart rate now appears on the Live Activity screen before recording begins.

Pinned activity bug: Fixed an issue where the pinned activity reverted to Timed Activity after changing the phone's language.

Workout editing: Fixed a problem that prevented editing reps during a workout.

Stability: General system stability improvements.

#3523. TV Legend Ed Asner Appeared In This Classic '60s John Wayne Western

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In 1966, John Wayne visited Vietnam and began formulating one of his biggest on-screen blunders, "The Green Berets." Before he could get around to making the one John Wayne film that Roger Ebert called "cruel and dishonest," however, he had another couple Westerns to get through. "El Dorado" was the first. It premiered in the United States in June 1967, exactly one year after Wayne made the rounds in IndoChina. At the time, the Duke was becoming increasingly irrelevant as the Western genre began its shift into the revisionist age. Nonetheless, "El Dorado," which saw Wayne reunited with his frequent directorial collaborator Howard Hawks, became a success. It also remains the only film to feature Wayne and Ed Asner, who at the time was just three years away from debuting in his best-known role as Lou Grant on "The Mary Tyler Moore Show."

Asner began acting in the mid-1950s. He made his TV debut in 1957 on "Studio One" and his film debut in 1962, appearing alongside Elvis Presley in "Kid Galahad." Oddly enough, he didn't appear in a Western film until 1966 when he joined Wayne in "El Dorado," which considering any working actor of the 1960s was bound to wind up in a Western at some point is surprising.

Asner did, however, appear in some classic Western TV shows, guesting on "Outlaws" in 1962 and "The Virginian" the following year. He also appeared in two episodes of "Gunsmoke" and in 1965 joined Robert Horton for a single installment of "A Man Called Shenandoah." When he set foot on the "El Dorado" set, then, while he hadn't yet appeared in a big screen Western, he was well acquainted with Hollywood's vision of the Old West. Now all he had to do was face down John Wayne.

"El Dorado" is directed and produced by Howard Hawks. His frequent collaborator Leigh Brackett wrote the script, which she considered to be her finest work. In Todd McCarthy's "Howard Hawks: The Grey Fox of Hollywood," Brackett is quoted as having said, "I wrote the best script I have ever written and Howard liked it, the studio liked it, Wayne liked it, and I was delighted." Unfortunately for her, Hawks wanted to play things a little safer by essentially remaking "Rio Bravo," the 1959 John Wayne-led Western that launched an unofficial trilogy.

"Rio Bravo" was the result of Hawks and Wayne's hatred for "High Noon," which featured a sheriff too scared to confront the antagonists alone. Hawks and Wayne's retort featured a more muscular hero who had no problem facing evil solo. It proved so successful and seemingly suited Hawks' sensibility so well he essentially remade it twice, once with "El Dorado" and again with 1970's "Rio Lobo" — both of which starred the Duke. The former was a more lighthearted movie, however, with James Caan as John Wayne's sidekick providing much of the comic relief due to his poor aim.

Otherwise, "El Dorado" starred Robert Mitchum, the film noir legend who was also no stranger to the Western, as the alcoholic sheriff of the titular town, J.P. Harrah. His old pal, gunfighter Cole Thornton (Wayne), arrives in El Dorado after being been hired by local tycoon Bart Jason (Ed Asner) to drive the poor MacDonald family off their land so he can claim it for himself. After talking to Harrah, however, Thornton refuses Jason's offer, and things don't exactly go smoothly.

Ed Asner — who passed away in 2021 at the age of 91 — played the villain of "El Dorado." It must have been intimidating for the early-career Asner, then in his mid-30s, to have to square up to John Wayne. "I found myself going into uncharted territory," he told Jake's Takes in 2021. "I regarded myself as a big liberal. I hadn't been proved yet as a liberal, but a big liberal, and here I was going against one of the biggest reactionaries of the times. I didn't know how I'd be treated." According to Asner he was "roasted on the first day" but "passed the roast test" and ultimately found the Duke to be "a nice reasonable fellow."

It probably helped that "El Dorado" was a success. Roger Ebert called it "the most entertaining Western to turn up this year" and according to "Howard Hawks: The Grey Fox of Hollywood," the film did "outstanding business" following its 1966 debut in Japan. It then went on to generate "rentals of $6 million on box office receipts of $12 million," which ultimately made it the 12th biggest picture of 1967. Not bad for Asner's first big screen Western.

Ironically, considering his initial collaboration with Wayne was so amiable, the very series that made Asner a star, "The Mary Tyler Moore Show," came to represent a form of TV entertainment that heralded the end of the TV Western as a result of the "rural purge." Not that Wayne himself was affected, but the more urban-focused TV slate of the 1970s was one major signifier that the world was moving on from the days when Wayne and his fellow Western heroes proudly rode the plains.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there’s one thing I know about Rebecca Yarros and her Fourth Wing books, it’s that she’s not afraid to kill anyone. That was clear from the moment Violet and co. stepped onto the parapet, and it became painfully obvious after our dearly beloved Liam’s death in the first book. Now, as we wait for book four (and the book-to-screen adaptation that just found its Violet and Xaden), the author has revealed that she had plans to kill off more characters than she did in Onyx Storm, and they’ll have to go in the next installment. So, yeah, I’m worried, and I’m really anxious about one specific character.

Listen, I spiral over comments Yarros makes about what’s going to happen in her books even harder than I spiral over updates and fancasts for the Fourth Wing TV show. So, you can imagine the panic I was sent into when she said the following at Iron Flame Night (via domloves2read):

So, I know when I’m in the book, when I start the book, who is going to die. Now, when I wrote Onyx [Storm] I actually was going to kill off other people at the end. And the way I had to shift the plot, and the way I had to shift things so that it wouldn’t feel like other books and it would have its own separate ending, it left some people alive that should not be alive that I will have to take care of in this book.

Yarros went on to clarify that she didn’t tell the audience if said characters “were good or bad,” and she poked fun at them, saying they are prone to jumping to conclusions that often involve her “plotting Ridoc’s murder.” She also said she always knows who she’s going to kill in a battle before she writes it, and she plants seeds ahead of time so we feel connected to those characters.

So, with all that in mind, I’ve realized I’m actually super duper worried about one character who (at least for now) is alive.

I know, I know, I can’t believe I’m writing this either: I really think Rhiannon could die in book four, and maybe Yarros had plans to kill her in Onyx Storm. So, let’s walk through why.

I actually got to this conclusion through a weird process of elimination. I was mostly thinking about what characters are either dealing with loose ends or are such a vital part of the story that they can’t die. Think characters potentially involved in the brother mystery, like Bodhi and Garrick, or those involved with Violet’s memory loss, like Imogen. Along with that, characters like Aaric are so powerful that it feels like they have a greater purpose to serve.

Plus, with the death of Violet’s mom, I don’t think Brennan or Mira will go (yet). I also don't think Dain or Sloane will die, considering their seemingly budding relationship. Then, just from a vibes perspective, I don’t think Ridoc will die (yet). And Swayer has already been through too much with going through first year twice and losing his leg.

Through that process, considering whose death would hurt Violet the most and just thinking about what’s happened in the first three books, I landed on Rhiannon as the character who was maybe going to die in Onyx Storm.

Other than Xaden and her siblings, I think Rhi’s death would hit Violet the hardest since she’s her best friend.

Now, adding to all that, a brutal Fourth Wing parallel led me to this conclusion, too. Think about it, of all the people in Violet’s crew, Rhi is probably the best of the bunch. She’s a natural leader, she was born to be a rider, and she’s simply a very good person. You know who else was near-perfect and all those things? Liam. And he died toward the end of Fourth Wing.

Yarros specifically said she didn’t kill a character in Onyx Storm because she didn’t want it to feel like the end of other books. If Rhi had died, it could have felt a whole lot like what happened to Liam. It would hurt Violet in a very similar way, and it would be the death of another hero, a good one, in this story.

So, yes, going into book four, I’m very worried for Rhiannon. However, for now, I’m going to choose to be very happy that she’s still alive and will live to see another page (for now).

#3520. You Can Get This 65-Inch Toshiba Mini-LED TV for $550 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has dropped the price of the 65-inch Toshiba Z670R to $549.97 from $748.99, taking nearly $200 off and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. The deal also includes free delivery to a room of your choice, which normally costs $19.99, though it does not cover unpacking, setup, packaging removal, or haul-away services. You also get a 90-day free trial of Amazon Music with your purchase.

Beyond the discounts, the Z670R has quite a bit going for it, starting with a 4K Mini-LED panel that combines QLED color with local dimming to help bright highlights stand out without washing out darker scenes. It also supports Dolby Vision IQ and HDR10+, so you can enjoy compatible HDR content across a wide range of movies, shows, and streaming services.

Gaming is another area where this TV makes a strong case for itself—its panel can run at up to 144Hz, while Variable Refresh Rate, Auto Low Latency Mode, and AMD FreeSync Premium are there to keep fast movement looking smoother and cut down on screen tearing with a compatible console or gaming PC, making it well-suited for racing games, shooters, and sports titles. You also get four HDMI inputs, with support for 4K at 144Hz, so there is room for a console, PC, soundbar, and another device without constantly swapping cables.

Fire TV is built in as well, which means Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, and other major streaming apps are available without adding a separate streaming stick, while Alexa handles voice searches and basic controls. The built-in audio is also more substantial than what you get from many slim TVs, with a dedicated bass woofer and Dolby Atmos support, so you may be able to live without a soundbar at first if you are setting up a bedroom or smaller living room. One potential downside is that Mini-LED does not give you the perfect blacks of OLED, so movie fans who watch mostly in a dark room may still prefer to pay more for one. For someone who splits time between movies, sports, and gaming, though, the Z670R gives you a lot of flexibility for about $550 without immediately requiring extra equipment.
