#3519. I'm Not A Star Trek Fan – Here's What I Learned After Watching Patrick Stewart's Best TNG Episodes

I love my job and promise I'm qualified to do it, but sometimes, I have to admit that I, as the kids or Taylor Swift might say, don't "know ball." After admitting that I'd never seen "Jurassic Park" or ever sat down and watched "The Mummy," I wrote about the experience of watching these gems for the first time right here at /Film, and across the board, I'm always excited to learn about some new corner of the pop culture world for the first time.

Then my editor asked me to watch "Star Trek."

I need to be exceedingly clear: I don't have any actual beef with the Star Trek universe, but I am a spiteful and deeply stubborn person who has been asked — begged, at times — to watch this show by some of its more passionate fans who have flitted in and out of my life. There came a point where I felt like proving some sort of inane point by not watching this show, even though my refusal to do so affects nobody and nothing anywhere in the world. Then, Sir Patrick Stewart died, and my lead editor asked if he could give me a list of five particularly fun Picard episodes of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and I could write about them. I said yes, because despite my well-documented spite, I'd like to pay my respects to Stewart's legacy. (A note! "Best of Both Worlds," "Family," and "Chain of Command" were only excluded from this list because they're multi-part episodes.)

Some important context! I've never watched this show before. I don't really know who most of the characters are, nor do I know what's going on at most given moments. So what do I think of these handpicked Picard episodes of "Star Trek: TNG?" Let's see.

I started with "The Measure of a Man," a relatively somber Season 2 episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" that involves a legal, ethical, and moral dispute over whether the ship's android guy Data (Brent Spiner) is a sentient being or the property of Starfleet, to be dismantled and studied. The whole thing progresses into a miniature legal drama where Captain Philippa Louvois (Amanda McBroom) has to oversee Data's case and make a declaration one way or another. (Also, I love that this show goes out of its way to remind us, regularly, that Patrick Stewart's Captain Jean-Luc Picard is way hot. Louvois is practically panting at him during most of their scenes.)

"The Measure of a Man" is a relatively somber treatise on what it means to possess a soul, artificial intelligence, and what can and should be sacrificed in the quest for more knowledge, but I really can't stress this enough: it's also the first Star Trek anything I've ever watched. With that in mind, I admittedly didn't follow every single plot beat but instead paid close attention to Stewart's performance, which is, obviously, outstanding. The way he approaches a world where the guy next to him is in full body paint as if it's a Shakespearean drama is incredibly rad, but it also lends some gravity to the entire situation. (Get it? "Gravity." The show's about space! Nevermind.)

As news spread of Stewart's passing, it became quite clear to me that he was a massively important actor for so many people thanks to the Star Trek franchise, and this episode was a perfect first introduction that helped me understand why. How could you not side with the guy arguing to save his friend?

"The Drumhead," the second Patrick Stewart episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" that I turned on, is a tiny courtroom drama focused on an explosion on the Starship Enterprise that may or may not have been outright sabotage. After the arrival of retired rear admiral Norah Satie (Jean Simmons), the crew tries to officially get to the bottom of it, as Worf (Michael Dorn), a Klingon dude that I referred to as "the guy in a Chewbacca mask" to tick off one of my Trekkie coworkers for fun, reveals that his hilariously named fellow Klingon J'Dan (Henry Woronicz), is betraying them; it turns out he is, but he didn't cause the explosion.

Satie turns on Picard, angry that he's vehemently defending his own crew — even though the explosion wasn't sabotage at all, as it turns out. The reason that "The Drumhead" ended up on this list is, indisputably, because of Picard's masterful monologue defending himself; Stewart, of course, performs it beautifully and with the solemnity of a soliloquy delivered by Hamlet or Macbeth. (The scene with him and the Klingon whose name is definitely Worf and not Not-Chewbacca is also quite nice.) Again, there's a steadiness to Stewart's performance that's obviously what drew in "Star Trek" fans for decades. Even as you know that Picard is falsely accused, Stewart's real concern and frustration in the moment is palpable, and his moral center remains clear even as he deals with political scapegoating and fear-mongering. That's not just a prescient message for our current times; it's a message that has remained relevant in the decades since Stewart turned in this performance in "The Drumhead," and it's easy to see why Picard is so important to so many.

In this episode, which my editor insists is a must-watch because it shows off Captain Jean-Luc Picard's sillier side — and Patrick Stewart's by extension — Picard is bullied into going on vacation by his colleagues because he won't stop working and just go already. (As a freelance writer, I find this sadly and disturbingly relatable.) Picard finally agrees to go to a planet called Risa when he finds out that Deanna's (Marina Sirtis) mother is coming to visit — I asked around, and apparently, she's a real pain in the butt — and when he gets there, a woman he ultimately learns is named Vash (Jennifer Hetrick) kisses him to try to get away from an enemy. (They do it later, probably crazy style. I don't know what the sexual norms are in the Star Trek universe and am only sort of afraid to ask.)

After that, Vash and Picard have a whole subplot involving some sort of MacGuffin called the Tox Uthat — and a brief borderline kidnapping by that aforementioned Ferengi character Sovak (Max Grodénchik) — and by the end of the episode, Picard goes ahead and destroys the Uthat with the Enterprise's help because I guess it's very dangerous or whatever. I don't know about all that. What I do know is that "Captain's Holiday" is an episode of "TNG" that reminds you that Picard is a hot captain who f***s. In that sense, it's incredibly effective, and I am sorry for how much I objectified Sir Stewart throughout this episode. (No, I'm not.) In all seriousness, though, Stewart took the challenge of this silly, relatively fluffy episode and performed it with the utmost sincerity and wit.

I was given next to no information about "The Inner Light" and the assigned episode that follows (more on that in a second, obviously), and that definitely improved my viewing experience ... because not only do these feel like relatively standalone episodes, they're also both incredible showcases for Patrick Stewart as a performer. After getting hit by some sort of energy beam in a probe on the Enterprise, Jean-Luc Picard wakes up in another universe as a guy named Kamin, who lives with his wife Eline (Margot Rose) on a planet called Kataan. Picard then spends several decades there hanging out with his wife and his friends, raising children, and noticing, all the while, that the sun's radiation will eventually cause widespread drought, something he hopes to prevent despite the government repeatedly telling him that they don't have the technology to prevent it.

Spoilers for this pretty old episode, but when I learned that the whole thing was a series of memories implanted in a probe to show others what life on Kataan was like before it was lost to time, I was pretty shaken! (Also, the fact that 40-odd years only take 25 minutes for Picard is nuts.) All in all, this was the most emotionally resonant episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" I watched in this bunch. As I watched Stewart's Kamin try, over the course of years, to save the planet he calls home and protect his loved ones in the process — despite that mission ultimately being doomed — I ended up weirdly hoping that Picard wouldn't return to the ship, only because Kamin seemed so happy and comfortable with his loved ones. Picard was a cultural father figure, and this episode explains why pretty perfectly.

A sort of "Sliding Doors," "A Christmas Carol" episode completed by journey into the Star Trek universe — and yes, I'm talking about "Tapestry." (No, I did not know who John de Lancie's Q was going into this, and I still don't! Sorry!) After Jean-Luc Picard is wounded on a mission — an understatement, considering it's a large sucking chest wound — he's taken something that may or may not be the afterlife where he meets up with Q and is able to revisit a crucial moment in his life, seeing what would happen if he didn't get wounded in a bar fight and receive an artificial heart in the aftermath.

After changing his past and sleeping with his fellow cadet Marta Batanides (J. C. Brandy) — I love that all of these episodes drive the point home that Picard is super popular with the ladies — Picard decides to not fight the alien who stabs him in the heart, only to learn that, without taking that massive risk and nearly dying, he doesn't become the captain of the Enterprise ... but becomes a loser junior officer that nobody really respects. I genuinely did not see the "Picard goes back and gets stabbed" conclusion coming here, but it ends up making a weird amount of sense that he needs to push himself to end up on the correct life path. Once again, Stewart delivers a deeply considered and serious performance as a man grappling with a fork in the road that he actually has the power to change (or not), but this is probably the most complicated look at Picard in this bunch, and Stewart sells that conflict in him throughout every single second. Stewart was one of our finest actors, bar none. Episodes like "Tapestry" prove that handily.

"Star Trek: The Next Generation" is streaming on Paramount+.

#3518. 'It Follows' Star Officially Addresses Her Return to Another Iconic 2010s Thriller Franchise

In a new interview, Monroe addressed the possibility of returning for a sequel

Maika Monroe has built a career as a modern scream queen. After a breakout 2014, when she starred in both It Follows and The Guest, she became a key figure in horror, continuing to revisit the genre in everything from Longlegs to Victorian Psycho. This year, both It Follows and The Guest have been a part of the horror conversation: It Follows just wrapped a sequel, wonderfully titled They Follow, while The Guest just received a quasi-sequel with Onslaught, which director Adam Wingard set in the same continuity as his previous 2014 film.

Monroe notably doesn't appear in Onslaught (there are no repeat characters), but will she ever return to The Guest universe? In a recent interview for her upcoming film, Victorian Psycho, Monroe sounded hopeful.

“I love Adam so much,” she tells Polygon. “We grabbed coffee not too long ago, and he's awesome, so I would love to work with him again, so we'll see.”

The Guest remains one of Wingard’s most beloved films (and this is the guy who directed Godzilla vs. Kong). Written by Simon Barrett and starring Monroe and Dan Stevens, the story follows a charming visitor named David (Stevens) who arrives at the Peterson family home. There, he reveals that he is an army veteran and was a close friend to their son, who died while on tour in Afghanistan. David soon integrates himself into the grieving family, coinciding with strange and violent events taking place in the town. Anna (Monroe), the family’s eldest daughter, begins to grow suspicious of his behavior and past. The Guest marked one of Stevens first freaky roles, an edge that has since become a defining aspect of his career.

Onslaught came out earlier this year and marked a reunion between Wingard and Barrett, who’ve built a long partnership throughout their careers, collaborating on films like A Horrible Way to Die, You’re Next, and the V/H/S franchise.

The film stars Adria Arjona as an army vet with PTSD, who’s forced to defend her community and her daughter against three Terminator-like army experiments who’ve escaped a nearby facility.

Onslaught also features Stevens as Dr. Hans Kammler, an aging German scientist with Nazi ties and the mastermind behind the super-soldiers stalking the protagonist. Wingard confirmed that the events of Onslaught take place near the town that’s featured in The Guest. Both films are a part of his and Barrett’s "KPG-verse," named after the shadowy organization that runs the super-soldier experiments and appears in several of their projects.

Even though Stevens plays different characters in both films, Wingard suggested there might be a connection between them. “I think he’s related to the genesis of the David character in some form [or] fashion, and I think that’s something that maybe we’ll more literally explore hopefully in future installments,” he told The Wrap.

Stevens, for his part, is happy to continue to explore that universe. “We’re definitely open to more KPG-verse. I don’t know whether a Guest 2, per se, is on the cards anytime soon, but you never know,” he told The Hollywood Reporter. “We’ve teed everything up for an Onslaught sequel as well, so watch this space.”

Whether we get a sequel to David and Anna’s stories or something new set in the same universe, the door is open. Monroe, Wingard, and Stevens all seem to agree: The world of The Guest is one they’d be happy to return to.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I can't imagine what it feels like to learn you've been cast as one of the most recognizable characters in the Harry Potter franchise, especially when you're following in the footsteps of the late Alan Rickman. That's exactly the position Paapa Essiedu found himself in when he landed the role of Severus Snape in HBO's upcoming book-to-screen series adaptation. While you'd expect some excitement after getting that phone call, the actor admitted his celebration lasted about as long as it takes to say "Expelliarmus" before reality came crashing down.

With the highly anticipated series arriving on the 2026 TV premiere schedule this Christmas, Essiedu recently spoke with People at the Time100 Next Gala about taking on the iconic Potions professor. The 36-year-old actor admitted he initially experienced "five to 10 seconds" of excitement when he found out he'd gotten the part. Then he remembered that accepting the job meant actually having to play Snape, and his reaction was wonderfully blunt:

It's like, wow, what an honor, what a privilege. And then there's a kind of crushing kind of reality of the reality of what is to come. 'Oh, fuck. I've got to do it now.'

I love how quickly that went from being honored to realizing he'd signed himself up for one heck of a challenge. Honestly, I get it. Rickman's portrayal of Snape remains one of the most beloved performances in the original eight-film franchise. His delivery, intimidating presence and ability to make even the simplest lines sound vaguely threatening helped turn the character into a fan favorite.

Those are some pretty big shoes to fill, and Essiedu knows it. He's already faced considerable backlash over his casting, including racist abuse and death threats from people upset about the decision. The actor previously addressed those reactions, explaining that he understood there would be criticism but remained committed to the role.

Still, despite the pressure surrounding the production, Essiedu seems genuinely excited about the experience. During the same interview, he credited the people working alongside him for making the enormous responsibility feel manageable:

It's a beautiful thing. And with something like this, it's also so much about the people that you're collaborating with, and I feel so much trust and endeavor in the people who I'm standing alongside on this journey. There's a lot of feelings, but they're all good.

That confidence extends to the show's young stars, too. Essiedu had particularly kind things to say about Dominic McLaughlin, Alastair Stout and Arabella Stanton, who are taking over the roles of Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, respectively.

Essiedu acknowledged the tremendous responsibility the three child actors carry, especially considering how closely audiences associate the characters with Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, and Emma Watson. He described his young co-stars as mature, hardworking performers and said he couldn't wait for audiences to see what they've accomplished.

I think that's worth remembering as we approach the premiere. Much of the conversation surrounding HBO's new Harry Potter adaptation has understandably focused on how the cast will compare to the original movies. But these actors also have the chance to explore the characters across an entire television series, potentially giving them room to develop aspects of the books that the films couldn't fit.

The eight-episode first season, Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, premieres Dec. 25 on HBO and streams with an HBO Max subscription. John Lithgow will play Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer takes over as Minerva McGonagall, and Nick Frost steps into Hagrid's enormous boots.

As for Paapa Essiedu, I have to appreciate his willingness to admit that the thrill of getting the job wore off almost immediately. Hopefully, once audiences finally see him teaching Potions at Hogwarts, he'll get to enjoy a little more than 10 seconds of excitement.

#3516. WhatsApp announces four new features to make group chats easier to manage

In a blog post this week, WhatsApp confirmed that it is rolling out four new features designed to make it easier to manage group chats and keep track of what’s going on in each one. Here are the details.

WhatsApp this week announced that the filter drawer, which appears when users swipe down on the conversations list, will now include a “Mentions and replies” button alongside other filter options such as Groups, Favorites, Unread and custom filters.

Once tapped, the chat list will show only “unread group conversation[s] where you were either mentioned or received a direct reply, including @all messages,” says WhatsApp.

Additionally, WhatsApp will now let users pin messages indefinitely in group chats, rather than choosing between 24 hours, 7 days, or 30 days.

Another in-chat feature coming to groups is the ability to “send someone recent messages retroactively after they’ve joined a group just by tapping their name in the chat.” Previously, this was only possible when adding someone to a group, rather than after they had joined.

Finally, WhatsApp is rolling out group status sharing, which lets users post updates visible only to members of a specific group. Other members can view, react to, and add their own statuses, which disappear after 24 hours.

As is often the case with WhatsApp updates, it may take some time for all four features to become available to everyone. To check out the full announcement, follow this link.

#3515. Jake Gyllenhaal's 124-Minute Sci-Fi Disaster Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

In 2004, "The Day After Tomorrow" clumsily delivered a message about climate change via a movie in which Dennis Quaid and Jake Gyllenhaal try to save the world from a new ice age. The questionable part of the film was the science, which as NASA Goddard Space Flight Center meteorologist J. Marshall Shepherd told USA Today, warranted "a D minus or an F." Otherwise, "The Day After Tomorrow" was a grand old time at the movies, and now it seems modern audiences are having a similarly wonderful time with the end of the world over on Netflix.

The sci-fi disaster film was co-written, co-produced, and directed by Roland Emmerich, who prior to this had taken a break from big-budget sci-fi fare to make "The Patriot" with Mel Gibson. "The Day After Tomorrow" saw him return to familiar territory, with a film based on on Art Bell and Whitley Strieber's 1999 book "The Coming Global Superstorm."

Dennis Quaid stars as Paleoclimatologist Jack Hall, who's dismayed to find that global warming has finally brought about a new ice age that's preceded by extreme weather events which batter major cities around the world. His son Sam Hall (Gyllenhaal) happens to be in New York just as the big freeze sets in, prompting Jack to set off on a rescue mission.

The movie isn't the most critically acclaimed thing Emmerich has ever done. But it did gross $552.6 million on a $125 million budget and remains an impressive showcase of early 2000s CGI and arguably the best natural disaster movie of the era. If it's been a while, or you're yet to catch "The Day After Tomorrow," why not join in the celebration over on Netflix?

"The Day After Tomorrow" hit Netflix on November 1, 2026 and immediately took over the streamer's charts like an unstoppable climactic event. Streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol shows the movie debuted at number one on the Netflix Top 10 movie charts on November 2, 2026 in the United States. What's more it maintains that position at the time of writing and it will be interesting to see just how long Jake Gyllenhaal's disaster flick can hang on to the top spot.

Otherwise, there are plenty of other disaster movies streaming on Netflix, just in case you don't necessarily fancy the early 2000s stylings of Roland Emmerich and co.

#3514. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Is 'Ballhog'?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's zeitgeist snapshot explains what ballhog means, how a video of someone wrapping a burger led to a new meme format, and the dangers of Benny tripping. So strap in, and let's go.

Ballhog or ball hog is a streetwear fashion style growing in popularity among younger people. The cool ones, anyway. The idea is to wear vintage clothes that look normal, even drab, to most, but that people in the know can recognize as interesting or unique. Like the best youth trends, it's an insider vs. outsider thing that takes connoisseurship to understand. Some examples: If you're wearing a late 1990s Helmut Lang denim jacket, most people will think "thrifted," but a ballhog-enjoyer would recognize it as a seminal piece of streetwear history. If you want to be ballhog, rocking a pair of skinny jeans isn't going to cut it unless they're from Dior Homme or at least Cheap Monday.

The style is named after the Ball Hog Collective, a group of rappers, Twitch streamers, and content creators founded by the Atlanta-based indie record label Ballhog. It was popularized by streamer Brady Goodwin, seen below looking quite ballhog:

The #ballhog hashtag is blowing up (as people used to say) lately with a growing collection of kids posting videos to show off their ballhog fits, like so:

The popularity of the style comes down to, I think, how difficult it is to commodify. Most truly organic trends are recognized quickly by culture vulture types, and in a few months, there's a line of clothes at Target, but you can't do that with ballhog. There's no way to make "new" ballhog gear, as that would mark it as inauthentic immediately. Gotta hand it to the kids for adopting a style that is at once exclusionary and impossible to rip off.

On the opposite edge of the spectrum from ballhog fashion is the "while they're out partying btw" meme, videos made to show off the strange, specific, and usually useless talent one develops while others are out wearing cool clothes and socializing. The phrase has been kicking around since last year, when TikToker @tacobella posted this video

but it's taken off more recently, thanks to the huge number of views on this video showing off some truly mind-blowing burger wrapping skills:

This led to an influx of videos of people showing off what they were doing instead of partying. Like this mechanic:

This is the second youth trend I support wholeheartedly. We can't all be cool ballhoggers and we don't all have talent, but we can all learn to do a thing really well through brute force and repetition.

The past tense of "cringe," "crunged" is often used to describe extreme cringe, like "I cringed so hard I crunged."

As for "scuba," it now describes something that is very smelly, which might be because the word conjures the dead air of unventilated, underwater spaces. But it's often accompanied by a pinch-your-nose gesture, which looks like the gesture in the Scuba Dance that was popular on TikTok a few months ago, so that's a more likely origin for the term.

There has been a steady stream of news stories about kids overdosing on Benadryl over the last few years. They call it "Benny tripping," and it's achieved by taking too much of the allergy medicine, like 10 times the amount recommended. Among the active ingredients in Benadryl is Diphenhydramine, and it's a particularly nasty drug. Unlike most recreational substances, tripping on Benadryl is not fun. It's a deliriant, and taking too much results in hallucinations that are usually described as terrifying—swarms of spiders, shadow people, whispering voices, etc. Benadryl overdoses can result in loss of short term memory, displacement from time and space, and panic attacks that last for hours or even days. Or you die from tachycardia. Here's how Reddit user Reasonable-County971 described their experience,

I lost access to my memories. I couldn’t recognize my mom—I mistook her for a 'pretty nurse'. Early in the trip, before you lose yourself, you develop tremendous anxiety, far far beyond anything else I can compare it to. Also, you have motor skills affected, including losing access to your bladder.

So yeah, it's a bad drug. And it's easy to get—just pop down to CVS. On the plus side, despite sometimes overly hysterical reporting on Benadryl as an "online trend" or challenge, tripping on Benadryl is such a harrowing, not-at-all-fun experience, its use isn't particularly popular among young people. But if you want to scare yourself, read some trip reports, watch this YouTube video, and imagine someone you love going through this.

This week's viral video is very meta, and it's hilarious to anyone who follows the trajectory of viral internet sensations. Brought to us by the great @ariisaysso, this video lays out the history of the fictional Cheezit Girl as she becomes an internet sensation, quits her job, sells merch, releases a rap single, releases a remix, reheats the nachos, and falls into obscurity, all in about two and a half minutes. We've seen this story before with the Hawk Tuah Girl, Dah Bih Gah Kid, and many more future members of the "remember that thing" club, and we'll no doubt see it all again soon. Such is the circle of life.

The process of reading a Christopher Nolan script sounds like a spy thriller.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Director Christopher Nolan is the rare unicorn filmmaker who can draw audiences to the theater and bring in the kind of box office numbers that every major movie studio dreams of. Seeing a Nolan movie feels like special event viewing, partly because audiences go see his films with a level of anticipation and excitement that only comes with not having many details and never fully knowing what to expect. And, apparently, the head of Universal had an even more unique experience when Nolan pitched her The Odyssey.

There is a level of secrecy surrounding the Oppenheimer director’s projects, though I'm only now finding out that it carries over to even the Chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment, Donna Langley. During an interview with Maria Sharapova for Pretty Tough, Universal’s Head Honcho described her experience with reading Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of The Odyssey, which sounds a bit like its own spy thriller. She revealed this about the IMAX savant's method, which includes his wife and producing partner, Emma Thomas:

It’s terrifying…. I’m terrified. Because well the way that Chris does it, or the way he did it on The Odyssey and on Oppenheimer, actually is I was invited over to their house, and I went by myself both occasions. And I didn't know what I was going to read because he doesn't say ahead of time. So you don't know until you're sitting in his library on the couch and he hands you the script. And so it’s a bit intimidating.

Not only does that sound intimidating and terrifying, I can’t imagine what would happen if you had a negative reaction while you were sitting in the home of the filmmaker responsible for writing it. Granted, Nolan is considered to be one of the best filmmakers in the entire world, but even the best at something has a bad day (or project) every once in a while, don’t they?

What strikes me as particularly interesting is the fact that even the biggest of big wigs at Universal doesn’t get to know ahead of time what she’s going to read when she knocks on Nolan’s door. I can’t imagine the level of heightened emotions that one experiences when reading a script from such an expert storyteller for the first time, as everything unfolds. But according to Langley, the pitch experience for this book-to-screen adaptation doesn’t just end there:

Then they leave, and I get a couple of hours to read the script on the same sofa…. And they leave me to it with a cup of tea. And then they leave, and then they come back when I'm finished and we talk about it.

It would probably be hilarious to watch the facial expressions of someone as they read a Christopher Nolan script. Especially someone so high up at the studio, as they realize what kind of budget they’ll need to do the story justice when it’s a story as epic as The Odyssey, one of the biggest blockbusters from the 2026 movie schedule. But knowing that, once finished, the Memento director and Thomas, will return to chat about it seems even more daunting. I wish I could have been a fly on the wall to hear everything that they talked about once Donna Langley finished reading the Odyssey script. Langley added:

It’s a process that — I love it, because it feels very old school, and it’s very intentional. And it makes you pay attention, but it is slightly intimidating. But I think, in the best way possible, it makes me feel very alive.

I have to admit, there is something really cool about making everyone involved with getting a movie into production feel like they’re a part of a private little club of people let in on a secret that the world is not yet ready for. It’s an old-school approach, keeping technology out of it, and that tracks for Nolan, given he doesn't even own a smartphone. However, I understand how exhilarating it must be to be a part of the cool club. And Langley said that the scripts for The Odyssey and Oppenheimer were both brilliant and easy to talk about once she finished them.

The Odyssey's reviews were largely positive from general audiences and critics alike, even if some did point out historical inaccuracies and that side character problem. This historical epic lit up the 2026 box office in a big way, proving that if you release a movie people want to see, they will go see it, likely over and over again. Now, I'm just wondering when Nolan and Thomas might reach out to Langley with another script that would lead them to repeat their unique process.

#3512. Skydance Inherited Massive Flops From Warner Bros. Deal - And Things Could Get Worse

There's a new mega-studio in Hollywood, and it's got a lot to prove. The Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger was recently made official, with the new company named Skydance. This $111 billion deal has been met with intense scrutiny, in no small part because Skydance is now saddled with billions of dollars in debt. So, to make all this look even remotely tenable for the foreseeable future, that means Warner Bros. has to deliver at the box office.

Unfortunately, the new owners at Skydance inherited a string of massive flops ... and it may get worse before it gets better.

Indeed, a report from Page Six has examined Warner Bros.' ex-film bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy's "free spending" ways. Recall that Warner Bros. set a huge box office record in 2025, with six movies in a row earning at least $40 million on opening weekend. But this year has not been kind to the studio, with this report stating that Warner Bros.' 2026 slate will lose around $800 million. Can it really be that bad? Yes, it can.

Here's a full breakdown of Warner Bros.' 2026 at the box office, movie by movie:

"Wuthering Heights" — $80 million budget/$241 million worldwide

"The Bride!" — $90 million budget/$24 million worldwide

"They Will Kill You" — $10 million budget/$19 million worldwide

"Lee Cronin's The Mummy" — $22 million budget/$90 million worldwide

"Mortal Kombat II" — $80 million budget/$129 million worldwide

"Supergirl" — $170 million budget/$126 million worldwide

"Evil Dead Burn" — $20 million budget/$72 million worldwide

"The End of Oak Street" — $90 million budget/$121 million worldwide

"Practical Magic 2" — $75 million budget/$106 million worldwide

"Digger" — $180 million budget/$49 million worldwide

"Clayface" — $44 million budget/$84 million worldwide (still in theaters)

I previously broke down how movie box office actually works. Basically, without getting too far into the weeds, theaters keep around half of all money from ticket sales, and budget figures don't include marketing expenses. Taking that into account, we can see that only "Wuthering Heights," "Lee Cronin's The Mummy," "Evil Dead Rise," and "Clayface" will go down as hits for Warner Bros. this year, when all's said and done. And some of those are rather modest successes at best.

The rest of the slate is either filled with big disappointments or crushing flops. Tom Cruise's "Digger" will lose a lot of money at the box office, potentially as much as $250 million. That's just the tip of the iceberg, too. "The Bride!" also lost a fortune, while "Supergirl" flopped in a rather terrible fashion. Movies that were expected to be blockbuster hits instead became shipwrecks, with the debris washing up on the rocks. It's been bad.

The validity of that $800 million figure is somewhat irrelevant. It's crystal clear that WB's 2026 slate, overall, is going to lose a lot of money. Even if movies like "They Will Kill You" eventually made money on VOD/streaming, Skydance needs big hits. What it's gotten is a string of disastrous flops.

Even "One Battle After Another" was still a box office bomb ($213 million worldwide/$170 million budget) despite winning Best Picture at the Oscars. This Page Six report estimates it lost around $75 million. The Oscar helps, but probably not quite that much. Hence, Skydance needs Warner Bros. to deliver at the box office more than ever, and the hope is that 2027 will deliver green pastures. But that's far from a sure thing at this juncture.

On paper, there are some surefire bets on Warner Bros.' upcoming slate in 2027. 2024's "Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire" became the highest-grossing "Godzilla" movie ever, so it stands to reason that its sequel, "Godzilla x Kong: Supernova," will be a hit as well. But Warner Bros. will have to split that revenue with Legendary, so that's a somewhat qualified winner.

There's also the studio's much-anticipated return to Middle Earth. Even though Peter Jackson isn't directing "The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum," it has a lot of appeal and revives a multi-billion-dollar global franchise. Optimistically, that should pan out pretty well, too, though how well remains to be seen. On top of that, there's the "Minecraft Movie" sequel, James Gunn's "Superman" follow-up "Man of Tomorrow," and "The Conjuring: First Communion," the latter of which ought to deliver. Remember, only six horror movie franchises have made over $1 billion at the box office, and The Conjuring Universe is one of them.

Outside of that? It gets far more murky. Director J.J. Abrams' "The Great Beyond" was pushed back to 2027, presumably because WB wanted an IMAX release. It's expensive and far from a sure thing. Even riskier is the new Nancy Meyers rom-com tentatively titled "Paris Paramount," which reportedly cost a dizzying $120 million. As for Sam Esmail's $60 million "Panic Carefully" and the CGI/live-action hybrid movie "Animal Friends?" They're big question marks.

For seemingly every sure thing on WB's 2027 slate, then, there's a real risk. Skydance film bosses Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg have a lot of decisions to make. For now, though, It's be less about the movies they want to make and more about how they're going to handle all the dicey prospects they've inherited.

#3511. The Fitbit Edge Is Everything the Charge 6 Should Have Been

I’ve been using the new Fitbit Edge for a little over a week, and am happy to report that it’s quite good at its job. It shipped with more features than I expected (Google Maps directions were there from the jump) and corrects the missteps that Google made with the Fitbit Charge 6. After running the Fitbit Edge through its paces, here’s my breakdown of what works well, what doesn’t, and what I think of the device overall.

When I reviewed it in May 2025, I liked a lot about the Charge 6, but found it had a few serious flaws. Tightening the strap messed up its GPS readings (weird but true), and some of its features required a subscription (like the music controls that only worked with YouTube Music). Its promised side button wasn’t really a button, and didn’t even always work.

I’m happy to report that all of my biggest gripes have been fixed in the Fitbit Edge. Or to put it another way: the Edge is what the Charge should have been in the first place.

Accuracy tests are always one of my top priorities in testing, but honestly I wasn’t expecting much from this device. A Fitbit can still be successful in my eyes even if its heart rate sensor is only “good enough.” Nobody should expect lab-level precision from a Fitbit.

But I was pleasantly surprised by just how capable the Edge is in this regard. It sometimes takes a few minutes to lock on to a heart rate signal (as most optical devices do), but after it does, it is spot-on—I think it might be in the running alongside the Apple Watch and high-end Garmins as one of the better heart rate wearables on the market. The Edge’s accuracy is notably better than the Fitbit Air's, even though they seem to share the same sensor hardware.

Location accuracy is also quite good, only deviating slightly from a Garmin I tested alongside the Edge. It may not be the best out there, but it’s miles ahead of what the Charge 6 was able to do.

The Fitbit Edge has real music controls, unlike the Charge 6. I can play something in Spotify or in Castro (my favorite podcast app) on my phone, and then control the audio from my wrist—and you no longer need to use YouTube Music or have a subscription to get this feature.

When the Fitbit Air and the Google Health app first launched, it was possible to pair both a Fitbit and a Pixel Watch to the same phone, but not two Fitbits. That has finally changed: I was able to connect the Edge to my phone without losing my connection to the Air. It also works to swap seamlessly between the two Fitbits. For example, one night the Edge was low on battery, so I slept with the Air on, and then swapped back in the morning once the Edge was charged. The app happily showed my sleep data from the Air and my activity data from the Edge without my having to do mess around in the app.

As a nice bonus, the charger for the Fitbit Edge is the same as for the Fitbit Air. (The chargers for the Pixel Watch and for the Fitbit Charge 6 are not compatible with the Edge.)

The Fitbit Edge is a similar size as the old Charge 6, but with noticeably more screen real estate. The strap fits pretty much the same way as a Pixel watch band—that is to say, normally, not with the strange hang-off-the-wrist stiffness of the Charge 6.

The Fitbit Edge also has a physical button—not a haptic nub like the Charge 6, but an actual, physical button. And it even works (to return you to the home screen) nearly every time I press it. The Charge 6’s nub was not as reliable.

Overall, I’m quite happy with the Fitbit Edge. It’s much better than the Charge 6, and adds accuracy and a screen to the things I already liked about the Fitbit Air. But there are a few things I don’t totally love.

One is that there is no NFC chipset, which means no option to use Google Pay. I don’t mind using my phone or card at checkouts (and I always carry my phone), so this isn’t a big deal for me, but I know a lot of folks love a wrist-based payment, and that’s missing from the Fitbit Edge. (Google reportedly said most Fitbit users didn’t actually use Google Pay, so they removed the functionality—presumably to fit in the other components while keeping the device small.)

The other downside is, I hate to say it, the Google Health app. It’s OK, but I still find myself arguing with the AI when it assigns me workouts I never asked for, and I have to agree with the redditors who are commiserating about the lack of a “yesterday” view. (On the bright side, Google recently added a feature that lets you turn off the AI insights, which helps a lot.)

Overall, the Fitbit Edge is a great fitness tracker. It measures heart rate and running/walking mileage accurately; it can control music in a sensible way; and it looks good, feels good to wear, and works smoothly. The price also tracks: It’s definitely worth the $20 premium over the Charge 6, and it’s not quite double the price of the Air, which I think is fair. For anyone who doesn’t want a smartwatch or a running watch and will be satisfied with just “a Fitbit,” this one is pretty much perfect.

Why Geography Always Seems To Be A Problem For Prince Harry And Meghan Markle

#3508. Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir's Sci-Fi Recommendations For Capturing His 'Vibe' [Exclusive]

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you're an aspiring science fiction novelist, you would do well to take the advice of author Andy Weir, who's red hot in publication and Hollywood thanks to the runaway successes of "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary." That the former was self-published before getting turned into a bestseller and a blockbuster film directed by Ridley Scott — one that starred Matt Damon and earned seven Academy Award nominations, including a nod for Best Picture — is the dream of every up-and-coming writer.

So, genre authors have good reason to hang on Weir's every word, especially when it comes to capturing his profitable vibe. And while I'm a firm believer in finding your own vibe, there's a time-honored tradition in this industry of proving you can write comfortably within established formulae. With Weir, it's about straddling the line between hard science and uplifting, humanistic engagement with a vast universe that needn't be as harsh as we've been led to think. We can always, as Damon's character in "The Martian" says, "science the s*** out of" our various predicaments. I think that's naively hopeful in an age where the United States government is vehemently anti-science (unless it lines the pockets of AI-shilling tech billionaires), but Weir's got that storytelling magic that makes you want to believe we're not too far gone.

Weir is but one man, though, so if you're wondering where you can find his vibe in other work, he shared some suggestions with /Film's Jeremy Mathai, starting with his go-to recommendation:

"Well, if you consider an Andy Weir vibe to be just hard science fiction, with accurate science in there, then you got to go for [James S.A. Corey's] 'The Expanse.' That's really, really good hard sci-fi. That's really solid."

"The Expanse," for those not familiar, deals with a relatively realistic colonization of our solar system that does not initially involve interstellar travel. There's literally a lot of space to fill, but it's subject to the kinds of territorial disputes that have sparked wars on Earth. Ultimately, the narrative expands, bringing in aliens and the like, but, in its television incarnation, Mark Fergus and Hawk Ostby (who brilliantly adapted P.D. James' "The Children of Men" in 2006) approach the scenario with intellectual rigor.

Andy Weir also voiced enthusiasm for Blake Crouch's "Dark Matter," a frantically paced sci-fi novel that's been successfully adapted into an Apple TV series via the author himself. The small screen version of Crouch's parallel universe thriller stars Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly, and it finds the former's character struggling to skip back to his reality (where his family is being appropriated by an alternate universe version of himself).

Finally, Weir is a proponent of Ben Bova's "The Grand Tour" novels, most notably the fourth entry in the book series titled "Mars." As Weir explained:

"That's a fairly hard sci-fi approach to a mission to Mars. It's about the first mission to Mars. It's got some pretty interesting twists in there that turn out to be ... at first, they look a little bit woo-woo, aliens, oh no. Then you find out the twist reveal of what's going wrong, and the thing is absolutely scientific and completely sensible and you're like, 'Ah, nice one.'"

Again, I'd advise you to find your own vibe, but if you want to catch the eye of publishers or studio execs, maybe check these works out and find your way forward the Weir way.

#3507. GTA 5’s Unsolvable Mystery Broke Fans for Over a Decade, and GTA 6 Should Do It Again

Mount Chiliad spawned thousands of theories

In Grand Theft Auto 5, one landmark was visible practically no matter where you were in San Andreas: Mount Chiliad. "Claimed by the Spanish in 1769, Mount Chiliad is the highest peak in San Andreas, sitting at a height of 2,744 meters," reads a sign at the nearby Silent Probe Mountain art installation. "Taken under Mexican control in 1821, it was then, and remains in American hands since 1847."

It's more than just a mountain, though. Once the player has achieved 100% story completion, standing atop the mountain at 3 a.m. during cloudy weather reveals a UFO, hovering in the night sky. It's marked with an F.I.B. logo, aka the Federal Investigation Bureau, implying that it was created by the government. However, there's also reason to believe that the mysterious aircraft is a hoax, because it doesn't react to bullets, and raindrops nearby become pixelated.

The running theory is that it's a hologram, as opposed to the two other functional UFOs in the game, which are physical objects. They're located high in the sky above both Fort Zancudo and the Silent Probe Mountain respectively, they can both be collided with, and they emit electromagnetic pulses that cause the player's vehicle to shut down if they get too close. There's reason to believe they're both also government-controlled: the former visually looks somewhat similar to a real-life B-2 Spirit stealth bomber and, when viewed using third-party software, has two human pilots inside. The latter also has F.I.B. printed on the side, much like the UFO above Mt. Chiliad.

Players knew there was at least one secret at the top of the mountain, thanks to graffiti on the back of the observation deck that reads "come back when your story is complete." GTA Online revealed that the mountain is also home to a nuclear launch facility. But some players are convinced that Mt. Chiliad holds one final mystery that is still unsolved to this day.

Inside the tramway station near the summit, a mural depicts an abstract interpretation of the mountain itself. At the top is an eye, while the exterior of the mountain has lightning bolts emanating from it. Inside the mountain is a maze of perpendicular connecting lines. Each one connects to one of eight squares. Five of them are small, marked with an X inside. The three larger ones at the bottom of the picture show, from left to right, a UFO, a cracked egg, and a person wearing a jetpack.

One week after GTA 5 was released, on Sept. 24, 2013, fans created the Chiliad Mystery subreddit. For the last 13 years, users there have been dedicated to uncovering the secrets believed to be held within. The community worked out that the X's correspond to petroglyphs hidden around the mountain, each of which depicts a weather status required for the Mt. Chiliad UFO to appear. There's also a theory that each X also represents the roman numeral for 10, and since there are five of them, it's representative of the 50 collectible spaceship (aka UFO) parts scattered across San Andreas.

In the GTA Online mission involving the nuclear facility, the player escapes by using a jetpack. Is that what the jetpack drawing on the mural is referring to? It’s one of the mural’s lingering riddles. It's certainly plausible, if a little underwhelming, because the common belief was that unraveling the mystery would result in a permanent jetpack vehicle, usable in GTA 5’s single-player mode, not exclusive to Online. However, some think the jetpack just refers to the UFO above Fort Zancudo, because in GTA: San Andreas, the jetpack is found at the military base.

Then there's the cracked egg. This has been the biggest source of confusion for the sleuths working on the mystery, and there are a number of theories. It could refer to the Epsilon cult, as they believe the world hatched from an egg. It could also tie in to the fountain by the Maze Bank Tower in Los Santos, as the two bear a close resemblance. Or there's the most common theory, which is that it is simply a hint to the underwater UFO found in Paleto Bay, on the northern coast of San Andreas.

So with all of that in mind, there's every chance that the mural is simply one giant hint to finding each of the UFOs in GTA 5. But believing that would also mean believing that the Chiliad mystery is solved, and there's no fun in that, because it would be a seriously disappointing outcome. And for the users on the subreddit, that isn't even a possibility.

There are hundreds of loose ends and theories players have discovered. Even in the last year, they’ve posted dozens of new ideas. Here's user Alexisuwuu23, who is convinced an in-game film, "Capolavoro," holds the secret because a billboard ad for it can be found at the location where streetlights form a question mark if looked at from the observatory, and it all ties into a disappearing ladder. "Intentional, obviously," reads one reply. "Gotta be a marker or something. The hunt continues."

In September, AntelopeIcy6558 posed a theory about the eight lights on top of the Maze Bank Tower helipad. "I believe that to solve the secret, you need to shoot these eight lights in a certain order," the post reads. "Why? I believe there are eight locations around Los Santos that we need to find. Each of these locations from some angle resembles a keyhole, which is one of the main symbols of this mystery."

There are other theories that think the mystery stretches beyond GTA 5, and also includes Red Dead Redemption 2. Cancelled DLCs and datamined files have revealed a vast array of potential clues, but since those projects were never officially released, they're unlikely to ever provide a definitive answer. Then there are those who predict GTA 6 will provide a resolution.

Twelve years ago, user talkol made a post titled "pretty solid proof that the game was released without a jetpack or flyable UFO," which outlined what is still the most damning evidence we've had: there is nothing hinting at either of those vehicles in the game's files. Of course, that didn't dissuade the masses, because posts like these have been non-stop for the last 13 years.

Last year, as reported on by IGN, YouTuber Gator Keys uploaded a video titled "This is The End of the Mount Chiliad Mystery." He kicks it off by stating what many realists would agree with: "I'm not claiming I'm the first person to come to this conclusion. I'm sure many other players did in 2013, but for some reason, the Mt. Chiliad mystery remains in 2025. So there needs to be a video that puts an end to it before GTA 6 releases."

Gator Keys goes into plenty of detail in the eight-minute-long video, but to sum it up, his explanation is that the mystery is nowhere near as deep as the community had believed. The answer is essentially that the government is all-seeing and all-powerful, as represented by the F.I.B. logos on the UFOs and the eye on top of the mural. It's simply a satirical take on real life, similar to the idea of the Illuminati.

Ultimately, the "true" answer for the Chiliad mystery is irrelevant. The mystery itself spawned a thousands-strong community, with everyone cooperating and theorizing. It's reminiscent of when that kid at school promised they'd found Mew underneath a truck in Pokémon Red and Blue. Easter eggs and gaming mysteries these days are usually solved within days, thanks to datamining and the sharing of information via the internet. GTA 5, on the other hand, whether intentionally or not, gave players something to talk about for 13 years.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

There's no doubt GTA 6 will spawn plenty more theories and Easter eggs, whether they're a continuation of the Chiliad mystery or something entirely new. It'll also likely be the biggest video game of all time, whether it includes a decade-long mystery or not. But the longevity of the Chiliad mystery makes one thing clear: Rockstar is the champion of this type of lore, and including something similar, where the game never truly feels complete without it being solved, will keep a huge portion of the community occupied for years to come.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3506. If You Loved 'Crystal Lake,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Peacock’s Crystal Lake is an unexpected treat in a lot of ways, taking one of horror’s most iconic figures—Jason Voorhees of the Friday the 13th franchise—and digging into the universe’s background by focusing on his mother, Pamela. Famously the actual serial killer in the original film, Pamela’s development into a psychotic killer who inspired her son to become the psychotic killer of all time is the engine that drives Crystal Lake, finding the damaged humanity behind the terror. If you’ve burned through all eight episodes of Crystal Lake’s first season, and you’ve worked through the streamalike series with similar DNA, it’s time to check out some movies—starting with the perfect companion film, 2022’s Pearl.

The second film in Ti West’s X trilogy (starting with X and concluding with 2024’s MaXXXine) is the ideal film to watch after Crystal Lake. Like the series, it explores a female serial killer’s backstory and recontextualizes your understanding of their motives and psychology. It also requires that you be familiar with the original story—while you can certainly watch Crystal Lake or Pearl without having seen the Friday the 13th films or X, you’ll be missing out on a lot if you do.

In X, a group of young people descends on a dilapidated old farm to film an adult movie in Texas in 1979, and by the end of the film most of them are dead, killed by the farm’s elderly couple Howard (Stephen Ure) and Pearl (Mia Goth), with Pearl presented as the most deranged and dangerous of the two. It’s a riveting update to the classic splatter movie template, and Goth nails her dual role as the Final Girl Maxine and the psychotic, murderous Pearl. The prequel, Pearl, jumps back to 1918, when Pearl (Goth again) was a young woman living with her strict mother and paralyzed father. Pearl has big dreams of being an entertainer, but her mother tries to trap her to ensure she’s there to care for her parents and work the farm. Pearl’s lonely unhappiness and frustration (both mental and, er, physical) inspire a slow boil of tension as her grip on sanity frays, and her anger toward her parents curdles into something frightening.

Like Crystal Lake, Pearl takes a killer who seems fairly one-dimensional in their original presentation and gives them a deeper back story and psychological framing. Pamela Voorhees wasn’t just crazy—she was driven to madness by the horrible things that happened to her and her son, and the awful way she’s treated by her fellow humans. Similarly, Pearl is a hopeful and innocent young woman who is slowly molded into a killer by the events of her life. Both the series and the film serve as reminders that monsters are rarely born—they’re made. And it’s usually the casual cruelty of the people around them that does the making. If you loved Crystal Lake’s fresh take on Pamela, Pearl is the perfect choice for a movie night. Stream Pearl on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Need more serial killer movies that hit the Crystal Lake vibe? Never fear—here are some other excellent choices to pair with the series.

If you’ve never actually seen the original Friday the 13th (or if it’s been a while), this is a must-watch for fans of Crystal Lake. Although the series takes some liberties to update the timeline, it’s still intended as a glimpse into the events that shaped both Pamela and Jason Voorhees into inhuman (and somewhat supernatural) monsters. Initially given savagely bad reviews, the film was a surprise blockbuster and is now regarded as a classic of a genre it helped to create in the first place; rewatching it today not only helps contextualize Crystal Lake, it puts the entire slasher genre into perspective. Stream Friday the 13th on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

The success of Friday the 13th led to a rush of copycat films, of course. Most of those weren’t particularly good or even interesting, but Sleepaway Camp is an exception (although it was similarly savaged by critics at the time). Now a cult classic, Sleepaway Camp has two things that recommend it to fans of Crystal Lake and Friday the 13th: a weird sensibility that gives it an otherworldly atmosphere that enhances the sense of dread, and what is probably the most unexpected twist ending in the history of slasher films (and it’s probably a Top 10 twist in general). Stream Sleepaway Camp on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

One reason Crystal Lake exists is the enduring power and influence of slasher films in general and Friday the 13th specifically. Few recent films have tapped into that dreamy nightmare feel like Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. As with most of Schoenbrun’s work, the film delves into themes of identity, subverting queer tropes, and the malleable nature of reality itself. If you’re looking for a slasher story that’s less straightforward than Crystal Lake while dealing with some similar themes of transformation and destiny, this is it. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

If you’ve seen all the Friday the 13th movies and want more slasher horror with a bit more edge, check out The Burning. Is it a great film? Not really. Combining the straightforward slasher thrills of Friday with some of the villain motivations of fellow classic franchise A Nightmare on Elm Street, The Burning dials the blood and guts up to 11 (and beyond) and remains notoriously gory even by today’s standards. But if your fave part of Crystal Lake is the frequently over-the-top gore and violence, this is an ideal movie choice. Stream The Burning on The Roku Channel or Kanopy.

Want a slasher film that explores the psyche of a female killer the way Crystal Lake deconstructs Pamela Voorhees? Check out May. A fragile young woman, May struggles to find connection with the people around her, and slowly descends into a fantasy world that inspires her to literally make her own ideal friend. What makes May so interesting is the depth of the exploration of May’s personality that’s similar to how Pamela is handled in Crystal Lake, tracing each step of her stumble into a bloody hell. Stream May on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

#3504. DC Studios Officially Casts Mason Thames As Robin — Will He Play Him In Live-Action?

We might not know when the DC Universe will unveil its version of Batman, but we just got news that the franchise has cast its Robin. Well, at least we know who'll be voicing one of the Robins in the upcoming "Dynamic Duo" movie. In an interview with Collider, DC Studios co-head Peter Safran confirmed that Mason Thames has been cast as the voice of Dick Grayson in the upcoming film.

Thames is best known for starring in "The Black Phone" and its sequel, as well as playing Hiccup Horrendous Haddock III in the live-action "How to Train Your Dragon" movie. But it seems he's been gunning for a DC role. "We always talk about wanting volunteers and not recruits to be part of the DCU, to be part of DC Studios," said Safran, "and Mason always wanted to be Dick Grayson. He just did."

According to the producer, Thames came in to read for Grayson and "auditioned the s*** out of it." "He's a wonderful young actor," he continued. "But boy, did he want this. He was just obsessed. When he came over to the DC offices, he came over with his dad at the time, and we've got tons of great archives and stuff in there, and wanted to take a picture of everything and with everything. He's a fan."

That certainly bodes well for a committed performance from the 19-year-old, who most recently appeared alongside Dave Franco and O'Shea Jackson Jr. in the most startling comedy of 2026, "Idiots." The question is, will Thames actually play Dick Grayson in live-action? According to past comments from Safran's DC Studios co-head James Gunn, that's exactly what will happen. But there's no confirmation as of yet.

"Dynamic Duo" is an animated film that's being developed by DC Studios in collaboration with Swaybox Studios. The latter's unique animation style combines puppetry and CGI to create a stop-motion-like effect that will be used to tell Jason Todd and Dick Grayson's origin stories. Mason Thames' casting as the latter had previously been rumored, with scooper Jeff Sneider reporting it in September 2026. But now it's official, meaning Thames will join Logan Kim, who's playing Jason Todd, in "Dynamic Duo" — much to the dismay of "Titans" star Curran Walters, who reacted to the news of the Jason Todd recasting with disappointment.

The movie is set for a September 22, 2028 release, with Arthur Mintz, who co-founded Swaybox with Theresa Andersson in 2013, directing. For now, further details about the film are scarce, but Lee Pace and Steve Buscemi have reportedly been cast as members of the Red Hood Gang.

As it stands, we at least know who will be voicing two of the most significant versions of Robin in the DC Universe. The question is, will Thames and Kim portray their characters in live-action? They certainly should, given James Gunn's prior comments.

When he and Peter Safran became co-heads of DC Studios in 2022, they promised this latest on-screen superhero franchise would not simply be more of the same. Gunn touted a shared universe without a house style and confirmed that DC Universe actors would portray their character across film, TV, animation, and even video games, streamlining the franchise in a way that sounded as though it could be bad news for animation voice actors. But it remains to be seen whether he will stick to that claim moving forward, especially since much has changed since 2022.

James Gunn has repeated his claim about actors portraying their DC Universe characters across mediums on several occasions. In 2023, he told DC.com "Television, movies and games all intertwine within the same universe. We're going to cast actors that are going to be able to play the characters in this, as well as in other things, some of which we've already cast." Thus far, Frank Grillo has played Rick Flag Sr. on the big screen in "Superman," on TV in "Peacemaker," and voiced the character for animation in "Creature Commandos." As such, it would make sense for Logan Kim and Mason Thames to follow a similar path.

But as we've seen in recent years, nothing is set in stone. Leaving aside the Warner Bros. Discovery/Paramount merger becoming official in October 2026, James Gunn and Peter Safran announced a slate of movies back in 2022, some of which have now been scrapped. Gunn confirmed that DC had cancelled the planned "The Authority" movie, for instance, and he has spoken openly about how plans for the DC Universe otherwise shifted following Warner Bros.' initial announcement. All of which raises the question of whether he's sticking to his plan for actor continuity across mediums.

It would certainly make a lot of sense given his previous explanations. In 2023, Gunn spoke to The Hollywood Reporter about how Aaron Pierre would be playing Green Lantern John Stewart in both the HBO series "Lanterns" and on the big screen in the upcoming "Man of Tomorrow." "We don't want the series to feel in any way like step-children or lesser-than," he told the outlet. "[The show is] just another way to tell a story." Time will tell if the same holds for Kim and Thames.

#3503. Apple @ Work: Next to a growing token bill, Macs might start looking like a bargain

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple hardware costs more than it did a year ago, and if you have purchased a fleet recently, you are feeling it. Now, one thing I should mention: Macs have not risen in price with inflation or performance. If you think about what a Mac mini or MacBook Air cost when they launched vs. today, I would still say they are extremely affordable. With that being said, there’s a scenario taking shape in the enterprise where the price of a Mac matters a lot less than it used to. If open-weight AI models become a real part of how companies work, Apple Silicon might end up looking basically free compared to the token bill it supplements.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Cloud AI in the enterprise is priced by the token, and that’s a fine model when usage is moderate. The problem is that usage isn’t staying light. Agentic tools that write code, analyze documents, and run multistep tasks consume tokens at a pace a chatbot never did, and the bill scales right along with them. Earlier this year, Fleet’s IT leadership research cited a company that burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in four months after rolling an AI coding tool out to roughly 5,000 engineers. That’s the risk with a variable cost by token usage. Finance is somewhat in the dark on what the number is until the invoice shows up.

Local hardware works the opposite way, where you pay once, and the cost is capped. Every hour that machine spends running a model after that costs you very little, aside from power usage.

Someone I’ve long respected, Horace Dediu, showed some interesting numbers in a recent Asymco piece that really shows the opportunity ahead for Apple. In one example, a 26-billion-parameter model used for analysis four hours a day, around 150 million tokens a month, runs $450 to $850 per user per month through a cloud provider. A 16″ MacBook Pro with an M5 Max and 128GB of unified memory costs about $6,500 and can run a model locally. That’s a payback period of 7 to 14 months. He gives a lot more examples, and it’s worth a read to see Apple’s opportunity here.

The reason Apple Silicon is so well suited to this is unified memory. On most PCs, the GPU has its own small memory pool, and the model has to fit within it. On Apple Silicon, the GPU shares the entire memory pool, so a laptop with 128GB can hold a model that would need a far more expensive setup elsewhere.

Viewed through this lens, a price increase on a Mac Studio is a rounding error. If the machine pays for itself in under a year, and Apple Silicon Macs can stay in service for four to five years, it’s practically free over a normal refresh cycle. Now, if agentic coding keeps improving at such a rapid pace, you might end up upgrading sooner than that.

All of this hinges on one assumption: the math only works if an open-weight model running locally is good enough for your task day-to-day. For a lot of everyday work, like summarizing docs, drafting, content analysis on internal data, and basic routine coding, the gap between open-weight models and the frontier has narrowed significantly recently. For the hardest reasoning and coding tasks, frontier models still lead, and that isn’t changing anytime soon.

There are other caveats, too: his usage figures in those examples are high, and a typical employee isn’t burning through 150 million tokens a month. Token prices have also been falling, narrowing the gap over time. I am really interested in a hybrid model as well. Cribl recently launched StreamAI, an AI gateway for telemetry that routes each prompt to the right model and includes built-in budget control. At JNUC 2026, Jamf showed on-device AI support that deploys models through blueprints, routes prompts through an on-device AI gateway, and governs all of it with AI policies. Apple is clearly thinking about this too. At JNUC, Apple’s Jeremy Butcher had this to say regarding cloud and on-device AI:

“We think our platform makes for the best way to do both,” said Butcher. “We continue to have these conversations, and we look forward to working with all of you to bring it to life.”

A hybrid model might be the best of both worlds, with routine work running locally and the hardest tasks routed to frontier models in the cloud. Either way, Apple is well positioned. Even with RAM and GPU shortages driving up hardware prices, the ROI on Apple Silicon looks promising if open-weight models end up handling a decent share of enterprise AI workloads. Mac prices are going up, but token bills are going up faster (even if token prices continue to fall).

#3502. Jurassic Park's Lost Animated Series Pitch Has Finally Surfaced In Video Form

It's been over 30 years since "Jurassic Park" changed movies forever, with Steven Spielberg's 1993 adaptation of Michael Crichton's sci-fi thriller novel delivering not only a perfect film, but a production that brought a systemic change to how Hollywood made movies. It also marked the last time a dinosaur franchise would become a bonafide hit, as Hollywood continues to try and fail to make audiences care about dinosaurs unless the title includes the word "Jurassic." (David Robert Mitchell's "The End of Oak Street" is the latest example of audiences largely avoiding non-"Jurassic" dino movies.)

Given how incredibly successful the "Jurassic Park" franchise has been, it's no wonder it's expanded to include spin-offs, including video games, cartoons, and more. But what is surprising is just how slow this franchise has been to grow. After all, the first film came out in 1993, at a time when practically every big movie somehow got turned into a cartoon, regardless of whether the original was for kids or not.

"Jurassic Park" did almost get an animated series back then, but it never made it to production. Still, we've heard about this show on and off over the years, and now, we finally have the very first bit of footage, reportedly titled "Escape From Jurassic Park." The trailer surfaced on Twitter/X, and it quickly spread. Watch for yourself right below.

After all of these years, it has finally been found!

Fans of Jurassic Park, I humbly present to you, the animated Pitch Trailers for the canceled Jurassic Park Animated Show!

More info coming soon! pic.twitter.com/UGT5lOvvd5

— Jurassic Library (@JurassicLibrary) October 31, 2026

The trailer for the "Jurassic Park" animated film, thought lost forever, doesn't show much, but it does perfectly capture the look and tone of the Spielberg classic and mixes it with that recognizable '90s Amblin animated look we saw in "Animaniacs" and other shows of the time.

There's not a whole lot of information about the lost "Jurassic Park" animated series. We do have old pitch decks and story treatments that give an idea of what the series could have been about, as well as old concept art from cartoon veterans Will Meugniot and artist William Stout, who were meant to spearhead the show.

Perhaps most importantly, the "Jurassic Park" TV series was meant to be a direct sequel to the first film, with the first season reportedly focusing on BioSyn creating its own rival dinosaur theme park, leading to — you guessed it — another dino outbreak.

According to William Stout, this "was not going to be a kiddy show (although kids of all ages, including myself, could enjoy it)," he said in his blog back in 2014. "They wanted the show to be a mature prime time series with top writers and state-of-the-art television animation augmented with quite a bit of CG animation."

That much is clear from the leaked trailer for the "Jurassic Park" animated series. Though it still features kids, a big sense of adventure and wonder, and a visual style reminiscent of Don Bluth, the trailer also makes it clear this is a show about man-eating dinosaurs, and seems to hint at an appropriate amount of violence.

We also know from reports about the series bible and its proposed episodes that the "Jurassic Park" cartoon would have been serialized, with each episode building up to the next and the first season ending with the rival park opening. That's a quite approach surprising for 1993, when serialization was virtually unheard of in animation.

Though the series never made it to production, we eventually did get a "Jurassic Park" cartoon (seen in the photo above), and it remains the best sequel to that original movie.
