#3492. These Are Lifehacker's First-Ever 'Gift of the Year' Award Winners

Maybe this is the year your spouse finally wants to ditch physical books and embrace the e-reader; or maybe you want to help make your parent's home a little smarter. As the gift-giving season approaches, Lifehacker's staff of tech experts and product reviewers has selected our inaugural Gift of the Year winners across 15 categories. From smartphones, tablets, and e-readers to fitness trackers, gaming equipment, power tools, and more, these are the items we think are the most gift-worthy in 2026.

And while you're shopping, Lifehacker's sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at CNET, PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET, and Popular Science.

If you’re buying a smartphone for someone on your list, you have no shortage of options. But for most giftees out there, the iPhone 17e is the best choice. This isn’t the best iPhone, but that’s the point. For a starting price of $699, you get an iPhone with a high-quality display, a solid single rear camera, and Apple’s A19 chip, the second-best processor the company currently makes. You sacrifice some features here, like a high-refresh-rate display, higher-quality cameras, and a faster USB-C port, but those things won’t matter to most. The majority of us want an iPhone that can take great photos, send iMessages, take FaceTime calls, and run our favorite apps. The 17e can do that, without the exorbitant price tags of Apple’s more premium iPhones. If your giftee needs an Android, that’s a different conversation, but for Apple fans, or the platform-agnostic in your life, the 17e makes a great smartphone gift.

Apple’s best iPad for most people is the one simply called the “iPad.” This tablet, sometimes called the “iPad A16” or “iPad (11th generation),” comes with all the features you’d expect from an Apple tablet. It has a solid 11-inch display, Apple’s A16 chip to run iPadOS 27, a camera on the back for scanning documents and light photography, a camera on the front for video calls, and the option to use an Apple Pencil if you wish. It’s compatible with all of the apps on the App Store, and it can handle almost every iPadOS feature Apple makes—minus Apple Intelligence, but that might be a perk for some. While it’s far from Apple’s best iPad, it’s really the best for most people—that’s why it’s our pick for the best tablet to gift.

Our pick for the year's most desirable gift for readers isn't one of Amazon's slick new Kindles, but a tiny, 4.3-inch Chinese import that can pack hundreds of books into a device not much bigger than your library card. The Xteink X4 Pro may have a funny name and a form factor that suggests an e-reader left too long in the dryer, but it's packed with features, including a touchscreen and a temperature-adjustable front light, that belie its $99 list price ($50 less than the cheapest Kindle). Sure, there's a learning curve involved (the native firmware is merely fine, but easily replaced with a crowdsourced alternative developed by a community of online fans), and it won't work with your existing library of Kindle books. But once you've gotten it set up, you'll realize its biggest benefit: It's small enough to fit into any pocket—or even magnetically attach to the back of your phone—so you can easily carry it with you everywhere, and read instead of doomscrolling. After all, the best e-reader is the one you actually use.

Picking headphones for someone can be tricky. Some people love long battery life; others are just looking for whatever pair offers the most features. At the end of the day, price is what sets the best headphones apart from the rest. However, there is one outlier that offers a great value for the money and does well enough in most categories to make most people feel like they're upgrading: the Sony ULT WEAR headphones. At their new low price, there is no other pair of headphones that offers better quality active noise cancellation, app experience, comfort, battery life, and audio quality with LDAC support for Android devices. Not to mention the ULT button, which has two levels of extra bass that will have heads rattling like they're front row at a concert.

If you’re looking to buy a smartwatch for someone in your life and you know they don’t have any strong preferences going in, the Apple Watch SE is likely the best choice for you. It might not be Apple’s most powerful smartwatch, nor does it have the biggest, brightest display, but it does just about everything you’d expect an Apple Watch to do. It pings you with your iPhone notifications, tracks workouts and sleep, and lets you send and receive texts. It has the previous-generation S10 chip, which is plenty of power for watchOS (including Apple Intelligence), and Apple should support it for years to come. You can spend more to get more features on watches like the Series 12 or Ultra 4, but for most, the SE is all the Apple Watch you’ll ever need. And, if your giftee wants the cellular option, the SE can connect to 5G, just like Apple's more expensive watches.

These relatively inexpensive display-style glasses have that Christmas morning "woah" factor: Once the recipient plugs them into any device with USB-C video, they will instantly see a virtual display that's the equivalent of a 147-inch TV at 1080p. They’re particularly good for frequent travelers and dorm-dwellers who can’t agree on what to watch, but really, they're for anyone on your list who likes to play games, watch movies, or use their computer. (So, basically everyone.)

Buying a smart home gift is a tall order. There are so many different categories to choose from, and, within each, there are many considerations to keep in mind, like platform compatibility, feature set, and price. That’s why I think the Amazon Echo Dot Max is the best smart home gift of 2026. It supports a variety of smart home platforms, including Zigbee, Matter, Thread, and Alexa. That way, your giftee can likely connect the Echo Dot Max to most, if not all, of their existing smart home devices, as well as future devices they may pick up. It’s also one of Amazon’s better smart speakers: It isn’t as small as the Echo Dot, so it’s able to fill your room with sound, but it’s also not as expensive as the Echo Studio. It’s a great balance at this price, considering the versatility it offers as a smart home hub.

No single gift will please every gamer, but the Steam Deck comes close. This device blurs all the lines in gaming: It’s a PC that’s the size of a handheld, and it plugs into your television like a console. Fans of gaming on the go will love the portability and the touchscreen. Console gamers will love the friendly user interface, thumbstick controllers, and finally getting the chance to play “PC exclusive” games. PC gamers will love being able to move away from their desks and play video games on the couch or at a bus stop for a change. The Steam Deck is a win-win-win.

You’re probably not going to buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can buy the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing your watching and gaming is the mission of the Philips Hue Play Sync Box. It’s a middleman between a TV and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for making gaming more immersive, and it also improves just watching TV by projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals. The result is the illusion of a larger screen and a very cool special effect.

If you work out at home, investing in some adjustable dumbbells is a no-brainer, and you'd be hard-pressed to find a "best home dumbbells" list without the PowerBlock Elite Adjustable Dumbbells near the top. The futuristic cubic look is stylish, but more importantly, it's a seriously economical, space-saving design—which is the whole point of going adjustable over a traditional rack of individual weights. The weights have flat edges so you can hold them on end on your lap, and unlike a lot of adjustable models, they're compact enough that they won’t bump into each other on shoulder or chest presses.

Fitness trackers come in many forms, including watches, rings, and smart bands. I have favorites in every category, but when it comes to the overall best fitness tracker for most people, the Fitbit Air is the clear winner. It does all the essentials without a subscription, including step tracking, sleep tracking, and automatic workout detection. Its battery lasts a week, and your giftee will have the option to either use the new Google Health app (which I mostly like) or bypass it and use a third-party app like Bevel. More importantly, it's a fraction of the cost of any other tracker out there, so it's a lot more likely to fit your gifting budget than something like an Oura ring.

If you gift a subscription to Bespoke Post, you’re giving the chance to open a different gift every month, like Christmas is lasting all year. Unlike some hyper-niche gift services, Bespoke Post lets users customize their loot boxes: One month, they can choose an outdoorsy vibe, and the next, go for a high-end coffee collection. They can even skip a month if they don’t like what’s on offer. This is an essential gift subscription for anyone buying a present for a hard-to-shop-for dude.

Makita invented cordless drills in 1978, and it has been known for making quality drills ever since. Its new 18-volt LXT combo set is even better than its predecessors because it has a longer battery life with improvements to motor control, overheating, and dust and particulates. The drill has about 70% more power than previous models, allowing you to drill into tough materials like pressure-treated lumber more easily, and the impact driver has a three-speed control, allowing you to adjust the power to match the material you’re driving fasteners into. Since a drill and driver are the foundation of a cordless tool kit, this set, which offers better battery life and more power, stands out—it comes with two batteries, a charger, and a tool bag.

Buying a kitchen gift can be challenging because our kitchens are so personal—some of us know what a braiser is, and some of us keep shoes in our ovens. No matter who you’re shopping for, the Our Place Wonder Oven is the perfect gift. This countertop appliance combines six functions into one stylish unit with a small footprint. If the recipient has a small kitchen, they will love it for its compact nature and for the way it replaces at least three other countertop appliances (a toaster, an air fryer, and a convection oven), clearing space. If the person on your shopping list is an accomplished cook or always busy feeding a family, they’ll love it because it makes preparing fast, casual, and healthy meals a breeze without having to fire up that six-burner behemoth and use 16 pans. It can air-fry, bake, roast, toast, broil, and reheat with aplomb, and it sports an amazing steam infusion feature that makes everything come out moist—even those undated leftovers you pulled out of the freezer in desperation. It also comes with everything you’ll need to start cooking: a wire rack, air fry basket, bake pan, and crumb tray are all included. Did we mention it just looks cool?

A lot of tech might be expensive these days, but that doesn’t mean all of it is. In fact, there are plenty of excellent gadgets you can buy friends and family for $50 or less. Our favorite option in this category is the JBL Go 4. This portable Bluetooth speaker is small but mighty, able to get quite loud for such a tiny device. You’ll get seven hours of playback on one charge, plus an extra two hours with “Playback Boost” enabled. The Go 4 has an IP67 rating against dust and water, so you can bring the speaker with you outdoors without worrying about ruining it. If your friends have JBL speakers of their own, not just Go 4s, you can connect them all together for a quick multi-speaker setup. It really is a versatile device, especially when you consider both its size and its price. The JBL Go 4 makes for a great stocking stuffer, Yankee Swap contribution, or gift for anyone looking for a portable speaker for home or on-the-go use.

#3490. Everything Coming to Prime Video in November 2026

Sports fans can catch the four Friday night doubleheaders from November 6 through 27 featuring Emirates NBA Cup 2026 Group Play action, as well as Thursday Night Football. If you want sports with some added drama and fun acting, look out for Nicolas Cage as John Madden when the Madden biopic makes its way to the streaming platform this month. And finally, the most-anticipated sci-fi event of the year that Prime Video and fans have been waiting for, Blade Runner 2099 will surely take your breath away. There’s a lot to look forward to, so here’s your guide to everything coming to Prime Video in November 2026.

The first-ever television production in The Lord of the Rings franchise, The Rings of Power serves as a prequel to The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings film trilogy and is adapted from J.R.R. Tolkien’s extensive history of Middle-earth, drawn from the appendices of The Lord of the Rings. Set during a time of relative peace, the series covers major events from Middle-earth’s Second Age, including the forging of the legendary rings and Sauron’s rise to power as the new Dark Lord. Morfydd Clark, Robert Aramayo, Benjamin Walker, Ismael Cruz Córdova, and Daniel Weyman reprise their roles for Season 3, with Jamie Campbell Bower, Eddie Marsan, and Simon Pegg as new characters.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has thrilled fans with its opulent production ever since its premiere in 2022. The first and second seasons were highly praised for their earnest tribute to Tolkien’s universe and the innovative expansion of the history of Middle-earth. Rings of Power Season 3 is set five years after the fall of Eregion during the War of the Elves and Sauron, when Sauron secretly begins to craft his weapon of ultimate power that would give him final victory over all Middle-earth.

Inspired by the life and work of American football coach and commentator John Madden, Madden is an all-new biographical sports drama directed and co-produced by David O. Russell. Starring Nicolas Cage as the titular legend, the film chronicles his journey from a Super Bowl-winning partnership with Al Davis and the Oakland Raiders to becoming football's most recognizable voice and building the worldwide Madden NFL video game series. Christian Bale, Kathryn Hahn, John Mulaney, Sienna Miller, and Shane Gillis star as other real-life personalities.

Described officially as “a celebration of a brilliant mind whose once-in-a-century spirit and personality, partnership with his daring wife Virginia, lifelong friendships, and infectious love of people and football transcended the world of sports,” Madden is a must-watch for sports fans. The Pro Football Hall of Fame NFL coach and sports commentator is one of the most recognizable figures in football history and a beloved icon who famously never had a losing season and has won 16 Sports Emmy Awards. Madden will make its streaming premiere on Prime Video on November 18, following its theatrical release on November 11, 2026.

Created by Ben Watkins and produced by Lonnie Ali and Michael B. Jordan, The Greatest is the first-ever authorized scripted series about Muhammad Ali, presenting an intimate exploration of his phenomenal life as a boxer, humanitarian, and global icon. Jaleen Best stars as the titular legend (who fans might recognize from All American: Homecoming), while showrunner Watkins is best known for creating shows like Hand of God and Cross. The series also stars Omari Hardwick, Dana Gourrier, Kai Parham, and Amin Joseph as main characters, with Michael Ealy and Giovanni Ribisi in recurring roles.

Since his landmark gold medal win at the 1960 Olympics, Muhammad Ali has been the subject of several feature films, TV shows, animated TV series, and over a dozen major documentary films and TV specials. But the Prime Video original is special for touching upon his personal life and candid moments. The eight-episode limited series not only traces his journey from Cassius Clay to Muhammad Ali, but also looks at his life beyond the fame and fortune and depicts him as a son, brother, husband, and father.

The latest installment in the Blade Runner franchise, Blade Runner 2099 is a direct sequel to Denis Villeneuve's Blade Runner 2049 and Ridley Scott’s Blade Runner, all of which are based on Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?. The miniseries is set 50 years after the events of the 2017 film and focuses on Olwen, an aging Replicant Blade Runner, and her mysterious partner, Cora, a human pretending to be a replicant, who are tasked with hunting down a gang of rogue Replicants. Michelle Yeoh stars as Olwen and Hunter Schafer plays Cora, with Dimitri Abold and Lewis Gribben as other main characters.

Between 1982 and now, Blade Runner has grown into a robust cyberpunk media franchise that includes two feature films, three shorts, an animated series, and several games. Created by Silka Luisa and produced by Ridley Scott, Blade Runner 2099 is one of the most anticipated sci-fi shows of 2026 and the second TV series in the titular franchise following 2021’s Blade Runner: Black Lotus. As revealed in the trailer, the upcoming miniseries shares the core atmosphere, textures, and grungy world-building established by Ridley Scott in the 1982 film but features higher stakes and a major shift in the power dynamic between humans and replicants.

Directed by Nanette Burstein, The Boy Who Stole Billions? is a deep-dive documentary series about Sam Bankman-Fried and the collapse of his $32 billion cryptocurrency empire, FTX. The three-part series delves into one of the biggest frauds in U.S. history with unprecedented access and exclusive firsthand accounts from Sam Bankman-Fried himself, provided during his prison sentence. The documentary also features never-before-seen interviews with various other figures involved with Bankman in his personal life and business, including his co-CEO and former girlfriend, Caroline Ellison.

Founded in 2019 by Bankman-Fried and Gary Wang, FTX became a major crypto exchange in its short-lived existence before collapsing in 2022 due to a major financial fraud. Bankman-Fried and his fintech empire have also been the subject of Ben MacKenzie’s 2025 documentary Everyone Is Lying to You for Money and a segment on 60 Minutes. A close-up look at the rise and fall of the poster boy of cryptocurrency, The Boy Who Stole Billions? has been described as “a series that will surprise many, bringing audiences closer to the people behind the headlines and opening up Sam's world in ways it has never been seen before.”

#3489. Where The Rings Of Power Fits Into The Middle-earth Timeline

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power explores a different point in Middle-earth history than past screen adaptations of Tolkien's work. While Frodo's story in The Lord of the Rings is at the foundation of the overall franchise, it is set at the tail end of a timeline over 60,000 years long. The Rings of Power is also set in this timeline, but several thousand years before the One Ring ever fell into the hands of Hobbits. Understanding precisely how all this fits together gets a little more complicated since Prime Video has made some changes to Tolkien's Middle-earth timeline.

The events of The Rings of Power are based on the various works that Tolkien constructed to outline the lore of The Lord of the Rings. This includes the appendices of The Return of the King, as well as posthumously published books like The Silmarillion and Unfinished Tales of Numenor and Middle-earth. The stories within begin at the very beginning of time and the creation of the universe and span all the way through tens of thousands of years, through the First, Second, and Third Ages of Middle-earth. Prime Video's The Rings of Power is set somewhere in the middle of all this.

The Rings of Power is set during the Second Age of Middle-earth, a period in Tolkien's timeline that spanned 3,441 years. It followed the First Age, an approximately 6,000-year period, and preceded the Third Age, a 3,021-year period. Since Prime Video's series is predominantly about Sauron's Rings of Power, and these were created in the year SA 1500, this is approximately when The Rings of Power season 1 and season 2 are set. This means the events of the series take place about 7,500 years after the start of the First Age and 4,959 years before Frodo leaves the Shire in The Lord of the Rings.

The beginning of Rings of Power season 1 featured moments from the First Age, when the Dark Lord Morgoth was the central antagonist of Middle-earth.

While Sauron made his Rings of Power in SA 1500, the timeline for Rings of Power is a little more complicated than just this. For example, Isildur, the future king of Gondor, isn't born until SA 3209, over a thousand years after Sauron's deception at Eregion. Prime Video condensed the timeline, making Isildur a young man when Sauron forges the Rings of Power in season 2. This was necessary because it would have been difficult to cover the stories of the mortals and immortals of Middle-earth at the same time.

Rings of Power has also done things out of order. Sauron's story is the foundation of the series, and Rings of Power season 1 covered his actions between about SA 50 and SA 1500. However, Pharazôn taking power and the downfall of Numenor didn't happen until around SA 3261 and SA 3319, both events that have been teased to be on the way in Rings of Power.

Second Age Events Relevant To Rings Of Power Seasons 1 & 2

Future seasons of Rings of Power are sure to dive into the Last Alliance of Elves and Men, which forms in SA 3430, as well as the Battle of Dagorlad, which is when Sauron is destroyed and the One Ring claimed by Isildur. This will likely happen sometime near the end of the Prime Video series, but it's certainly possible that Rings of Power will take things forward into the Third Age of Middle-earth.

The Third Age kicks off right after Sauron's downfall, and this period in Middle-earth's timeline sees a lot of important development for the characters of The Rings of Power. Isildur becomes king of Gondor, Elrond marries Celebrian (Galadriel's daughter), and Gandalf the Gray makes his official arrival in Middle-earth (though Rings of Power has moved that up with the Stranger). It's certainly possible that Rings of Power will carry on into this period, exploring Isildur's decline to the One Ring and the dwindling of Sauron's remaining Rings of Power in Middle-earth. Only time will tell.

#3488. How to Make IndieWire a Preferred Source on Google

Do you rely on IndieWire‘s film and TV coverage? If so, please consider taking a moment to ensure you never miss an important story via Google‘s new Preferred Sources feature.

Choosing IndieWire as a preferred source ensures that Google will prioritize IndieWire stories in all of your queries, including traditional searches, Discover, and AI Overviews. Whether you’re searching for movie release dates, TV recommendations, or the latest breaking news, you’ll have access to IndieWire’s reporting and analysis.

If you want to add IndieWire as one of your preferred sources, you can either click this link, click the “Add Us As a Preferred Google Source” button at the top of this article, or manually adjust your preferences by following the instructions below.

First, head to Google.com and search for any entertainment topic. A movie, a TV show, or a film festival will all work perfectly.

Head to the “Top Stories” section of your results that links to news websites. In the top right corner, you’ll see a starred icon that says “Customize.” Click it.

Clicking the customize button will open a new search bar that asks you to type in your preferred sources. That’s where you can add IndieWire.

Once you’ve selected IndieWire as a preferred source, simply click the “Reload Results” button in the bottom right corner, and you’ll be all set!

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As Android Authority reports, Google typically doesn't personalize ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos by default. However, the policy now makes these data available for that purpose if you've connected these apps to other Google services—like Personal Intelligence—that do support personalized ads. Personal Intelligence is the opt-in Gemini feature launched earlier this year that links with other Google apps to give you more tailored, contextual responses in Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode.

Personal Intelligence is opt-in by default, but as Ars Technica points out, users are presented with opportunities to enable this feature and connect apps to it without realizing it or understanding the potential consequences of doing so.

If you remember the Festivas menu bar app from Mac year, Pumpkin Lights is very similar in concept.

Pumpkin Lights brings a jack-o-lantern to your menu bar, just in time for halloween. It’s a nice decoration, and there’s plenty of different ways to customize it. You can “grow” many different pumpkin designs, as well as pick between four different color variants.

When you click on the pumpkin or pull on it, your Mac will toggle between light and dark mode – at least by default. Pumpkin Lights also has the option to open an app/website, keep your Mac awake, mute a sound, run a command, or run a shortcut of your choice.

The jack-o-lantern does have proper physics, so you can actually toss it around a bit and move it around in a novel way. You can customize the rope it hangs from, and much more. There’s also an option to have a hanging light bulb that serves a similar purpose.

Why Pumpkin Lights? Here’s what the developer has to say:

The idea came from something most of us do every day without thinking: switching between Light and Dark Mode. It’s always a toggle buried in Control Center or System Settings, and it never feels like anything. I wanted it to feel like touching a real object. So instead of a flat icon, the pumpkin and the bulb are real 3D models, ray-traced in real time, hanging on cords you can swing and spin. When the candle lights, its glow comes through the carved face. I spent most of my time on small details like how the cords move and how light falls on the pumpkin, because I wanted it to still feel delightful the hundredth time you use it, not just the first.

Pumpkin Lights is a completely free utility. You can download it from the developer’s website here, and it’s available for any Mac running macOS 14 Sonoma or later. You can also follow the developer on Twitter.

#3484. To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release “Being Heumann” in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.]

After I watched Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in the weeks leading up to its world premiere as the opening night film at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, I had a long list of things to talk to the filmmaker about.

Curb cuts — those graded concrete ramps at the edge of sidewalk corners that allow anyone and anything with wheels to glide gently onto the street below — aren’t really the sort of thing most people think about. But if you need them, if you’re in a wheelchair or pushing a stroller or dragging a heavy suitcase, they’re tough not to think about. It’s hard to jump off a curb if you can’t, well, jump. At best, you need help. At worst, you just can’t do it. Related Stories How to Make IndieWire a Preferred Source on Google Taika Waititi’s Delusional ‘Klara and the Sun’ Instagram Post Exemplifies the Dangers of a Growing Divide Between Critics and Artists in the Digital Age

Starring British actress Ruth Madeley as the iconic activist Judith Heumann, “Being Heumann” wastes no time putting our star in the middle of a busy New York City street, with not a curb cut to be seen. She doesn’t really have a choice. A wheelchair user for most of her life (Heumann contracted polio as a toddler), Heumann grew into the “Mother of the Disability Rights Movement,” and the film finds her at an important crossroads.

First, she needs to be able to navigate the world around her, which was simply not built for her. No curb cuts.

But things are changing. When the film begins, the first U.S. federal civil rights protection for people with disabilities, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, has been signed, but no one is putting it into actual action. Heumann set out to change that. The film jumps ahead four years, following Heumann as she leads hundreds of fellow activists and disabled people into a massive protest, including a historic sit-in in the San Francisco Federal Building that lasted a month.

It’s real history, but it’s also rousing and funny and entertaining. And deeply human.

It is, of course, very similar to Heder’s previous film, “CODA,” which followed a deaf family and their one hearing child as they navigated a world not built for them. The film premiered at the 2021 Sundance Film Festival, where it proved to be a huge crowdpleaser (no easy feat, as that edition of the festival was held entirely online). A year later, it won Best Picture, changing Heder’s life forever.

After her big Oscar win, Heder had some immediate needs to meet. “I had worn these high heels for so many hours the night of the Oscars that my toes went numb, and it took maybe two months to come back to life and have feeling in my toes again,” she told IndieWire with a laugh. “But there was a moment of recovery, not just from the energy that it took to go through an awards campaign, to do a Q&A every night, to fly all over the world with the movie, but also the adrenaline leaving your body, which was a very intense feeling.”

Choosing what project she’d take on next was also top of mind for Heder, who admitted that it took awhile for her to get back into the process of actually creating after spending more than a year sharing “CODA” with the world. That was intense, too.

“It’s shocking moment as a filmmaker, because suddenly there’s a bunch of eyes on you that were never there before,” she said. “‘What are you going to do next?’ and ‘How are you going to follow that up?’ It took some time for me to tap back into why I tell stories and what moves me. I developed a lot of projects. I had maybe five different movies that I was developing or writing or overseeing a writer on and didn’t really know which one would come together first.”

And then there was “Being Heumann,” which Heder has been working on in earnest for about five years. She first met Heumann at Sundance in 2021, when Nicole Newnham and James LeBrecht’s documentary “Crip Camp” premiered, in which the irrepressible Heumann appeared as a young woman. (Heder also co- wrote the script alongside Rebekah Taussig, based on Heumann’s autobiography.)

“It was before ‘CODA’ had come out, it was before I had taken the whole Oscar ride,” Heder said. “I had been drawn to this story because it was a great story, long before I was thinking about what’s the right move in the industry or how do you follow up a film that goes on to do [win Best Picture]. It was just very close to my heart.”

There was also Judy Heumann. Heder said she knew from her very first meeting with Heumann that she wanted to make a film about her. She hadn’t even been aware of Heumann until she saw the documentary, and then? She couldn’t take her eyes off her.

“There’s a scene where she’s yelling about lasagna in the cafeteria at summer camp, and I was like, ‘Who is this woman?’ She looked like she was conducting a senate hearing, but she’s talking about what they’re going to have for dinner,” Heder said. “I was very intrigued by her as a character, but I felt like there was a deadly version of this story, which would’ve been a traditional biopic.”

Heder had been working with Heumann for nearly two years before Heumann died in March 2023. Heder said she had a “a very strong feeling that Judy died having chosen me to make this movie and tell the story, and so there was a sense of responsibility to her and her legacy.”

There was also, by her own telling, “a little bit of fear of, if I follow up ‘CODA’ with another film that’s about disability, are people going to put me in that box? But after ‘CODA,’ I had a rare moment of power in the industry where a lot of people wanted to make what I wanted to make. There was a moment where I could have used that capital to go make a Marvel movie and get a big paycheck and move out of my small home in Eagle Rock or use the capital to try to tell the hardest story I could imagine trying to tell and probably a film that not a lot of people would’ve financed or gotten behind.”

She went with the latter. “I knew it was going to be an all-disabled cast with a lot of new actors and without movie star names, and it was a period piece and it was more expensive than your average indie movie,” Heder said. “So it felt like if there was ever a moment that I could push it through to tell this story, that was the moment I was in.”

And while it was not an automatic yes from Apple, which also distributed “CODA,” Heder said, “They believed in the movie for sure, and they believe in me as a filmmaker. But, on paper, this movie is a challenging film.” Those challenges went beyond the already-daunting needs around casting.

“Yes, on one hand, it’s a story about a disability rights activist in the 1970s,” Heder said. “It was important to me that the film not feel like ‘eat your spinach’ or that it was not there to educate people on something important that they should know about. What I pitched to Apple is ‘I want to make “Dog Day Afternoon” with disabled people. I want to make a story that has a lot of momentum and humor.’ These people were building sex tents in the hallway, they were smoking pot, and the Black Panthers showed up! That’s a movie that I think will be fun to watch and joyful and entertaining. They understood not just that I was trying to tell the story, but the way I was trying to tell it.”

While Heder eschewed any “eat your spinach” angles, she’s still very passionate about sharing the incredible impact of Heumann’s work in the disabled community. “Most disabled people at the time didn’t even really understand that they could demand to be a part of society or demand equal rights,” Heder said. “There was a feeling of, ‘Well, your body is broken, so you don’t deserve to leave your house,’ and I think a lot of people had internalized that, and Judy awakened that understanding in a lot of people.”

Judy Heumann’s story also awakened a different understanding in Heder herself. The film doesn’t canonize Heumann, instead showing her as dedicated leader who is also prickly, brash, and set in her ways. Heder didn’t just want to tell a story about a leader, but what it actually takes to be a leader and continue growing in that role.

“There are so many tropes around disability, so the idea of meeting this young person who feels invisible and finds her voice and becomes an activist and comes into her power was the more expected story,” the filmmaker said. “But meeting someone who is at the height of their power, who has this radical empathy where she’s fighting for people to be seen and heard, and yet has a really hard time seeing and hearing and including other people, was a much more interesting character arc. On one hand, Judy is fighting for this group of people to be seen as human. But being a human on a very basic, connective level? Saying thank you to the people who are helping you, being kind, putting the people first? That was also a journey Judy had to go on.”

There’s a moment in the third act of the film when Judy is unable to physically be at the San Francisco sit-in. She not only has to trust that the more soft-spoken Kitty Cone (Madeline Delp), who has become her closest confidant, can keep the sit-in going in her absence, but she must also say that to her. You can see how hard that is for her, but how revelatory, too.

“I do think, as a director — and not to say ‘woman director,’ because I hate constantly qualifying director with my gender — there was a feeling when I started out as a young woman that I had to always have the answers, always seem in control and I knew what I was doing because if I expressed any self-doubt or any waffling, it would be perceived as ‘she doesn’t know what she’s doing,’” Heder said. “It took me a long time to get comfortable enough with my skillset, with my ability to be on a set, and go, ‘I actually don’t know. I actually don’t know where we should put the camera right now. What do you think?’”

Casting that kind of powerful person to portray Judy was charged on many levels. There was no question that Heder would find a disabled actress, but how do you cast someone to be Judith Heumann, so naturally without peer? Heder had worked with the real Judy for years. She knew all the important people in her life.

“There was an intimacy that you almost never have with your lead character,” Heder said. “Yes, Judy was a wheelchair user, but that was one element of her identity. It was also about Judy’s blunt sense of humor, Judy’s directness, Judy’s drive, Judy’s sense of humor, and all of those qualities were things that I was looking for. It was trying to find someone that physically resembled her, who also could embody her energy, which was very specific.”

She likes to joke that her casting directors, Bernie Telsey and Adam Caldwell, had to take on the “casting Olympics, because every character was a unicorn.” “I was like, ‘Hey, go find me a 19-year-old Black blind man who can sing, who has this relentless optimism and just embodies Dennis Billups,’” Heder said with a laugh. (They did, with first-time actor Charlie Rush-Reese, a gem in a sea of them.)

She found Madeley in a slightly different way. “I was working with a deck designer to put images together when I was trying to get the movie greenlit at Apple, and he was British, and he said, ‘This character really reminds me of this actress, Ruth Madeley. Do you know her work?,’” she said. “I didn’t know her, but she was in this film called ‘Then Barbara Met Alan,’ and I watched the film and I could see exactly what he was talking about. She has an earthy, wry humor, and she exudes intelligence and has this big well of emotion and vulnerability.”

Still, Heder said with a laugh, she didn’t make it easy on Madeley. “Ruth had done so much work before I ever met her, but I put her through the ringer. I auditioned her many times,” Heder said. “I saw many, many actors for that role, and she truly won that part. I knew it was going to be an incredibly difficult film to make, and I felt I really had a partner with her. Even aside from performance, which is the most important thing, having a true collaborator in your lead actor is invaluable as a director.”

Heder’s film is filled with incredible star turns by a number of new (and, in some cases, brand-new) performers. Among their ranks is, however, one very recognizable name: Mark Ruffalo, cast here as Joseph Califano, the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. He’s the guy who needs to sign the meaningful regulations that would put 504 into actual action. And, for most of the film’s running time, he refuses to do it. He’s the bad guy of the story, sort of, and to have an outspoken activist like Ruffalo in that role adds real dimension to the part.

“Mark is someone who has been unafraid in his life to be principled and stand by those principles, whatever the cost,” Heder said. “And Califano was someone who really considered himself a good guy and had, throughout his career, protected the Selma March, pushed forth the Great Society Program, had stood with the students at Kent State, and really felt like ‘I’m on the right side of history.’”

When the film begins, he has just started to work for President Jimmy Carter, and the pressure is on. The president gave Califano a strict mandate: cut the federal budget by $3 billion. He was less than three months into his job when the sit-ins began. The moment he signed the 504 regulations, he’d have 60 days to enact the necessary changes to meet its requirements. And they would cost $3 billion.

“The more I read about Califano, the more I felt like you could tell this story from his perspective, you could absolutely understand that he was between a rock and a hard place, but that’s when people’s principles are actually tested,” Heder said. “In my first meeting with Mark, he was talking about fear, and there are a lot of politicians now who are living in a state of fear, whether it’s their reelection, whether it’s losing money that backs their campaign or offending lobbyists or constituents.”

She added, “The reality is, the movie is not speaking to a mustache-twirling villain who is out to make life hard for disabled people, it’s speaking to the good guys who are stuck in inaction because it feels too hard or too scary. That’s very timely for me, because we all have something to protect that you risk by going out on a limb and announcing what you believe in. There’s a lot of fear right now, and we see it real time, and so there are actual repercussions to speaking up and standing by your morals.”

Inaction isn’t Heder’s bag. In making a film like “Being Heumann,” which is literally about the fight for accessibility, there was no question she had to build a production that was comfortable, creative, and open for all. That didn’t scare her. Why should it? It’s attainable.

“With ‘CODA,’ we were trying to make a set accessible to a deaf cast, which was one very specific thing, and so it was about communication and ‘where do we put interpreters?’ and ‘how do I call action and how do I call cut?,'” she said. “But it was all working toward meeting a very specific set of needs on this movie because it was cross-disability. Someone who is paraplegic has very different needs than someone who is an ambulatory wheelchair user versus someone who lives in chronic pain. It was about making a set that is accessible to a deaf cast at the same time that you’re making that set accessible to a blind actor. And we didn’t know what we didn’t know.”

Heder and her crew had to figure out how to navigate everything from ramps to scripts. How do you do a table read with a blind actor? How do you do ADR when they can’t see their own mouth moving? How many braille scripts do you need? Will audio earpieces help? How many interpreters need to be there for the deaf performers?

“At every stage of the process, we were coming up against these hurdles that were unexpected, even though we had built an accessibility team and we had really done our best to do intake forms for every actor to understand what their needs were on set,” Heder said. “A lot of our cast had never been in a movie before, or some of them were non-actors and so didn’t even know to ask, didn’t even know what they would need to ask, because it’s very different to say, ‘Yes, I’m fine in a vintage wheelchair, but are you fine in a vintage wheelchair for 12 hours?’ Because that’s what a movie set is. There was a lot of real time adjusting that had to happen and problem-solving in the moment. It never stopped.”

Heder is clear, however: this was worth it. “I never want people to take from this at all that it is too hard to work with a disabled actor, I think it’s about knowing what you need,” she said. “Once we figured out what people needed, it really did flow and run as any other set would. It was just a learning curve figuring out what those accommodations were. Judy impulsively led a hundred disabled people into this federal building, many of whom went in without their attendants or their caregivers and then had to figure out how to survive in this building over this 30 days. They all had to find their superpower in their own disability.”

The challenges they faced (and overcame) also helped align them with what Judy Heumann and the rest of the protestors felt during the sit-in. “When I interviewed Dennis Billups, who is blind, he said he was standing lost outside the protest, and he offered to push a wheelchair user if they would guide him into the building,” Heder said. “There was all of this interdependence that started to happen in the protest that was about survival, and that happened in real life on our set, where our cast started jumping in to fill each other’s needs in a way that is very hard to describe and was incredibly profound.”

I mentioned how touching it is to see the way that Heder shows that on the screen, that everyone is useful and that everyone has something that they can do, when she added a compelling corollary. “Not only is everyone useful, but everyone needs help,” Heder said. “Everyone needs help. It’s not just the disabled cast that needed help. There were moments where my non-disabled cast needed help, and there were moments where people on the crew needed help.”

She continued, “It’s like the same way when I was a new mom and I was pushing a stroller around the city, ‘thank God for curb cuts,’ or getting off the subway in New York City and having to lug a stroller up the stairs, ‘thank God for the elevator.’ We all have these moments where you understand that accessibility helps everybody. We built ramps onto our set from every direction, and the grips were like, ‘Thank you. We are lugging thousands of pounds of equipment, and this is the first set I’ve been on where there are ramps everywhere you look, and we can wheel that stuff up.'”

It’s the exact lesson we see in the film, and one that people still need to be reminded of: we can make the world a better place for everyone, but we have to work together.

“I remember there being a big scandal or pushback when there were directors who came out and said, ‘I don’t allow chairs on my set,’ and what you are saying through that,” Heder said. “I understand the intention, which is ‘I want people committed and energized and not kicking back and not participating.’ However, you are also saying that you are not inviting anybody onto your set that cannot stand for 12 hours. … When you refuse to provide any accommodations, you are shutting off an avenue to so much talent and creativity.”

Heder added, “That was the thing I really felt more than anything on this. It was profound to me that what Judy did with these protestors, how this group of people physically changed our world. It’s things that we all take for granted, now that there are curb cuts or Zoom or FaceTime or even texting. All of these moments of innovation came out of inclusiveness that are now accepted as our reality.”

“Being Heumann” will premiere at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.

#3482. Here’s how the new MacBook Pro and macOS 27 are optimized for touch

Apple just unveiled the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, its first MacBook with a touch display. While Apple already added a handful of touch optimizations to macOS 27 Golden Gate earlier this year, there’s also a number of new optimizations that were unveiled alongside the new MacBook Pro. Here’s what Apple worked on.

With the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, the traffic light icons in the top left of an app window will get bigger when you’re tapping them, making the touch targets a little bit larger.

Gestures that you can normally perform on the trackpad can also be performed on the screen. Whether that be a three-finger swipe up for mission control, three-finger swipes to switch spaces, pinching to zoom, or scrolling on a web page. You can also access Spotlight from the Dynamic Island, similar to how iPhones handle it on iOS 27.

If you’re an app developer, you’ll really appreciate this change: with the new MacBook Pro, you can fully navigate the iOS simulator with touch. No need to try to replicate touch gestures on a trackpad.

When you interact with a context menu in the menu bar, each of the items within a menu will get a little bit larger for touch. Additionally, most optimized apps will have larger touch targets, even if the buttons don’t necessarily appear bigger.

All in all, there’s a handful of optimizations already in macOS 27 Golden Gate for the touchscreen MacBook Pro. On top of what was named here, Apple also added pull to refresh in Safari and slightly larger spacing between menu bar items to all Macs with macOS 27.

Yeeeeeeeah no. Interactions with any of the onscreen elements are incredibly tedious, sporadic, and glitchy. This isn’t the company Steve Jobs started, it’s just Microsoft with an Apple logo.

Apple also says there’s more to come on the Mac when it comes to touch optimizations, so we’ll likely see much more in store at the next WWDC.

What do you think about touch support on the new MacBook Pro? Are you looking forward to it eventually trickling down to every Mac? Let us know in the comments.

The film is none other than Cliffhanger, which, ironically, doesn’t end on one. #3479. Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch

You too, Netflix? Netflix’s whole thing has been that its algorithm was designed in such a way that it knows what you’ll want to watch, that even small shows with no hype or stars like “Baby Reindeer,” “Adolescence,” “Squid Game,” “Ginny and Georgia,” or even “Stranger Things” once upon a time can turn into massive, organic hits. They call it the “Netflix Effect” for a reason.

But even Netflix has had trouble keeping people consistently engaged and in getting them to find that next show or film. Last month it overhauled its creative leads to meet that challenge, so it is turning to where so many other companies have turned to shake things up: AI. Related Stories To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’

Netflix today launched AI Discover, which is a new tab on the streamer’s TV app where you can ask an AI assistant to help you narrow down a selection based on what you say you’re in the mood to watch. Fortunately Netflix didn’t do the Meta thing and come up with some cuddly meeple to be your virtual assistant.

The tool is built around themes, in which you select from a range of themes, each of which is previewed via a clip from a show or movie. You can say I want to watch “Something Light” or “Scare Me” or ask for something for families, something that’s popular, or something quick, to name a few options. The AI will give you recommendations, it will allow you to refine your selections further and you can continue doom scrolling, and you can finally “Tune Your Recommendations” to either keep a recommendation or tell the AI to not recommend it again.

What this is not is an AI chat bot. You don’t even type anything into it (TV remotes are sometimes hard for that), just pick from some pre-selected options until you get what you want. The AI also though won’t be available on kids profiles, for now it’s not available on mobile, just TVs, and the data collected won’t be used to inform future content decisions for what Netflix produces.

While this could be seen as just a fancy new search function with an AI label, Netflix clarifies that this is new tech they’ve been building with a predictive intelligence model that responds in real time and continues learning based on your preferences. It’s a function on top of the existing search that’s a bit more refined.

For now, AI Discover is only available for a handful of U.S. members who are using it in English and on supported TVs, but it’ll open wider in the coming weeks. The AI Discover function is indicated with a red gem icon and a “New” label on the top of your screen.

#3477. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

#3475. Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. A24 will release “Club Kid” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

The official Cannes synopsis for “Club Kid” is almost suspiciously vague: “A washed-up party promoter is forced to turn his life around when an unexpected visitor arrives.” Hmm…

Technically, that’s true. But it’s also the kind of carefully evasive logline you can only use if you’re an artist as charismatic and cunning as Jordan Firstman. A writer, actor, singer, comedian, and now debut feature filmmaker, Firstman has spent years making audiences feel like they know everything about him without fully surrendering the parts of himself that might actually hurt. Related Stories Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’

“People have trouble metabolizing me for a lot of different reasons, ” Firstman told IndieWire, ahead of his dazzling feature film’s world premiere at the Cannes Film Festival on May 15. “I think I remind them of someone they know, but also someone they don’t know. Or someone who deserves things, but also someone they went to high school with who’s just an annoying gay guy. Perception is weird.”

For years, Firstman’s public persona has existed somewhere between chaotic queer oracle and self-aware caricature — whether through his hilariously unhinged Instagram comedy, his writing and acting work on shows like “Search Party,” “The Other Two,” and “I Love LA,” or his caustic self-portrayal in Sebastián Silva’s “Rotting in the Sun,” which debuted at Sundance in 2023.

“I wanted the thing I did after that to be a bit softer and more like a version of me that I knew, but other people didn’t,” Firstman said. “There was a lot on me in that movie in terms of persona and people thinking about me in a certain type of way.” (Suffice to say, Firstman spends much of “Rotting in the Sun” cartoonishly chasing attention and ketamine on the beach.)

The “Club Kid” filmmaker also wrote the viral Laura Dern tribute that was performed by the Gay Men’s Chorus of Los Angeles at the 2020 Spirit Awards (“Top five moments of my life,” Firstman joked), which helped carve out space for his unique voice in Hollywood. Sliding effortlessly from incisive observer to chaotic flirt to exhausting narcissist, Firstman is never not in on the joke. But it took until now for him to finally explore what happens when that cyclical sense of self-parody stops working as armor and starts feeling like a weight.

“I didn’t want to win anyone over anymore,” Firstman said of his mentality heading into this project. “All I could do was tell the story I wanted to tell in the way that I wanted to tell it.”

A funny and melancholy look at one man’s deep feelings of isolation, appropriately set against the fast-changing experience of modern queer nightlife, “Club Kid” stars Firstman as Peter, a gay New York party fixture whose chemically accelerated existence is interrupted by the sudden arrival of a child he never knew he had. That setup could easily lend itself to a broader (read: straighter) comedy, but Firstman’s soulful consideration of finding both family and purpose hits a much more sensitive frequency than that.

Not nearly as interested in punishing Peter for his messiness as it is in helping explain why he built his life this way in the first place, “Club Kid” draws a lot of its tension from the inherent conflict between the pursuit of shallow visibility and the fundamental need for more meaningful types of intimacy. The damage and acceptance that kind of internal contradiction can bring to a person over an extended period runs through every frame of Firstman’s film, and the result feels less like a conventional dramedy than a decade-long discovery unfolding in real time.

With a slick, feel-good opening scene that smartly orients the entire experience, “Club Kid” charts Peter’s evolution from the mid-2010s into the spiritually scorched present with merciless specificity.

“I remember that era was the start of Europe coming to America gay-wise,” Firstman said. “Dark rooms were not really a thing before that. It was Molly, and maybe some coke, and that was kind of it.” Then came COVID. “I said this famously in the pandemic, but it’s like, you take sex away from gay people for a month, and they’ll make up for it for the next five years.”

According to Firstman, as the substances changed in many American clubs, so did the emotional atmosphere surrounding some parts of LGBTQ culture. “In 2020 and 2021, K got really big. Then G started in 2022. Then, the last couple years, the Mephedrone, the 3MMC, and 4MMC,” he explained. “You look around, and you see zombies where it should be a community. And sometimes that still feels like your community? It just changed.”

The brilliance of “Club Kid” lies in Firstman’s refusal to flatten those realities into an easy morality. His film understands the air of danger, loneliness, and instability often inherent in queer spaces — while warmly demonstrating why countless people keep returning to them anyway. No one in Firstman’s script is reduced to a victim or cautionary tale, least of all Firstman. And in the end, even his harshest skeptics will struggle to shake the affection they’ll feel for a character who has spent years finding and losing himself under the same strobe lights.

“Even when you strip back the surface layer of the drugs and the afters going on all weekend, beneath it is a bunch of queer people who are funny and sensitive and broken in some ways and artistic and just fully whole,” Firstman said. “That’s what I wanted to show.”

The heart of “Club Kid” is in Peter’s relationship with his son, played by newcomer Reggie Absolom, whom Firstman discovered after watching hundreds of audition tapes out of London. “I remember seeing the thumbnail and being like, ‘Please be able to act, please be able to act, because that’s him,’” Firstman said. “Then I met him, and we went for ice cream and talked about music. I sent all the kids the playlist I wrote the movie to. Reggie loved Massive Attack.”

At several points throughout our conversation, Firstman became emotional discussing his kid scene partner and their film’s larger themes of innocence, queer identity, and the cruel impermanence of self-perception. One moment in particular, in which Reggie bonded with the movie’s ensemble cast of queer and trans performers, overwhelmed him.

“For the rest of his life now he’s going to love trans people because he got to see how funny and creative [they are], and listen to music with them and joke around with them,” Firstman said, trailing off emotionally. “I think that’s the beauty of this story.”

That softness feels revelatory coming from an artist who has so often weaponized irony and overstimulation as an entertainment strategy. Moments earlier, Firstman had been casually breaking down the social consequences of post-pandemic partying and joking about his “level of hotness.” Then, he was crying and discussing chosen family.

“Everything shows on me,” Firstman laughed, describing the quality as a “gift and a curse.” “Maybe people have complicated feelings toward me because I can’t really hide anything.”

What makes “Club Kid” as hysterical as it is devastating? Its writer/director’s keen understanding that exposure and vulnerability are not the same thing. Peter has spent years being looked at — desired, consumed, partied with, projected onto — without ever fully learning how to let himself be seen. The arrival of his son has the power to change that, and viewers, too.

“A lot of queer people lose their innocence young and then go straight into this world that can be debaucherous,” Firstman said. “They don’t get a chance to go back to that. Then they don’t have kids. I think for a lot of people, kids bring out their inner child in ways they never expected.”

Speaking with IndieWire, the filmmaker repeatedly returned to the idea that queer adulthood can feel like an endless negotiation between freedom and self-destruction. But even at its saddest, “Club Kid” remains startlingly sweet. Firstman has an almost anthropological understanding of the contemporary queer social scene in New York, and his movie is packed with the kind of hyper-specific observations that can only come from somebody who has spent years studying how humor functions as both a tool for connection and an often unwieldy defense mechanism.

“I’ve softened a lot in the process of making it,” Firstman said. “I think I’ve struggled so much with my queerness, not in a traditional way, but more in the actual community and having so many mixed feelings about it. Because it isn’t simple. It’s very rich and full. And I think all this [with ‘Club Kid’] happened at the right time and when I could handle it in my life.”

For all its scenes of spiraling, “Club Kid” is ultimately about the terrifying decision to let yourself be loved without performing for acceptance first. The fact that Firstman can communicate a concept so psychologically naked suggests the arrival of a major new auteur unafraid to move forward on his own terms. “Club Kid” is the most honest Firstman appearance to date.

“Club Kid” premieres at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival in the Un Certain Regard section.

#3474. This 140W power station might be the ultimate charger for Apple users [Video]

I have tested and used countless charging stations over the years, and while many of them get the job done, I feel like there is always some sort of compromise. Whether it’s not enough power, lack of a certain port that I need, or slow wireless charging, I have yet to find one that truly checks every box for me. But over the last month, I have been using CUKTECH’s new 140W Powerstation, and it has nailed everything. It is a six-in-one desktop charger with a built-in retractable cable, magnetic wireless charging, and a dedicated diagnostic display, all in an aesthetic, compact package. Here is everything you need to know and why I think it’s worth considering.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video to see this CUKTECH 15 PowerStation in action!

At its core, the CUKTECH 15 PowerStation is a 140W GaN charger. It can charge one device at the full 140W, meaning it can charge your 16-in MacBook Pro PROLED XDR at max speed, or it can divvy up that power to charge up to six devices at once. It also offers a great combination of ports, a built-in cable, and multiple wireless charging options. You get:

Of course, the biggest selling point is the versatility of it all. You can charge your MacBook Pro with the main USB-C port, charge your iPad with the built-in cable, place your iPhone on the MagSafe charger, and place your AirPods on the wireless charging pad. After all of that, there are still more ports for other accessories that I use daily.

Do keep in mind that the 140W output is the total output, so if more devices are added, that output is shared across all the connected devices.

I am someone who is constantly switching between so many Apple devices. I switch between my iPad Pro and MacBook Pro all the time, and now that it is techtember, I am testing multiple iPhones at the same time, so I need to make sure all of my devices are charged up for when I need them. Not only that, but I also need a USB-A port for my camera battery charging station. So having a centralized hub to charge all of my devices is a MUST in my desk setup. So what immediately stands out to me about the CUKTECH 15 is how much functionality they were able to pack into this relatively compact charging station.

I am a huge fan of built-in retractable cables; they eliminate the need to remember to carry a USB-C cable, so you know you can charge at least one device. Then you add in the wireless magnetic charging stand that supports the new iPhone Duo and StandBy Mode, all while keeping the iPhone upright and visible. Also, when you set up that magnetic charging pad in the upright position, it reveals an AirPods Pro charger. The design is so well thought out.

The cherry on top of it all is the display. I love being able to see how fast something is charging. It allows me to see whether products meet their charging speed standards and how different devices are affected by their charge levels. CUKTECH was also smart to still include one USB-A port. Lots of companies have decided to omit that port because it is an old standard, but there are still plenty of older and wacky tech that uses USB-A, so the inclusion is appreciated. The only thing missing is a dedicated Apple Watch charger, but I just plug in my own when I need it.

The CUKTECH 15 140W Charging Station is available today on Amazon for $149. It has been out in Europe for a little while, but now it has finally made it to the US!

There are plenty of charging stations on the market, but CUKTECH’s 140W power station is the first to check off all the boxes for me. It’s compact, looks great, has all the ports and charging methods I need, and features a beautiful TFT display that lets me know things are charging as they should. If you use multiple devices throughout the day and need them charged at all times, this is worth considering.

#3473. Forget Rush Hour 4, Jackie Chan's Sequel To Hit 142-Minute Thriller Confirms His Best New Action Franchise

Jackie Chan is one of the most beloved martial arts movie stars, and his filmography is remarkable because it transcends genres. Chan is a talented martial artist, but he's also a stuntman. His action scenes are often as much about how he uses the environment as they are about trading blows.

Jackie Chan also has multigenerational appeal and has been a mainstay in action cinema for decades. Fans of 70s kung fu movies may know him best as Wong Fei-Hung in Drunken Master. Chan played Keung in Rumble in the Bronx, and even casual moviegoers know him as Chief Inspector Lee in Rush Hour.

The Rush Hour films are adored for many reasons. Chan teams up with Carter (Chris Tucker), an unpredictable LAPD detective, and the pair have incredible on-screen chemistry. The franchise also stands out among similar series because it's lighthearted and laugh-out-loud funny. Fans of Jackie Chan's stunt work won't be disappointed, and the movies are accomplished comedy action films even if you're less interested in the physical feats.

It's no surprise that Rush Hour fans are waiting for news about its fourth installment. However, the actor has also worked on numerous projects in China, and one of those recent Jackie Chan movies is set to become a franchise itself. It may be grittier and more violent than audiences familiar with Rush Hour are used to. Still, it remains an exceptional action movie, with jaw-dropping parkour, and Chan is as charismatic as ever.

The Shadow's Edge was released in 2025, with a sequel reportedly in the works. The movie introduces us to a skilled group of young thieves. They use a combination of high-flying martial arts and parkour, but they also have far more high-tech tools at their disposal. One member of the group is a professional hacker who uses the police force's own technology against them.

The authorities decide to call in a retired expert officer, Wong Tak-chung (Jackie Chan), to help bring the group down. He assembles a young task force, teaching them surveillance and fieldwork without relying so heavily on technology that could expose them. Tak-chung also discovers that the group has links to a mysterious criminal mastermind known as The Shadow (Tony Leung Ka-fai), who has eluded the police for years.

Jackie Chan's character is a great mentor, but he can still fight, and he's the highlight of several incredible action scenes. One particular brawl in a claustrophobic apartment is a big highlight. Leung's action scenes are also incredible as almost futuristic technology clashes with old-school training.

Without delving into spoilers, The Shadow's Edge does have a satisfying conclusion, but it leaves the door wide open for a sequel. It's too early to say when The Shadow's Edge 2 will release, but production officially began in October 2026.

Jackie Chan has been involved in several newer Western releases, including Karate Kid: Legends. He also starred alongside John Cena in Hidden Strike, which premiered in 2023. Several of Chan's latest movies have debuted in China. We've already covered The Shadow's Edge, and it's arguably a must-watch for fans of Jackie Chan movies, even if you don't enjoy subtitles.

Many of Chan's recent Chinese movies are quite different from what some Western fans may be used to. A Legend premiered in 2024 and deserves a special mention because it's a sequel to The Myth, which was released in 2005. Professor Fang (Jackie Chan) is an archaeologist. Ancient relics are discovered during a glacier excavation, and they are significant because Fang has seen them in his dreams.

A Legend tells a story in the present day and another in Ancient China as Fang learns more about the artifacts. Some action scenes set in Ancient China are particularly impressive, with stylish, large-scale battles and personal sword fights. Jackie Chan also starred in Unexpected Family in 2026. It's a charming comedy, though it's also very different from what general audiences may be used to, as it doesn't feature any martial arts.
