#3472. The 10 Most Elite Movies of 2026 So Far, Ranked

Each year, doomsayers are ready to pronounce cinema dead. Since the pandemic, 2026 has been the most triumphant and encouraging year for the medium, particularly regarding theatrical exhibition, with a handful of unexpected hits dominating the zeitgeist. This year has proven that you don't need a giant superhero epic to draw people to theaters, as everything from romantic horror movies to A24 documentaries have brought casual audiences to their local multiplex. 2026 has seen many of the highest-grossing movies of all time and a collection of gems and soon-to-be classics, including this list of the ten best of the year so far, ranked.

In a year filled with unexpected plot twists and revelations, The Drama took the cake as the most shocking cinematic confession of the year. The Drama, a hilariously macabre and provocative black comedy-drama by Kristoffer Borgli, was the first of three collaborations by Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and their most dynamic on-screen partnership. The film touched third rails, but it wasn't edgy for the sole purpose of shock value.

On the precipice of their wedding, Emma Harwood (Zendaya) discloses a horrifying and unsettling secret from her youth, which causes her fiancé, Charlie Thompson (Pattinson), to spiral, reckoning with his decision to devote his life to this woman. A film that's often hard to watch due to its cringe-inducing social faux pas and uncomfortable confrontations with society's most taboo subjects, The Drama is nonetheless fascinated by the politics of romantic relationships, as well as the conflicts that arise when people give themselves over to each other. There's a real heart to the romance between Emma and Charlie that balances out Borgli's pitch-black humor and dissection of American values. The Norwegian filmmaker asks: are Americans too prude or too crass? Either way, the combination is destructive.

A movie that's slipped through the cracks during the busy fall lineup, Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is the film that should keep Disney up at night. After failing to get their Blade movie off the ground as part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, director Bassam Tariq and star Mahershala Ali finally dropped out and teamed up to make Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, a bold action-thriller that's both rip-roaring and thoughtful as a reflection of Muslim identity.

Lesson learned for Hollywood: don't overthink the project and give Tariq and Ali enough resources to make a crowd-pleasing and socially conscious film, and you should expect greatness. The film was a glorious return for the two-time Oscar winner of Moonlight and Green Book, who gives perhaps his signature movie-star turn as Latif, an ex-military hitman who carries out jobs for a religious leader caught in the crossfire of Islamic and Christian forces while raising his kids as a single dad. Your Mother's fight choreography is as good, if not superior, to, anything you'll see in a major blockbuster, and its combat is a fresh evolution after years of John Wick clones. Tariq tells a deeply personal and urgent story of a conflicted assassin who struggles with his faith.

Trust us, accept Oliva Wilde's invitation to this raunchy, scintillating, and candid dramedy about all the things most people aren't ready to talk about. The Invite, a single-location, adult-oriented character study about two couples discussing sex, career ambition, and familial responsibility versus individualism, is the kind of movie that used to release regularly from the studio system. Now that they are a rare breed in 2026, films like The Invite feel like a festive celebration, but maybe not as freaky as whatever is going on in this film's apartment.

When an on-the-rocks, tense married couple, Angela (Wilde) and Joe (Seth Rogen), invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors, the quirky and feisty couple, Pina (Penélope Cruz) and Hawk (Edward Norton), they reconsider their entire lives and the status of their relationship, as truths unspool and hard feelings are laid out on the table during this wild dinner party. A stylish hybrid between a raunchy comedy and an intimate chamber drama, The Invite appeals to a wide audience, even with its commentary that's designed to reflect on your own discomfort. Wilde's precise behind-the-camera vision gives the film the edge of a psychological thriller, as the canted angles and intricate blocking create an uncanny vibe and awkward tension, a sentiment that everyone who's ever been paired up with an odd couple can relate to.

2026's first tentpole release, Project Hail Mary continues to linger in film culture since its release in March. Based on an Andy Weir novel and directed by Phil Lord and Chris Miller after a 12-year hiatus from the director's chair, the film was an inspired box office smash hit, as it offered a glimmer of hope for audiences that star-driven, non-franchise event movies can still thrive. The year was a big winner for Ryan Gosling and hand-crafted, practical effects.

A charismatic screen icon, a rock puppet, and an outer-space journey about going home and teamwork. What more else could you ask for? Project Hail Mary reinvigorated the traditional four-quadrant blockbuster after years of studios neglecting so many of its creative principles. The film, despite its PG-13 rating, is something that people of ostensibly all ages can enjoy, and its melancholic streak and sci-fi wizardry keep the cinephiles in the theater locked in. Dr. Ryland Grace (Gosling) is the idyllic movie protagonist—amiable, courageous, and sometimes naive. It is the part of a lifetime for Gosling, who has become a master of bumbling humor and dramatic sincerity, and Lord and Miller let their pop culture obsessions soar to the moon.

This is certainly a controversial pick, to put it mildly. Even when accepting some of the writing shortcomings and plot dynamics, Disclosure Day is yet another awe-inspiring, luminous vision by the legendary Steven Spielberg. One of 2026's most divisive movies left a bad taste in some viewers' mouths, but for those who were on its wavelength, the film's majestic scope and hyper-earnest tone made this feel like the most important cinematic statement of the year.

Featuring a career-best performance by Emily Blunt and Spielberg operating behind the camera as if he hasn't aged, time will be kind to this misunderstood achievement.

Disclosure Day, which saw Spielberg returning to the alien subgenre, is a mega-sized blockbuster/auteurist expression of many layers. A conspiracy thriller, sci-fi mystery, and existential drama wrapped into one, the film was criticized for being a retrograde and out-of-touch depiction of contemporary America and our relationship to government secrets coming from a septuagenarian filmmaker, but Spielberg's optimism is magnificently used to wrestle with contemporary cynicism. Disclosure Day posits a world where people's skepticism and ulterior motives shatter in the face of something truly profound. The film, filled with intense chase sequences and moving character moments, is far stranger and thematically inscrutable than Spielberg's usual fare. Featuring a career-best performance by Emily Blunt and Spielberg operating behind the camera as if he hasn't aged, time will be kind to this misunderstood achievement.

Why don't you have a seat over there? Primetime, starring Robert Pattinson (arguably the MVP of 2026) as To Catch a Predator's Chris Hansen, is an essential watch and one of the most striking films of the year. The first narrative feature by documentarian Lance Oppenheim, this surrealistic, unconventional biopic about one of the 2000s most polarizing media figures is a dazzling and off-putting morality fable about the sinister nature of performance art and vigilante justice.

Now 20 years removed from the height of To Catch a Predator's popularity on NBC, Primetime reflects on this bizarre and unruly era for culture from a contemporary lens. Oppenheim dives into this period by mimicking the visual and tonal style of an America obsessed with trashy reality TV, resulting in a hypnotic aesthetic that pushes the medium to new realms. Even if he has the moral high ground relative to the sexual predators that the show is incriminating, it takes a warped mind to make a living off turning federal prosecutions into performance art for millions at home on a Thursday night. Primetime, carried by Pattinson in the performance of the year, captures the world through Hansen's obsessions and unseemly desires. The film speaks to present-day perils by depicting an America where our heroes are on television, glorifying the hunt for sex offenders as a circus act, and where the media is our only outlet for justice.

One of the many movies of 2026 that needed to be seen to be believed, Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie is unlike anything audiences have ever seen on the big screen. Explaining Matt Johnson's style and the premise of the Canadian web series that the film is based on, which has no affiliation with the famous grunge band, is a tall task, but anyone with a good sense of humor and fervent passion for creative companionship will adore all the madness that's under the hood of this time-traveling music mockumentary.

For Matt Johnson and series co-creator Jay McCarrol, playing themselves in the film, the goal is to land a gig at the Rivoli nightclub in Toronto, but when inadvertently traveling back in time to 2008, they stumble into a chance to attain fame that will carry them to the present day. Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie's audacious concept doesn't disappoint in the final product, as Johnson and McCarrol put on the most electric, hilarious, and sweeping adventure that satirizes showbiz, movie history, and culture, best exemplified in the initial arrival in 2008, before the fall from grace of various canceled celebrities and societal rejections of insensitive humor. With the right crowd, Nirvanna the Band plays like a rock concert, with every joke and suspenseful, jaw-dropping set piece leaving the room completely enraptured.

Many inventive and groundbreaking movies entered the cultural zeitgeist in 2026, but there are still a handful of smaller, arthouse films that likely slipped past your radar. Look no further than Blue Heron, another crowning achievement of Canadian cinema and the announcement of a new visionary, Sophy Romvari. This personal, gut-wrenching, and transcendent portrait of grief and the erosion of memory is sure to leave you speechless and exploring your own soul.

The meaning of life, family, and distant memories are beautifully reflected in Romvari's debut feature film, which follows a filmmaker, Sasha (Eylul Guven as a child and Amy Zimmer as an adult), recalling a summer in the '90s when her brother's disruptive behavior, the result of untreated mental illness, caused a strain in her household in Vancouver. As a family drama, Blue Heron is palpably sensitive, sparking an array of Proustian memories where the minuscule incidents trigger the most harrowing sensations. The film's somber register evokes Romvari and her avatar trying to repress emotions, as the director is still trying to grasp why these memories continue to linger. This meta-textual, deconstructionist story about the stories we tell ourselves to make sense of the past shifts into gear in its second half, where the audience wrestles with how we treat male mental illness and the mind's constant longing to rewrite history.

In terms of scope, anticipation, critical discussion, and cultural omnipresence, The Odyssey will undoubtedly stand as the cinematic event of the year, if not the decade. Christopher Nolan, with yet another critically acclaimed, auteurist blockbuster under his belt, proved himself to be the most viable name in Hollywood, more than any other living movie star. His biggest swing yet gave you everything you wanted out of a major motion picture extravaganza ripe with humanity, grace, and pathos.

Rounded out by an absurdly stacked cast, including Matt Damon as Odysseus, Tom Holland as Telemachus, and Anne Hathaway as Penelope, The Odyssey was something everyone had to be part of in some way. Each star, even the surprise scene-stealers like Samantha Morton and Elliot Page, helped craft the modern-day classical epic. Nolan, who miraculously shot the entire movie on IMAX film, painted with his broadest canvas yet, but he never lost his control, momentum, and probing psychology that have made him the signature visionary of his generation. A stunningly intimate epic about trauma, destiny, and legacy, The Odyssey grounded the overwhelming scale of Homer's epic poem without minimizing the all-encompassing weight of the text. Nolan, who brought a fresh take on an ancient story, is perhaps the quintessential storyteller of our modern world.

Rarely do you see a feature film garner this much online buzz and sheer curiosity, let alone a documentary. However, anyone with an ounce of awareness of Nathan Fielder knew that You Can See Everything, a film we didn't even know existed two months ago, would break the confines of the documentary form. Chronicling convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes before she's sent to prison and much more, the film, co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, showed the glowing potential for cinema in the 2020s as a form-breaking artistic expression about everything and nothing at the same time, which is what living in the present day feels like.

No logline does You Can See Everything justice, as Fielder and Oppenheim's cinéma vérité coverage of Holmes and her partner Billy Evans evolves into a bizarre, unsettling, and hypnotic dissection of filmmaking, egoism, performance art, and parasocial relationships. For avid fans of Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, the shocking box office hit and potential awards player upends the Fielder we've grown to love or despise, as his deadpan awkwardness shatters in the face of the curious case of Elizabeth Holmes, who develops an uncanny relationship with her documentarian as Fielder attempts to read and connect with her. The film, which features a second-half shift in perspective that's becoming harder and harder to keep from being spoiled, reflects how some people are born incapable of truth and basic communication. You Can See Everything is the cultural text of the year, as its depiction of morally grey tech moguls and constant nonfiction image-making taps directly into our hearts.

#3471. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

If you’re like me and bought an iPhone Duo, you’re likely a bit disappointed by the options on the market to prop it up on a table. Apple’s official $129 folio with kickstand is expensive, flimsy, and gets in the way of the outer display. MagSafe wallets that turn into kickstands are too tall for the back of the phone, and there aren’t many good third party cases yet.

That said, the perfect option for an iPhone Duo kickstand might’ve actually been hiding in plain sight all along.

The reason why I say it’s been hiding in plain sight is because this accessory isn’t actually designed for iPhone Duo, it works on all iPhones. It’s the PopSocket Low-Pro, a low profile MagSafe PopSocket with a ring that flips out and serves as a kickstand. It also works as a normal PopSocket if you’re interested in that.

This PopSocket has a few strengths on iPhone Duo:

On the last point, you might’ve heard from some iPhone Duo reviewers that the phone can’t really work on a MagSafe stand while unfolded, because the weight of the left half of the phone drags it down. I’m happy to report that this PopSocket actually largely fixes that. It’ll still slip slightly over a longer period of time, but it’s good enough to make the experience usable.

I tested this across multiple MagSafe stands of mine and the slippage issue is improved across the board when using the PopSocket Low-Pro.

My favorite advantage to the PopSocket Low-Pro is the fact that it improves the iPhone Duo experience greatly while still allowing you to rock the phone without a case. The Low-Pro is truly low profile, and can’t really be felt when you’re holding the phone. It protrudes a fair bit less than the camera bump does.

#3469. Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was

One of 2026’s distinct pleasures (for lack of a better word) has been getting to know Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’ life partner and power of attorney holder who becomes the primary focus of “You Can See Everything.” Evans and Holmes have two kids together and are working to launch a new blood testing startup in the vein of Theranos. While Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film begins as a relatively straightforward documentary about Holmes and Evans’ life in San Diego during the last month before she reported to federal prison, it spirals into a larger investigation into Evans’ influence on Holmes and the nature of their partnership. Related Stories Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch

It’s a three-hour movie, but you’re not alone if you left with unanswered questions about the couple. Fortunately, Evans himself is still active as ever on X — both his own account, and the one he runs for Holmes. And on Monday, November 2, Evans spent some time answering questions from fans… everything was on the table other than his caveat that every question “needs to be legally permissible.”

He tried to clarify some of the film‘s more confusing moments, including his frequent onscreen sniffing, which he chalked up to allergies. As for rumors that cocaine might be to blame, Evans wrote, “Never been a fan.”

Solo parenting 2 toddlers you are sick approx 75% of days. Allergies in Austin TX are no joke.I take Claritin daily. Much less sniffling.

Evans also went into detail about his relationship with Holmes, denying that he has any real control over her but admitting that he’s still romantically crazy about her. He noted that he misses her presence and touch so much that the Theranos founder “should qualify as a medically necessary prescription.”

I miss everything about her.I miss her presence. Her touch. The way she runs her fingers through my hair. Her patience.She makes me a better person. And without her, I feel an emptiness that's hard to describe.People often say they need someone when what they really mean is…

Perhaps most importantly, he addressed the burning question of what his cousin’s “thing” was. Early in the film, Evans abruptly cuts off a conversation with Fielder on the beach when the topic turns to his family’s wealth by vaguely stating that he’s late for his cousin’s thing. Evans claimed that it was a marriage proposal, and implied that he ended up getting there in time.

She was getting engaged. Married now, has a baby, glad I went. Family over everything

And of course, the shower scene came up. Evans pushed back on the idea that he wanted to do full frontal nudity in the documentary, dismissing that suggestion from a fan as a “false narrative.” He also linked to a PEOPLE story that claims he was “violated” by the scene and wrote “trust the sources.”

Evans also did not limit himself to questions about the film. Other AMA questions focused on his cultural tastes, and Evans used the platform to express his love for Chappell Roan, Kendrick Lamar, Charlie Kirk, and Taylor Swift (he said he bought Holmes’ engagement ring at the Reputation tour merch booth).

Fielder and Oppenheimer’s film makes it clear that nobody can really see everything in a documentary, but Evans appears committed to proving that you can post everything if you try hard enough.

#3468. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3467. Three new iPad models are reportedly launching early next year, here’s what’s coming

After debuting the refreshed iPad mini with OLED this past week, Apple still has more in the pipeline for the rest of the iPad lineup in the first half of next year. That includes a new iPad Air, a new base iPad, and a new iPad Pro, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

To follow up the iPad mini refresh, Apple’s next iPad Air refresh will also gain OLED. It’ll likely stick with a 60Hz panel, and likely won’t make the switch from Touch ID to Face ID – but it’ll bring a nifty display upgrade to the iPad Air, a product that hasn’t had a major refresh since 2020.

In terms of chipset, while not confirmed, a jump from the M4 chip to the M5 chip is rather likely. It’ll also likely come with a higher price, likely around $799-899 for the base 11-inch model.

Next year, Apple will also finally update the base iPad for the first time since early 2025. It’ll upgrade it to the A19 chip and 8GB of RAM, finally enabling Apple Intelligence support on Apple’s cheapest iPad. It should also gain the N1 chip and the C1X modem for improved networking performance.

There shouldn’t be any screen or design upgrades with this iPad, at least as of now – though it could potentially see some refreshed color options.

With the iPad Pro, Apple will be adding a vapor chamber to the device, a feat it started last year with the iPhone 17 Pro. It probably won’t have any meaningful changes otherwise, except for a new chipset – likely M6 or potentially M7.

Hopefully, there’s some surprises in store with this device. The iPad Pro now starts at $1199 for an 11-inch model and $1499 for a 13-inch model. It’ll have been around 3 years since the last major revamp by the time Apple introduces the M6 model, and the company should probably do something to make it a more worthwhile refresh.

#3466. Upcoming Paramount+ Shows Reportedly Eying Move To HBO Max

The future of Paramount+ shows is getting clearer.

With Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, one of the biggest questions was what would happen to the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services. The post-merger company, which is now known as Skydance, appointed HBO's Casey Bloys as the Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer of Skydance Direct-to-Consumer, in which he is responsible for overseeing both Paramount+ and HBO Max, and co-CEO David Ellison has discussed plan to eventually merge the two services.

A new report from Deadline now shares that while no official decisions have been made yet, the possibility is being discussed of moving Paramount+'s upcoming drama series to HBO Max. Potential candidates include Nicole Kidman and Elle Fanning's legal thriller Discretion, the 9/11 first responders show The Best of Us led by Succession's Jeremy Strong, and other projects that are in the midst of waiting for an official greenlight.

Conversations about this move have reportedly reached the highest levels of Skydance, but all Paramount+ shows are staying on the platform for now as talks continue to progress. Meanwhile, Francesca Orsi, who was promoted from EVP to President of HBO Drama Series and Films, is working with Bloys to decide which drama projects belong on HBO.

As part of reviewing the Paramount+ slate with Sarah Aubrey, Head of Paramount+, Max Originals and International Programming, Orsi allegedly may also be tasked with looking at which Paramount+ series feel aligned with HBO, along with working on the select shows that stay on Paramount+, especially if they are akin to HBO's prestige dramas.

While the new streaming structure is still being worked out, moving upcoming Paramount+ shows like Discretion and The Best of Us to HBO Max could potentially expedite plans to merge the platforms together. From Kidman's time on Big Little Lies and The Undoing and Strong playing Kendall Roy in Succession, the stars of these series have plenty of Emmy Award-winning experience with HBO, making their new prestige dramas a natural fit.

This may be the trajectory for Paramount+'s upcoming shows, but it does not answer what will happen to the ones that already exist. From Landman to The Madison, there is no shortage of ongoing Taylor Sheridan shows on Paramount+, but it is unclear whether they will also move to HBO Max, especially before his NBCUniversal television deal begins in 2029. There's also the matter of where unscripted shows will go, including the many reality ones that also air on CBS, such as Big Brother, Survivor, and The Amazing Race.

If all Paramount+ content eventually shifts to HBO Max, there is additionally the matter of whether Skydance's streaming service will just be called HBO Max, if it will combine names, or if there will be a complete rebranding. Before the merger, HBO's streaming platform already underwent many name changes, including HBO Go, HBO Now, HBO Max, Max, and eventually back to HBO Max. Another major and more pressing question is what the subscription prices will look like if the two services and all their movies and shows are fully merged.

#3465. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3464. ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama

“The Intertwining” director Akira Yamamoto was mentored by Kiyoshi Kurosawa, and it shows. Yamamoto is one of many Japanese filmmakers to study under the legendary director of “Cure” and “Tokyo Sonata,” who was a professor at Tokyo University of the Arts from 2005 to 2023. And although he’s not Kurosawa’s most famous pupil — that would be “All of a Sudden”‘s Ryusuke Hamaguchi, whose style is also an influence here — he has clearly taken many lessons on composition and timing from his former teacher. To this end, Yamamoto’s latest feature takes a politically charged family drama and laces it with restrained, but palpable psychological tension, creating a film whose quietest moments are also its most uneasy ones. Related Stories Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut

Yamamoto’s primary tactic for creating this tension is the long take. Shots in this film frequently linger just a few seconds longer than they’re “supposed” to, reflecting the pauses in dialogue scenes where characters choose their words before they speak. Many filmmakers who utilize this tactic like to punctuate these moments with bursts of sudden violence, but aside from the elderly woman collapsing on a city bus who serves as a catalyst for the film’s plot — filmed in a very Kurosawa-esque long shot, by the way — Yamamoto contains himself here, too.

The struggle in “The Intertwining” is all psychological, as the two women who respond to the medical emergency — both medical students, as it turns out — begin to realize that they have a lot in common. Ji-hyun (Jiyoung) is a fifth-year Korean exchange student, although she’s frequently mistaken for Japanese — as Nakano (Karata Erika) notes with surprise when they formally introduce themselves afterwards. They exchange numbers and hang out a few times, eventually figuring out that not only are their parents both in the hospitality business, but they were born at the same clinic around the same time.

Ji-hyun’s parents briefly lived in Tokyo before going back to their home country, discouraged by the discrimination against Koreans that’s still pervasive in Japan today. This becomes extremely important later on as Nakano, who’s never felt at home in her family, decides to test her DNA against those of her parents and brother after learning about DNA sequencing in class. Nakano is both shocked and relieved to discover that the parents she grew up with are not her biological mother and father, and her new friend Ji-hyun supports her as she tries to process these feelings. Then a nurse at the clinic gives Nakano an envelope containing the names of her real parents.

As it turns out, it’s not a coincidence at all that Ji-hyun and Nakano’s parents both sought treatment at the same fertility clinic. Ji-hyun and Nakano were both the product of IVF, and their embryos were implanted in their respective mothers on the same day. Except the doctor made a mistake, meaning that Nakano is actually Korean, and Ji-hyun — who’s also faced prejudice for her ethnicity while living in Japan — is actually Japanese. The scene where the clinic’s current head tries to explain what went wrong more than 20 years ago contains another of the movie’s rare outbursts, as Nakano’s father angrily confronts the doctor for “putting a Korean embryo into [his] wife.” In his mind, this is the worst betrayal of them all, and the way he prioritizes his family’s honor over his daughter’s happiness is one of the reasons why Nakano feels no guilt about leaving him behind.

Ji-hyun, on the other hand, loves her family very much. She does not want to become Japanese, and the political undertones of their respective identity crises are one of the film’s most crackling unspoken undercurrents. Ji-hyun pities Nakano, but maintains boundaries between them even after the two go to South Korea to visit Ji-hyun’s warm and supportive family at their picturesque restaurant by the sea. By this point, the bubble of unspoken words between these two women is straining with tension. But Yamamoto is too subtle, and too savvy, of a director to let it burst.

Instead, we’re left with some challenging questions about identity, and what makes a person who they truly are. Although it’s the central conflict, the mix-up at the clinic is not the only outrageous coincidence in this movie, and “The Intertwining” could have been even stronger with a slightly tighter narrative focus. Still, it’s a testament to Yamamoto’s filmmaking that these feel less like plot contrivances and more like the invisible reverberations of fate.

“The Intertwining” does require patience and active engagement, both of which are made possible by committed, but controlled performances from Jiyoung and Karata, who also starred in Hamaguchi’s “Asako I & II.” One could easily imagine the premise of this movie as the stuff of Sirkian melodrama. But Yamamoto asks his leads to internalize these big emotions rather than externalize them through his filmmaking, and the controlled intensity shown by all three key players is key to what makes “The Intertwining” work.

“The Intertwining” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3463. Hands-on: ESR’s 45W Xtend charger is an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go

Last month, ESR released a new set of chargers under the xtend branding – all of which offer built-in retractable cables. They have a 45W wall charger that supports up to 60W with AVS, as well as a 100W car charger with two cables.

I’ll largely be touching on the 45W charger here, as that’s the one I’ve been utilizing the most.

Chargers with built-in retractable cables have been a larger trend in the past year or so, and ESR’s new chargers offer larger cables than usual. On the 45W Xtend charger, you get up to 3.1ft of cable length with the built in cable, compared to other offerings which are around 2.2ft.

I’ve been carrying around ESR’s new 45W charger for the past few weeks since it debuted, and I like it quite a bit. It comes in a few color options: black, white, as well as burgundy to match the iPhone 18 Pro.

You don’t only have to rely on the built-in retractable cable. The charger also offers a normal USB-C port for connecting any cable you’d like, including a longer one.

Personally, I love packing it for travel. Throwing a charging brick and a cable into a bag can be a little cumbersome at times, especially since cables can get tangled. I find chargers with retractable cables quite refreshing since they’re much easier to deal with in a pinch.

45W alone is plenty for fast charging any iPhone, but it also supports up to 60W dynamic charging with AVS, which’ll unlock the fastest charge speeds on iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.

ESR’s 45W xtend charger is normally available for $49.99, though right now it’s on sale for as low as $35.99 on Amazon in the white colorway. Burgundy is also available for $41.99, saving you 20%.

Their 100W car charger also offers two retractable cables, as well as an extra USB-A port. I don’t have many thoughts to offer on the car charger as I don’t drive, but I would imagine it’s nice to not have to deal with cables in your center console area. With 100W, you can fast charge pretty much any iPhone, iPad, MacBook Air, or base 14-inch MacBook Pro. It’s available for just $36.99 on Amazon right now, a $20 discount.

#3462. ‘VisionQuest’s T’Nia Miller Breaks Down Jocasta’s “Godlike, Badass” Moment in Episode 7

Taylor Gates is an Indiana native who earned her BFA in Creative Writing from the University of Evansville. She fell in love with entertainment by watching shows about chaotic families like Full House, The Nanny, Gilmore Girls, and The Fosters. After college, she moved to Los Angeles to pursue a career as a writer, editor, and filmmaker. Today, she’s a sucker for dramedies — especially coming-of-age stories centering around complex female and LGBTQ+ characters. She has been with Collider since May 2022.

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for VisionQuest Episode 7.

T’Nia Miller is a true powerhouse performer. Her range is incredible, spanning everything from intense horror and devastating drama to trippy sci-fi and political thriller. She has a long list of impressive credits, including Mike Flanagan series The Haunting of Bly Manor and The Fall of the House of Usher; Russell T. Davies shows Years and Years, Banana, and Cucumber; Apple TV’s Foundation; and Sex Education.

Her newest role is Jocasta in Marvel’s VisionQuest. Mysterious, ambitious, and endlessly fascinating, we are first introduced to Jocasta as the Butcherbird Killer before finding out that she’s actually an AI version of the brilliant scientist Josephine Carrington. She’s hellbent on controlling humanity, and yet, Miller doesn’t play her as a straightforward evil villain by any means. She’s highly complicated and morally grey, which really comes out during her spicy and twisted but also surprisingly moving scenes with Ultron (James Spader).

Collider got the chance to speak to Miller about her work on the series. During the conversation, she broke down Ultron and Jocasta’s complex, irresistible dynamic, all those references to motherhood and Edgar Allan Poe, those major reveals in Episode 7, and more.

COLLIDER: I absolutely love your character and performance. You're kind of playing multiple roles in one, between Butcherbird Killer, AI Jocasta, and human scientist Josephine Carrington. How did you approach bringing all of these identities together into this one character?

T’NIA MILLER: Well, I think she is just one identity. I think we're multifaceted — I think we're all of those people. Although Jo Carrington isn't a genocidal maniac, mass murderer, serial killer, I do believe that, at the core of Jocasta, she is Jo Carrington, right? So it all stems from that place. And then the other things are just circumstantial, as it were. It's just like, “Which hat am I wearing today?” I'm sure a different side of Taylor shows up when you're with your friends, when we're with your mom, when you're at work, so that's how I see it.

That’s so interesting. I think you're right — you peel back all of these layers of her. I absolutely love her dynamic with Ultron because it's so twisted and sexy, but also kind of pure and sweet at the same time. Were there any specific conversations or exercises you did with James to build that dynamic that's so unique and also authentic at the same time?

MILLER: The first time I met James was on set.

MILLER: Yeah, we were about to shoot a scene, but we were shooting chronologically. So that first meeting was in Episode 5, and we were sitting with [director] Vincenzo Natali. I love working with Vincenzo. I’ve worked with him before, so I instantly felt comfortable. It is a cat-and-mouse game. It's like, “I'm going to seduce and flirt with you” because it’s her language. “You have something that’s mine, so I’m going to get it.” And James is doing Ultron in that space. The writing is there, so you're doing what's on the page. It also happened to be my audition piece for Jocasta, so I sort of felt like I knew it. That was my intro into her world, and we just built it from there. And as the series went along, so did their relationship — Jocasta and Ultron’s — as did James and my relationship, and understanding, and care.

I remember there was one night where I couldn't remember my lines, and I was just having a moment. We were in Madripoor. It was tiny — it was, like, four lines or something — and he says, “I think he’d hold you. Is it okay if I hold you for this scene? I'll just hold you to support you. I said, “Thank you. I apologize. I’m so sorry.” He said, “You never have to apologize to me.” He held my arm, and I know that, at that moment, that was James.

That's so sweet. I love that. You can really feel the chemistry on screen. One of my favorite scenes in the show is the beginning of Episode 6 where Jo is like, “This is chess, except they're my pieces, my board, and I'm the queen.”

MILLER: I wanted to swear on that! I wanted to say, “I'm the MFB.”

We'll know in our hearts that she was supposed to say that! Can you talk about that line and that scene in general? There’s so much going on under the surface. It really is a chess game.

MILLER: It is chess. These are their tactics. They're just deploying whatever skills they have, and hers is, “Well, you obviously like me, so I'm going to lean into that.” Then that explodes in her face, but that was a lot of fun — the twists and turns and, at any given moment, who has the upper hand. Those peaks and troughs are so wonderful as an actor — it’s the really good stuff to play.

I noticed the language that's used to describe Jocosta is so maternal. She's called the mother of artificial intelligence, and she refers to the nanos as her children. I'm curious how that language impacted your understanding of her because I thought that was a really interesting choice.

MILLER: It really impacted it, actually. Because for me, I was going to rescue my children. She’s like, “I like you, and I'm attracted to you, but you are not gonna get in the way. You can't distract me from saving my children.” And I am a mother, so I was able to pull from those experiences of fighting for your kids. You have to. I've had to fight for my kids at times in their lives, so that really informed how, no matter what distraction there was, I had to keep my objective firm and clear until those later scenes. I’m like, “Okay, what is my objective? Why am I doing this? What is that about?” And she starts to crumble and question herself, and she begins to understand herself and what has happened to her, which is ultimately sad, and the scars of that trauma.

Four villains, and four arguments the films were honest enough to actually let them make. Here is the one you lean towards, the part of it that holds up, and the exact point where it stops holding up.

You align with the one who was right about the problem and wrong about the solution. Killmonger is the most persuasive villain Marvel has produced because the film never pretends his anger came from nowhere.

You align with the protector, which is the most understandable and most dangerous position on this list. Namor is not chasing power or revenge, he is doing whatever keeps his people hidden, and he has been doing it for centuries.

You align with the patient one, the only man on this list with no powers, no army and no hurry. Zemo lost his family in Sokovia and then spent years working out that you do not fight the Avengers, you introduce them to each other's secrets.

You align with the one who decided the answer was arithmetic. Thanos is not angry and not grieving in any way he will admit to, he simply reached a conclusion and never once revisited it, which is precisely what makes him frightening.

I thought it was also so interesting that there are all these references to “The Raven” and Edgar Allan Poe. I’m curious what you think her ties to that theme say about her, too.

MILLER: She looks to nature for her answers. It's not my first venture with Edgar Allan Poe because I did The Fall of the House of Usher. I was like, “Oh, this is great that it's showing up again.” It’s so funny because I kept seeing starlings all around me during that. I always see these starlings. There's so much to be taken from Poe and his view of the world, and I think that Josephine Carrington and Poe potentially have the same outlook in some ways on our humanity, or lack thereof, and where we should be heading. It’s a tale as old as time.

I love that you mentioned Fall the House of Usher. That and Bly Manor are where I first became familiar with your work. I'm curious if you had any conversations with Terry about your experience with that material or if it was a complete coincidence.

MILLER: I think it was a complete coincidence. Terry's got a million thoughts in his brain at once, and of course, there's a writers’ room.

Episode 7 sees the client wanting to restore Jo’s memories, which is a concept that really scares her. She says she's not really sure she's ready to be her again. Why do you think that fear runs so deeply in her?

MILLER: I think it's a fear that runs through all of us. It's a fear of the unknown. If I may, as humans, we feel like we have some element of control and that we know something, and actually, we know nothing, and we control nothing. I think that's just an echo of that. Why doesn't she want to know? Because that's a person. How did she get in this mess in the first place? Did she have a hand in it? Is it her fault? Who is she gonna have to face? Do I have to face my shadow self? Like, that's scary. What if I was wrong? What have I done? What's that going to unmask? I think she's genuinely petrified of what that means and where that may lead because she's unstable. She says, “I've got all these memories, and I don't know why I feel this anger, and I don't know where it comes from.” That's a trauma for so many women, especially as they get older — it starts to creep up on you. I've got this anger — this displaced anger — and I don't know where it comes from. You know you have to go back and do the work, don't you? I think that's it. I’m sorry to get all philosophical.

No, that's so beautifully said, and I think that's so true! It stands in such an interesting contrast to that moment in Episode 6 where Ultron insists that he wants to know her, even though it'll be painful. What do you think his desire to deeply understand her means to her?

MILLER: Here’s a really terrible analogy: It's like you're faced with a mountain of dishes, and someone says, “You wash, I'll dry.” [Laughs] It’s like, “Okay, I feel supported now. That's a surprise. Do I have a companion in you? Can I trust you?” I think, for her, it's everything — to be able to share it, to be able to be understood.

We get a flashback at the end of Episode 7 where it’s revealed that Josephine won the Stark Award with her partner, and the two of them vowed to be loving gods. I'm curious what that choice of words sort of tells you about her.

MILLER: Well, I think he says gods, and she says, “Yeah, but we'll be loving gods.” There’s a little bit of ego. They've managed to do this thing, and they're gonna save humanity. They're gonna save the world. She couldn't save her father, but she's gonna save everybody else from going through that pain and then some. That's kind of a godlike, badass thing to do, right?

I really hope that we get to see more of her in the MCU. Are there any characters you would like to see her interact with, in particular?

MILLER: Well, [everyone from] Black Panther. I've worked with Letitia Wright twice before, so let’s make it three. We did a play that was written by Danai Gurira, who is also in Black Panther, bizarrely and oddly enough. It was fringe theater earning pennies years and years ago. And then we did a queer show, Cucumber and Banana, with Russell T. Davies. That would be just interesting because it’s a small universe. I think Loki. Wanda.

MILLER: More of Ultron, please and thank you. I'm going to broadly say the Avengers. I'll just go on forever and ever and ever.

These are amazing. I'm wanting a Jennifer Kale moment. She has this potion background, so she’s in STEM, too. I think it could be really fun.

MILLER: Oh my god, that would be cool. That would be very, very, very cool. I see that.

You get to do so many cool action scenes in this show. You're kicking ass, to put it bluntly. What was stuntwork on this like for you? What was the training process?

MILLER: Very early on, I had a few rehearsals, and then I looked at Chloe Kibble, who is my stunt double, and I went, “Okay, Chloe — you're up. You are much better at it than I am.”

MILLER: In The Peripheral and Bly Manor, I got to do some of my own stunts — or part of them — and that was cool. Paul does a lot of his, but this was very, very much Chloe Kibble, who was brilliant and is brilliant. Shoutout to Chloe. I can do a few punches and kicks and stuff, but not the whole fight scene.

#3461. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3460. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.

#3458. Don’t Forget, Oscar Watchers: ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and Other Big Guns Are Coming Back

The fall festivals have come and gone, leaving specialty sugarplums dancing in Oscar pundits’ heads, from Netflix’s Spanish favorite “La Bola Negra” to Searchlight’s hilarious “Wild Horse Nine,” which just boasted a raucous Academy screening reception.

But don’t forget the big guns, movies of scale and scope that wowed audiences earlier in the year. Some will fill the craft categories (see “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”) or dominate Best Animated Feature (see Pixar’s “Toy Story 5,” which might land Taylor Swift an Oscar for Best Song). Others will wow not only cinephiles but the mainstream voters in the Academy. Their campaigners must push them back into voters’ consciousness, remind them of what they liked so much, all those months ago. Related Stories ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was

On November 11, “Disclosure Day” Best Actress contender Emily Blunt will launch her award season push for an “Oppenheimer” follow-up Oscar nomination with a SAG Q&A in New York, followed by November 13 in LA. On November 15, she’s conducting press conferences for the Critics Choice Awards and the Golden Globes. She’ll also do rounds of press interviews. And on December 10, she’ll accept the Kirk Douglas Award for Excellence in Film from the Santa Barbara International Film Festival.

In other words, Blunt is in it to win it.

Best Shots: Truth is, Universal is pragmatically putting Blunt front and center for “Disclosure Day” for her remarkable turn as a foreign-language-spouting weatherwoman inhabited by aliens, as opposed to filmmaker Steven Spielberg or costar Josh O’Connor. Craft contenders will include five-time Oscar-winning composer John Williams, possibly up for his 55th and last Oscar nomination, two-time Oscar-winning cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, Editing, Sound, and VFX.

The well-reviewed March blockbuster has come roaring back, with filmmakers Phil Lord and Chris Miller doing most of the promo duties so far. The heart-tugging sci-fi epic produced by Amy Pascal is competing at the Golden Globes for comedy as “The Martian” did before it. The DVD released in May. “PHM” will re-release in IMAX and IMAX 70 theaters starting December 11.

Best Shots: Ryan Gosling is a Best Actor contender as scientist Ryland Grace — not a trained astronaut — who is in way over his head on a space mission to save the Earth but uses science to figure out the many problems that come his way. Gosling carries the movie but also interacts beautifully with not only his commanding mission director Sandra Hüller (who is competing with herself in Supporting Actress for “PHM” and “Fatherland”) but James Ortiz, who was on set as puppeteer and voice for another solo space traveler, a crablike alien named Rocky. He’s contending for Supporting Actor. (Whether the actors branch will accept him is a big question.)

Lord & Miller are in the mix for Best Director, and “The Martian” Oscar nominee Drew Goddard could be in the running again for Adapted Screenplay. The movie could land several craft categories as well, including VFX, Sound, Cinematography, Editing and Daniel Pemberton‘s Original Score, which supports the different tones of the movie, through action, comedy, and pathos.

Universal just released their robust screening and panel schedule for “The Odyssey,” with Christopher Nolan and his cast and key crew to be grilled by the likes of Guillermo del Toro and Robert Downey, Jr. as they step in front of Guild and Academy voters. Not coincidentally, the movie hits DVD, Blu-ray, and 4K Ultra HD on November 17.

Best Shots: “The Odyssey” is in front-runner position for Best Actor. Matt Damon has wisely leaned into the degree of difficulty required to play the peripatetic wily warrior Odysseus in harsh locations that helped Leonardo DiCaprio win for “The Revenant.” Damon is a wily and charming campaigner who is well-liked not only in Hollywood — he has worked with everyone — but around the world. (Check out his Criterion Closet Picks.) He won a Screenplay Oscar with Ben Affleck (“Good Will Hunting”) but has never won an Acting Oscar.

The ubiquitous Anne Hathaway (who won for “Les Mis”) is leading the Supporting Actress field for her performance as the patient Penelope. Constantly promoting a slew of movies this year as she became more and more pregnant did not hurt her cause. She’s competing with two-time nominee Samantha Morton, a Brit, as the witch Circe. Veteran American John Leguizamo, never nominated, leads the British “Odyssey” Supporting Actor contenders Rob Pattinson and Tom Holland.

Of this group, “The Odyssey” and “Project Hail Mary” will dominate the Oscar nominations, likely scoring from 10-15 each. “Sinners,” a period movie with original music, holds the record with 16.

#3457. You Can Get These 'Nothing' Over-Ear Headphones for $55 Right Now

Nothing, the upstart U.K. brand that makes products like phones, smartwatches, and headphones, has quickly become one of my favorite players in tech. Its products offer unique features and designs, and the prices are competitive. For example, right now, Nothing's latest budget over-ear headphones, which were released in October 2025, the CMF Headphone Pros, are just $55 (originally $99). This is a great option for anyone looking to get reasonably priced over-the-ear headphones that punch above their weight when it comes to performance.

There is a companion Nothing X app that allows you to customize action buttons, among other things, but the cool thing about these headphones is the control you get without needing the app.

There is a multi-function roller on one side of the headphone that you can roll to adjust volume or press to control the ANC modes, which include adaptive ANC (adjusting cancellation/transparency in real-time) and Spatial Audio (creates an immersive, 3D soundstage for music/movies). On the other side, you'll find an "Energy Slider," which tunes your sound in real-time, instantly adjusting the treble and bass balance.

You'll get an impressive 100 hours of playback on a single charge (reduced to up to 50 hours with ANC turned on) as well as AAC, SBC, and LDAC support. They have an IPX2 rating for resistance against sweat, and there is a 3.5mm audio jack for wired listening.

Nothing is known for its minimalistic design, but these headphones do a bit more by allowing you to mix and match the earcups with different colors (sold separately for $25). These are a good option for those looking for stylish, budget over-ear headphones that have great battery life and excellent audio quality for their price point.
