#3456. 15-Year-Old MCU Easter Egg Officially Confirmed By Marvel Creator

WARNING: This article includes spoilers from VisionQuest season 1, episode 7.EXCLUSIVE: The Marvel Cinematic Universe is honoring one of its earliest Easter eggs all the way back to Phase 1.

The Multiverse Saga is currently getting close to finishing one of its remaining TV shows, with VisionQuest serving as the finale to the WandaVision trilogy. Throughout the whole season, the spinoff series have made various nods and callbacks to the larger mythology that began all the way back in 2008 with Iron Man.

In ScreenRant's VisionQuest cover story with Liam Crowley, showrunner Terry Matalas was asked about the major reveal of Jim Hammond, a.k.a. the Synthetic Man in episode 7, with Paul Bettany taking on another role in the franchise. As the story established that Phineas Horton created the first robot to honor his son, thus the connections to Vision, the executive producer elaborated on whether this was something he and Kevin Feige collaborated on from the Easter egg in Captain America: The First Avenger, or if it came to fruition organically within the creative team.

Matalas said, "No, that came up in the writers' room as we were digging in. I knew from lore that Vision was created from parts and components of Jim Hammond in the comic books. And even though there was a different kind of creation in the MCU, what if some of his source code came from Jim Hammond?" He continued by sharing "that shone a beacon on another kind of family story; a generational story where you have the grandfather of AI and his missteps as a father, not being able to connect to his creation, and that being passed down to Ultron and Vision through this code that Josephine Carrington wrote."

For the writers behind the VisionQuest TV show, the showrunner "felt like we were telling this big family story. There was a family tree being built as we were making the show." Jim was briefly seen in Captain America: The First Avenger when Steve Rogers and Bucky Barnes were attending Stark EXPO during 1943. It wasn't until the WandaVision offshoot that the android got re-explored and given its biggest exposure yet.

#3453. ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’s Most Terrifying Enemy Isn’t Inside the Dungeon

Dungeon Crawler Carl has completely taken over geek culture, which is impressive considering how hard it is to sum up the premise. The early novels take every big risk imaginable in a fantasy/science fiction story, and it does not make for a concise elevator pitch. However, even if you manage to break down this set up, the story evolves quickly to focus on much greater enemies outside the dungeon. This will be essential to understand when the TV adaptation premieres on Peacock, especially for new fans who may not realize what they're getting into. The show will have to balance the visual spectacle of the dungeon with the true story of Carl and his allies' secretive attempts to sabotage the game from within.

Dungeon Crawler Carl has come a long way from a serialized story self-published online to a best-selling novel series. Author Matt Dinniman has risen to the occasion at every step, coaxing the narrative to grow and evolve without straying too far from the wacky premise at its core. Still, it's been clear from the beginning that the dungeon itself is a sideshow, while humanity's real enemies are living amongst the stars. This balances well in the novels and makes for a fun, fast-paced adventure, but it may be difficult to bring to TV.

If you heard about Dungeon Crawler Carl via word of mouth, you probably got an elevator pitch something like this: Aliens take over earth and use advanced technology to instantly create a video game-like space inside the planet. Most humans are killed, and the survivors are encouraged to enter the dungeon to compete on an intergalactic game show called "Dungeon Crawler World." Awoken in the middle of the night, Carl enters with no shoes, not pants, and his ex-girlfriend's cat as his only companion. The dungeon makes his cat sentient and the two fight their way through the game in the hopes of surviving and restoring what they can of earth as they knew it.

That's all accurate, and it prioritizes what a new fan would need to know getting into the series without spoiling anything or focusing too much on details that will become important later. However, it could also give new fans some misinterpretations about the series. For one thing, recommendations like these tend to gloss over the fact that advanced aliens have been watching earth for thousands of years, and cultivating the planet to play this game one day. They gloss over the ancient technology already present on earth before the game began, and the tension between various alien factions as well as the System A.I. itself. It's true that these details aren't necessary at the beginning, but they become so integral later on that it can feel disingenuous to leave them out.

"There is some good in this world, Mr. Frodo... and it is worth fighting for."

Someone who actually picks up the Dungeon Crawler Carl novels will learn pretty quickly that the book isn't really about the game show itself. Carl and his allies look at the game only as a means of surviving, and they take every opportunity to undermine it for the viewers and the aliens involved. Ultimately, Carl's goal is to get the game shut down somehow and earn freedom for himself and the rest of the earthlings. It becomes a highly political story that some viewers might not be expecting, evoking themes of colonialism and violent uprising.

Meanwhile, the mystery of the alien technology is the central question of the series before long. To a newcomer, it's odd that this technology which is utilized for such an absurd, specific purpose can become a mystery later on, but in the context of the books it works beautifully. The question is whether the TV adaptation will pull it off as well — hopefully without softening the story's sharp edges in the process.

The best way for the TV adaptation to handle all of this confusion would be to broaden the audience's perspective early on. The books are written in the first person, and the audience learns about the worldbuilding and the conflicts at the same rate as Carl — more or less. However, adaptations often break out of this first-person perspective early on. It's harder to pull off in a visual medium, and it's difficult to disperse all the exposition needed from just one set of eyes.

Ideally, Peacock's adaptation will tease mysteries about the Borant Corporation, the various alien factions, and the System A.I. early on. If it needs to mix in scenes without Carl and Donut to do so, it will be worth it. The show has the luxury of looking ahead at what's important and interesting in the later books, and planting those ideas earlier than they were in the books. This is how adaptations get credit for strengthening their stories along the way.

For now, Dungeon Crawler Carl lives only on the page, and its transition to TV is a mystery on its own. There are eight novels available now in print, digital, and audiobook formats, with a ninth on the way and a tenth expected to finish the saga. Peacock's TV adaptation is in production now, but there's no word on when it may be released.

#3452. AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into the App Store

Hundreds of AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into Apple’s App Store after passing app review. The same apps were also available in the Google Play Store.

An investigation discovered more than 400 apps, apparently created by a single Chinese organization. The apps allow users to upload photos and then generate sexual and violent deepfakes which could be used to humiliate or threaten victims …

A Wired investigation discovered a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps with hidden abusive functionality.

Apps like Viefur [ostentibly used to add clothing to pet photos] often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

I feel like this going to be a never ending cat and mouse game. Much like Apple has always had with jailbreaks.

Wired says that the network is “hiding in plain sight,” thanks to thousands of video ads for them published on Facebook and Instagram. Some of the apps have been around for a year and have passed review by Apple, Google, and Meta despite each having clear policies prohibiting harmful deepfake content.

Bait-and-switch tactics were used to pass app review. The apps normally show benign content, but a server check can activate the hidden features. Downloading the app after tapping an ad for the deepfake functionality on Meta platforms appears to be one of the triggers. Dozens of pornography photo and video templates can then be downloaded, with credits purchased to generate deepfakes from user-uploaded photos.

Apple removed 19 apps after Wired shared details.

We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them. After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.

The company recently strengthened protections against this approach. Meta says it has taken action against more than 10,000 ad accounts linked to domains associated with these apps.

#3451. What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night?

What does an audience need from its movie theater on election night?

A provocation? A distraction? Something… else? Across our semi-united, Letterboxd-loving nation, new microcinemas are opening up, old movies are selling out, and local programmers are giving film fans tons of exciting reasons to hit the box office.

Also breaking, I guess: the U.S. midterms. (Go vote!)

This election cycle, the future of Hollywood remains an open question, as does the strength of our democracy. With control of Congress at stake, voters are debating what they want their country to become — and, in many cases, what they’re afraid it already is — to spectacular and exhausting effect. Related Stories ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was

Boarding yourself up in a movie palace like one of Joe Dante’s gremlins seems sort of reasonable under the circumstances. Thick walls, emergency snacks, and no checking your phone makes buying a movie ticket on November 3 an intriguing proposition in the U.S.

IndieWire spoke with 14 theater operators, programmers, filmmakers, educators, and authors across 12 states, including California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, and Wisconsin. Their answers offer a weirdly hopeful view of communities looking for comfort, perspective, and somewhere to be when the results come in.

At Las Vegas’ Beverly Theater at least, the connection is intentional: Reese Witherspoon and Matthew Broderick’s “Election” shares the day’s lineup with “The Devils” and “The History of Concrete.”

“We program The Beverly as a reflection of what’s happening outside our doors,” founding creative director and CXO Kip Kelly wrote. “Politics has become such an absurd spectacle that a dark comedy about a high school student council election might actually be one of the more sophisticated conversations you’ll have that day.”

Meanwhile, at Nashville’s Belcourt, a popcorn bag oversees the transfer of programming power. The theater’s monthly Staff Picks series typically falls on the first Tuesday, with a name drawn from a bag determining the employee who chooses the film. This time, someone picked “Under the Silver Lake”: the L.A. conspiracy thriller that’s paranoid enough to make anyone start connecting the deep-state dots.

“It’s totally a coincidence,” programming director Toby Leonard told IndieWire, laughing on the phone. “We realized what we had done after the fact.”

AFS Cinema programmer Lars Nilsen was similarly blunt about his Austin theater’s approach.

“We just programmed it as a regular week.” Nilsen resisted recruiting “The Good, the Bad and the Ugly” into any kind of election commentary, instead describing its Italian vision of the Old West as “the kind of dream America that Italians thought they understood about America itself.”

That said, tonight’s gathering still matters to Nilsen — even when the movie AFS is showing has nothing to do with the election itself. He pointed to the Texas organization’s addition of a third screen as a vote of confidence in people continuing to show up for one another through repertory culture.

“I think very intricately and carefully programmed cinemas are one of the places where community is being reborn,” Nilsen said. “Thank goodness.”

For Harlem’s Maysles Documentary Center, building community and considering who gets to tell that community’s story is the program’s point. Executive director Kazembe Balagun deliberately selected “BLKNWS: Terms & Conditions” for an evening that’s ordinarily devoted to watching the news.

He said he wanted to ask: “How do we imagine ourselves, represent our communities and think about power beyond the ballot box?” Plus, “I just think it’s a dope film.”

The “BLKNWS” screening is followed by a neighborly gathering echoing the center’s other events, from World Cup sidewalk screenings to group viewing for the Knicks playoff games. “I think that it’s not just what we put on the screen, but also the rooms that we create,” Balagun said. “The party afterwards is intentional because right now we live in a time where our communities are so fragmented.”

At Pennsylvania’s Gap Theatre, Spectral Cinema programmers Adrianna Gober and Dan Santelli are confronting power as an ambitious intellectual team. Their 35mm selection, Bresson’s “The Devil, Probably,” follows a young man overwhelmed by disillusionment with the institutions around him.

“The film speaks so much to the feelings of alienation and powerlessness that a lot of people are grappling with right now,” Gober wrote. She described the struggle to find meaning and control as “a tug of war between hope and despair.”

Santelli sharply cautioned against allowing that despair to become another reason to give up. “In the current political climate, it’s all too easy to fall into a feedback loop of despair and resignation, whereby the recognition of one’s apparent powerlessness becomes a justification for further inaction,” he wrote, adding he’s “less interested in offering audiences an opportunity for catharsis than one for reflection.”

That distinction runs through other programmers’ choices, too. Just look at “The Devils.”

At Minneapolis’ Trylon, John Moret chose Ken Russell’s film to cap the witchy “Evil Incantations” series after its restoration was announced at this spring’s national Programmers’ Jam in L.A., which he co-organized. The Warner Bros. Clockwork news sent a room full of repertory devotees into a frenzy months before “The Devils” mania got properly started — and Moret saw the opportunity to send his audience at Trylon from the voting booth straight into Russell’s religious nightmare back then.

Every screening has sold out since, Moret said. And personally, he often spends election night at the movies: “I think that there’s going to be plenty of people who are looking for distraction.”

Art can offer distance while leaving a lot to recognize on a deeper level, but even outrageously visual, avoidance and arthouse rarely mix. Moret praised the magical appeal of Russell and “The Devils” specifically, and said great film “should reverberate truth in a way that connects with you, but also allows you to be at a different time and place and truly put it into perspective.”

At Brookline’s Coolidge Corner Theatre, the 1971 film is sticking around for the same reason: The worshippers just keep coming. Now in its third week, “The Devils” shares the November 3 calendar with “Voting Counts: Elections in Film,” an adult film class that proved popular enough to require a second section. The program was conceived for election season, but “Network” also got its turn on Election Eve.

“We want this to be everybody’s movie house. We want our audiences to feel at home here,” Coolidge Corner artistic director Mark Anastasio told IndieWire. “There has to be a variety of programming appealing to the diverse appetites of the Boston area.”

In Milwaukee, author Matthew J. Prigge is about to discover what his favorite movie feels like in a theater.

His book event at the Oriental Theatre includes a screening of “Dog Day Afternoon,” which Prigge spent years researching for his nonfiction “Dog’s Day.” But somehow has never actually seen on the big screen. The election timing was mostly coincidental, though Prigge recognizes the relevance of Sidney Lumet’s film — about a man robbing a bank to fund his lover’s gender-affirming surgery — in 2026.

The actual robbery, the writer cautioned, has a more complicated history than its Hollywood adaptation. Still, Prigge said, “I think that the movie works just because it’s such a human story and it gets to the actual people that are involved and it makes it relatable, it makes it very raw.”

He also noted that for one evening watching the 1975 title wouldn’t be work for him: “That’s a big deal for me to see it as a communal experience. It’s been a while since I’ve been able to just sit back and enjoy it.”

For Hyperreal Film Club’s Blake Williams in Texas, finding an audience to join helped make a new city feel like home — but things are “definitely tense” in Austin, he said. After moving south from Indiana, Williams discovered the organization through its eclectic programming and eventually joined their team.

Now, he says his closest LGBTQ friends in the local film scene are considering leaving the state because they feel unsafe. His election-night offering to a community he wants to keep together? “Hardball.” After a month of Halloween horror, Williams wanted the kind of crying that comes with a good ol’ sports movie, and Keanu Reeves coaching a group of kids offers a true tale of common ground through weepy comfort.

“You kind of want to see a change in these things happen and you hope that it’ll happen, but at least film can kind of make people forget about these things,” he said. “I think it’s cool that we’re able to offer our comforts to the community to put them at ease, even if it’s just for a few hours.”

Relief means different things to different moviegoers, and at North Kansas City’s Screenland Armour, co-owner Adam Roberts is offering the new “Wild at Heart” restoration, alongside animation studio Laika’s first-run “Wildwood.” The former’s booking followed the remaster’s pre-planned release schedule, but Roberts nevertheless sees David Lynch’s dark vision of American life as an prime excuse for escapism.

“We are highly engaged in our local community and routinely show political films,” he wrote to IndieWire. “I think for patrons looking for a distraction on Election Night, there is no better place than the cinema.”

Charlotte’s Independent Picture House discussed special election programming before deciding its existing lineup already had the assignment covered, too. Creative director Jay Morong, also a senior lecturer at UNC Charlotte, pointed to “Wild at Heart,” “The Devils,” and specifically “Digger.”

“These are all movies that are addressing very specific things that are in the consciousness of the voter at this moment in time,” he said. “Let’s just roll with what we got because this is what independent and art house theaters do.” IPH’s monthly filmmaker meetup also happened to fall on election night, giving North Carolina’s indie community somewhere to discuss results that could affect their livelihoods.

“We are constantly battling against the state government and the incentives and them cutting back on budgets here,” Morong said, lamenting a decline in area film and TV productions. “So the film community is very actively involved in who is winning these state and federal elections and how they’re [using their voice] or cheerleading for the film industry in North Carolina.”

In Los Angeles, moviegoers can leave the voting booth for something that looks suspiciously like… another one? At WHAMMY, Julie Orlick’s One Person Cinema fits a chair, a television, and a viewer wearing headphones inside a five-by-three-by-six-foot room. The resemblance wasn’t intentional, but when someone pointed it out, an election-night opening felt fitting.

“We all just thought it’d be a good fun thing to do after a serious day of activities,” she said.

The premiere offering features her erotic short “DÉSIR,” and unlike an actual voting booth, this one has a peephole through which someone outside can watch the person watching.

“The only people who get to experience it are the people that go inside the room,” Orlick said. “And I think that also brings a secrecy to the film.” The experimental artist said she built the installation as a final project at UCLA, conceiving a private encounter with intimate images she wanted to keep off the internet. With WHAMMY and TAPE, she developed a residency featuring other filmmakers’ work, too.

An accompanying screening of “Les fantômes du hard” in WHAMMY’s larger microcinema rounds out an evening with considerably more erotic material than the average polling place — and you can find Orlick’s One Person Cinema inside the Echo Park microcinema all month.

Alternatively, over in Illinois, audiences at Chicago’s Gene Siskel Film Center can travel the globe without leaving their seats. Jia Zhangke’s “The World” — set among workers at a Beijing theme park filled with miniature global landmarks — screens as part of “Contact Zones,” a public series and lecture class taught by School of the Art Institute of Chicago professor Daniel Quiles.

“We’re given a sort of official line that we’re a polarized country or that we have arch enemies around the world,” Quiles said. “How can art give us a different way of framing these things?”

The professor’s interest in globalization’s recent past grew from questions about what retreating from it might cost. The screening film’s he’s chosen bring students, museum curators, and other moviegoers together to consider their stakes seriously: “I think by watching a film like ‘The World, ‘we might see parallels to the underclass in our own country rather than seeing China as some big bad guy.”

Finally, among respondents to IndieWire’s latest Reddit inquiry, several welcomed a few hours away from the election. Being “expressly forbidden from looking at my phone” was a selling point for one; but another, invested in a tight race, couldn’t contemplate the disconnect.

Meanwhile, others had already discharged their civic duties to make room for a different national emergency: Godzilla. “I voted early specifically so I can see Godzilla Minus Zero on Godzilla Day without having to worry about making it back to vote on time,” one kaiju fan wrote.

In Washington, D.C., another moviegoer plans to see A24’s “The Drama” at Suns Cinema.

“I didn’t realize it was election night when I bought the tickets, but I love supporting Suns any day of the year,” they wrote in an email to IndieWire. With its would-be wedding mired in finger-pointing, the popular flick from earlier this year feels well-suited to the socially charged D.C. setting — even if this moviegoer’s turnout concerns are more personal than political.

“I will hopefully be going with my crush (fingers crossed) if they respond to my texts,” they said.

DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Those numbers line up with what you’d expect from a unit this size, and they make it useful for both emergencies and planned outdoor use.

You also get a solid mix of ports—there are three AC outlets, a 30-amp port for heavier appliances or RV setups, multiple USB-C ports (including a 140W option for laptops), and DJI’s own SDC ports for direct drone charging. If you use DJI gear, that alone makes life easier in the field, notes this Mashable review. Recharging is also fast for a battery this size. Plugged into a wall outlet, it can go from empty to full in about 90 minutes. You can also top it up with solar panels or from your car, which makes it workable for longer trips. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.

#3448. Marvel Studios Brings Back Thanos' Black Order With A Shocking Twist

Warning! This article contains SPOILERS for VisionQuest episode 7.VisionQuest's new episode marks the end of an era for the Marvel Cinematic Universe series, as this is the first time that the Disney+ show releases a single episode, rather than two. Next week, episode 8 will mark the end of VisionQuest, setting up Tommy Maximoff, Vision, Ultron, and more for new MCU adventures. On last week's VisionQuest episodes, the live-action MCU TV show brought back Raza, a villain connected to the shadowy Ten Rings organization who made his debut in the franchise's very first project, Robert Downey Jr.'s Iron Man, back in 2008. Raza was unable to take Vision.

VisionQuest episodes 5 and 6 also touched on whether Ultron was fully behind Jocasta's plan to enslave humanity, which the Marvel series' new hour further explores. Lisa Molinari was the first victim of Jocasta's nanotechnology, and it could lead to her Marvel Comics fate, with the character becoming a villain Tommy will have to deal with. In VisionQuest's new episode, the MCU has finally turned to the comics to shine the spotlight on an underrated character that has a long history in the franchise, while also putting two major VisionQuest players in danger ahead of the series finale next week.

One of the biggest secrets in the MCU series has been related to the identity of The Client, the mysterious character that keeps sending bounty hunters like Paladin and Raza after Paul Bettany's Vision. Disney+'s VisionQuest finally answers the question of who The Client is, at least partially. Over the course of six episodes, fans came up with different theories for whom the character might be, with some of the debated names including Jim Hammond, Marvel Comics' first Human Torch, and Captain America franchise villain Arnim Zola, among others. However, The Client turned out to be none of those.

VisionQuest is a phenomenal contribution to the wider MCU, delivering a series that not only smashes superhero fatigue but also transcends the genre.

At the end of the episode, The Client is revealed to be played by none other than James Spader, the MCU's Ultron actor. The character's name is not revealed in VisionQuest episode 7, with Marvel leaving that part of the surprise for the series finale to unwrap. However, given that Spader plays him, the MCU has already revealed who The Client is, partially. He is the human that the Ultron AI based his human design on. Much like how E.D.I.T.H. discovered in past episodes that she was based on Stark Industries test pilot Edith Marks, the other AIs follow a similar pattern.

VisionQuest episode 7 sets up the finale with two major characters' fates hanging in the balance. One of them is F.R.I.D.A.Y., who seemingly fell to her death after Ultron threw her off a balcony inside Jocasta's mind. That said, it would make no sense for her to die here. After all, Ultron previously showed that he was not fully onboard with Jocasta's brutal plan for humanity. Additionally, in the Marvel series' new episode, Spader's MCU villain reveals to F.R.I.D.A.Y. that not only did he know she was hiding in Jocasta's mind, but he was actively hiding her from the new Marvel foe.

It was always Ultron's plan to find out who was behind Jocasta's creation, but nowhere did it seem like he wanted to really kill F.R.I.D.A.Y. as part of his course of action, so she might still be alive despite how the fall looked. The other character in trouble heading into the VisionQuest finale is Paladin. The bounty hunter went from a foe to a friend of sorts in episode 7. After delivering Vision to The Client, just like Bettany's MCU hero wanted him to, The Client's security team hit Paladin's van with a missile. Following the TV rule of "no body, no death," he could still be alive.

After being teased multiple times in past episodes, VisionQuest episode 7 finally brought in the first Human Torch from Marvel Comics, who goes by the Synthetic Man in the MCU, J.I.M. The android was created by scientist Phineas Horton a couple of years after he lost his son, James, serving as a stronger replacement who would not leave the saddened character so easily. However, Horton's obsession with crafting J.I.M. eventually led to his wife and young daughter, Victoria, leaving him. Horton is played by an aged up Paul Bettany, confirming that he is the one who inspired Vision's human persona.

Bettany ends up pulling triple duty in the latest episode of VisionQuest, as not only does the actor give life to Vision, but also to Phineas Horton and J.I.M., with the latter helping White Vision understand that he and the original Vision are one and the same. Previously, he kept referring to that Vision as the original and the one who experienced love with Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch, but by looking deep within his mind and understanding where Horton and J.I.M. failed, he embraces all sides of himself. Horton died being consumed by fire alongside J.I.M. when the latter lost control after being sent spinning when he found love.

VisionQuest episode 7 also continues the trip down memory lane for Vision with a not so happy memory. While Thanos and the Black Order might no longer be part of the MCU, Marvel Studios just brought back a powerful weapon one of them wielded in a creative way that perfectly fit the story being told in the Disney+ series. Vision needs an immensely powerful power source to be able to tap into the depths of his code to find Phineas Horton and J.I.M. He ends up going after Paladin for help, and the bounty hunter possesses the perfect item.

Corvus Glaive's scepter/spear, the very same weapon that he used to impale Vision in 2018's Avengers: Infinity War, returns as the modified power source that allows Vision to find exactly what he needs to not only accept himself but also save Lisa Molinari. It is a fitting way to reinterpret something from Vision's past to serve his present journey, which is all that VisionQuest is about. Now, it remains to be seen how all these threads will come together when VisionQuest episode 8 releases on Disney+ on November 10.

That’s enough to cover the front and back doors, a couple of ground-floor windows, and a main hallway in an apartment or smaller house. It also doesn’t require a subscription, so once you’ve paid for the system, you won’t have to worry about ongoing monthly fees.

With the sensors in place, you’ll get an instant notification through the free Eufy app whenever someone opens a protected door or window, while the motion sensor can detect movement in areas like a living room or hallway. Not everyone in the household needs the app to use the system, though, since the included keypad lets family members or a house sitter arm and disarm it right at the door. Everything connects back to the HomeBase Mini, which serves as the central hub with built-in storage that keeps everything stored locally.

Setting up the system takes minutes, as the battery-powered sensors require no wiring and the app guides you through each step once the HomeBase is plugged in. That said, you will need to replace the sensor batteries periodically, and a larger home with several entrances may require more than the four entry sensors and one motion sensor included in the kit—you can add more Eufy sensors and accessories as needed, but each comes at an extra cost. And if you want to see what triggered an alert, you'll have to purchase compatible cameras separately, since no cameras are included in the package.

#3446. Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

Clipfarming, influencer screenings, and meme-bait popcorn buckets: promoting a movie in the internet age is often a full-court offensive to get noticed. In that spirit, why not just get down to business and resort to modern civilization’s oldest method for seeking attention: dangling some money in people’s faces?

That’s what the marketing teams behind “How to Rob a Bank,” from Amazon MGM Studios, and “Ebenezer,” from Skydance’s Paramount Pictures, have tried in the weeks leading up to their shared November 13 release to North American theaters.

For the former ensemble heist thriller, a branded ATM was moved between multiplexes throughout the Los Angeles area over the course of four days. Those who learned of the campaign on the film‘s social media channels could gain clues about the machine’s location and a specified PIN number, which would spark payouts of a single one-hundred-dollar bill to those who bothered to seek out (or stumble upon) it. Related Stories What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night? Don’t Forget, Oscar Watchers: ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and Other Big Guns Are Coming Back

“Ebenezer” took a more cheeky, trifling approach, promoting an official Venmo account for Johnny Depp’s Christmas crab apple that users could request funds from. Those who scrolled through the account’s transactions would see it shares the character’s penny-pinching spirit: the only completed transactions were those giving away one single cent. The Venmo account was only active for a few hours, though a Paramount Instagram post from last week teases followers to “check back” as “Ebenezer might be feeling generous on @venmo again.”

Several film news aggregation accounts like Culture Crave and DiscussingFilm reported that the account “crashed” due an overwhelming amount of requests, though Paramount declined to comment on if such a description was accurate. Venmo did not respond to a request asking if the company partnered with the studio on the sponsorship.

Much like that line, there is also a tackiness du jour to both money-mindset stunts, especially in a world where awards shows, professional sports and geopolitical events can hardly be watched without outlets asking you to bet — erh, predict — on them. A video posted to Paramount’s socials opens with a Venmo request for $500, asking Scrooge to help pay off a user’s student loans.

Not to mention the real inadvertent quirk: the account has been able to receive payments from users. Considering the scant number of one-cent payouts from the account and the number of influxes, it is almost certain that Paramount could have made money on the stunt, though an individual with knowledge of the account shared that all received funds were sent back to users via private transactions.

Krystyna Ursta, a 27-year-old actress, video editor, and Depp fan in Los Angeles, shared that she gave about $30 to the account and received a full refund a few days later — plus an extra penny and an invitation to a special screening of the film in New York on Monday. She will be attending a local press screening instead. Ursta also posted a video of herself reacting to the account, one of many fan responses that flooded in on social media.

“I kind of figured that they will probably return it,” Ursta wrote over text after being reached through her Instagram handle, which she included in her Venmo transactions. “I’m such a big fan. I was happy to support the film.”

The rather gimmick-less gimmick of waving around money also helps capture the attention of people that aren’t necessarily interested in seeing the movie, but are going through the average modern experience of thinking about one’s financial situation. Aggregation accounts were quick to post graphics reporting on both stunts, with captions like “HOW TO ROB A BANK ATM’S ARE BEING SET UP AROUND LOS ANGELES AND GIVING PEOPLE FREE MONEY AND IT COULDN’T HAPPEN AT A BETTER TIME” and “EBENEZER SCROOGE WILL SEND YOU REAL MONEY ON VENMO BUT THERE’S A CATCH SWIPE FOR MORE.”

There’s also people like Scott, a 35-year-old based out of Atlanta that couldn’t help but engage with the “Ebenezer” Venmo account after seeing it on X. He sent a penny, then received one in return. (A disclaimer: six Venmo users were reached for interview about their Ebenezer experience by sending them $0.01 with this reporter’s contact information in the caption; Scott was the only response that timed out before publication.)

“Seeing Ebenezer is now on Venmo was too funny and stupid to not engage with,” he wrote over text. “There’s something very boring dystopia about it: the idea of a fictional character from a 200-year-old Christmas story being commercialized on Venmo just shows how dumb Hollywood can. … It’s like McDonald’s Monopoly: take our slop and we might give your money.”

Also helpful for the studios is how little dangling the potential of money actually costs. Sans staffing fees, producing the “Ebenezer” Venmo account and its activity used a sum less than the coins between the couch cushions on the Paramount lot. Per the “How to Rob a Bank” promo’s website, each location’s prize pool gave away ten one-hundred-dollar bills and twenty twenty-dollar-bills ($1,400 total), plus some theater-supplied prizes like gift cards. An employee at the Regal Sherman Oaks that worked on the day of the on-site promotion said the ATM seemed to deal out the rewards in a random order, as opposed to $100 dollar bills for the first finders. Amazon MGM declined to comment, while Stellar Agency Inc., which sponsored and administered the promotion, did not respond to a request.

Both had much smaller overheads than a “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t” promotion than ran in April 2025. To launch the magician threequel’s first trailer, Lionsgate reportedly gave away roughly $250,000 to those that texted a mysterious phone number displaying in Times Square in the hours up to the drop. Like “Ebenezer” and “How to Rob a Bank,” it was a promotion that sparked a viral moment with plenty of user-generated content, each sharing the widely desired fantasy of receiving free money.

Neon handed out basic resources for an “I Love Boosters” promotion in May, where stars KeKe Palmer and LaKeith Stanfield took over a Shell gas station in West Pico to give out complimentary refills to the first 70 cars that arrived. The stunt played on then-peaking fuel prices, which had skyrocketed in the wake of the U.S.’ initial bombing of Iran in February and the subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

In the months since, President Trump has promised $5,000 checks to every adult U.S. citizen if the Republican Party retains control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Trump announced the idea, his approval rating was at a dismal 35 percent, per a CNN aggregate of various polls. Though the offer is unprecedented and dubious on its face, it has been covered extensively — and it cost nothing to float it.

#3445. Affinity for iPad all-in-one design app now available, free for individuals

Design app Affinity has long been popular with Mac users, and a long-awaited iPad version has launched today. Canva promises that Affinity for iPad offers “the same pro-level power” as the Mac app.

It’s been a year since the company’s vector, photo, and layout tools were unified into a single app on Mac, and the same is now true on iPad …

Created specifically for the touch-first interface and unique capabilities of iPad and Apple Pencil, the app brings professional sketch, vector, photo and layout editing together with the same pro-level power of Affinity on the desktop […]

With Affinity for iPad, creatives can take a project from first sketch with Apple Pencil to print-ready file on iPad alone. And it’s free for individuals, just like Affinity on desktop, which has recorded more than seven million sign-ups since launching a year ago.

“Creative work doesn’t stay in one discipline, so your tools shouldn’t either,” said Duncan Clark, CEO of Pro Design at Canva. “Since we brought Affinity together on desktop, our biggest user request has been the desire to bring it to iPad. Today we’re delivering it: a fully-fledged, professional app built for touch.”

Being able to carry out all of the work within a single app on a single file is a key attraction of Affinity. The integrated app replaces the separate Affinity Photo, Affinity Publisher, and Affinity Designer apps.

Sketch: Rough out concepts the moment they land, with the unique capabilities of Apple Pencil like pressure and tilt in every mark, thick where you press and soft where you tilt. A full brush library comes with controls to shape each brush into the exact tool you need. Sketches stay live in the file to build on, rather than trace again.

Vector: Responsive, smooth and under control. Build a full logo or icon system with real curves and precise nodes, or bring a rough drawing through from Sketch. Sketch to Shapes turns hand-drawn forms into clean vector shapes.

Photo: Fine-tune RAW files, make intelligent selections, retouch in real time and build full composites at the shoot or on the go. Users can even sketch over a photo first to plan where a subject or prop should sit. The Mask Tool finds the boundary as the Apple Pencil pixel precision runs along a challenging edge, so hair, fur and foliage take a stroke rather than an afternoon. Every mask, grade and retouch stays live and undoable, even thousands of layers deep.

Layout: Create multi-page documents such as ‘zines, lookbooks and photo books, with text and images flowing across pages; master pages and grids keep everything consistent, and typography exactly right. Projects go all the way to a print-ready file with proper colour handling.

Canva says the app supports all of the advanced capabilities of Apple Pencil Pro: pressure, tilt, barrel roll, squeeze, and hover. AI features include generative expand, upscaling resolution, and adding attributes like motion blur. A Decompose Layer feature even splits a flat image into editable layers.

Affinity for iPad is a free download from the App Store.

#3444. HBO Max's 10-Episode Sci-Fi Series Could Be the Perfect 'Lanterns' Replacement

Lanterns is the kind of success no one expected. The more grounded take on Green Lantern lore, combined with excellent character work from leads Kyle Chandler as Hal Jordan and Aaron Pierre as John Stewart, created a winning formula and made Lanterns one of the most-watched shows on HBO Max. While a second season of Lanterns remains in development, that doesn't mean DC Studios is done with Green Lantern. Pierre is set to return as John Stewart in Man of Tomorrow next year, while Nathan Fillion is reprising his role as Guy Gardner for Mister Miracle. Another series looks to embrace all the cosmic elements of Green Lantern while building out the world of another fan-favorite DC series.

Appropriately enough, this new series is titled My Adventures with Green Lantern. Spinning out of the events of My Adventures with Superman, My Adventures with Green Lantern will see Jessica Cruz (Auli'i Cravalho) joining the Green Lantern Corps. There's just one catch: while the Guardians of the Universe usually choose Green Lanterns, Jessica becomes a Green Lantern when a power ring literally lands in her lap. She's then pulled into the fight of her life "when more debris from the Lanterns’ ancient space war arrives – along with their alien foes," according to the official logline.

One of the major debates surrounding Lanterns is that its narrative felt better suited to a terrestrial DC hero like Batman or the Question than to two men charged with defending the universe from interstellar threats. While the show mentions other Green Lanterns like Ch'p the squirrel and Mogo the living planet, some viewers felt there could have been more Green Lantern elements in a show called Lanterns. My Adventures with Green Lantern is about to fulfill their wish, as the series is set to bring in plenty of characters from the comics. A preview at Annecy Festival reveals that Jessica attends Hal Jordan Memorial High, with her classmates, including future Green Lantern Kyle Rayner.

Jessica will also have to deal with other Green Lanterns, most notably the Corps' drill sergeant, Kilowog. She will also be fighting Yellow and Red Lanterns in the series, hinting at the presence of two iconic Green Lantern villains. The Yellow Lanterns are usually part of the Sinestro Corps, led by the titular Sinestro — Hal Jordan's former mentor and Green Lantern who now wields the yellow power of fear. The Red Lanterns, on the other hand, draw on the red power of rage thanks to their leader, Atrocitus. The presence of Yellow and Red Lanterns hints that My Adventures with Green Lantern will explore the emotional spectrum established in Geoff Johns' Green Lantern run, and that it'll be a more cosmic affair than Lanterns was. Producer Jake Wyatt also said that he wanted the villains to stand out at Annecy:

“We wanted to get weird with the bad guys. We needed hot evil people to scare the hell out of Jess and her buddies.”

Your answers point to the iconic sci-fi hero who shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of facing the impossible.

You carry a weight most people would crumble under — the knowledge of what you're capable of, and the burden of what you might have to become.

You lead with instinct, warmth, and an absolute refusal to accept a no-win scenario — because you've always believed there's a third option nobody else has thought of yet.

You are the kind of person who holds the line when everyone else is losing faith — not because you're fearless, but because giving up simply isn't something you're capable of.

You are not reckless, not grandiose, and not particularly interested in being anyone's hero — you just refuse to stop when it matters.

You have been through fire that would break most people — and what came out the other side is something the world underestimates at its peril.

While My Adventures with Green Lantern is spinning out of My Adventures with Superman, it's inspired by another iconic series. My Adventures with Superman draws heavily on shonen anime like Dragon Ball Z, while My Adventures with Green Lantern draws heavily on Sailor Moon. A clip shown at Annecy features Jessica singing the iconic Green Lantern oath and transforming into a costume that largely resembles Sailor Moon's, putting another unique stamp on the Green Lantern mythos.

Lanterns was only the beginning of DC Studios fully embracing the Green Lantern comics, as My Adventures with Green Lantern looks poised to revamp the mythos for a new generation. It's a far cry from the days of Ryan Reynolds' box-office bomb, and the "brightest day" that these characters deserve.

#3443. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3442. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3441. Here’s everything new Apple TV has coming in November

Apple TV’s November lineup includes the return of a beloved comedy, a heist thriller with big stars, the follow-up film to its Oscar winner, and a lot more. Here’s everything new coming to Apple TV in November.

“Stick” is a sports comedy series created by Jason Keller and starring and executive produced by Owen Wilson. Wilson stars as Pryce Cahill, an over-the-hill, ex-pro golfer whose career was derailed prematurely 20 years ago. After the collapse of his marriage and while working at an Indiana sporting goods store, Pryce hedges his bets, and future, entirely on a troubled 17-year-old golf phenom named Santi (Peter Dager). “Stick” is a heartfelt, feel-good comedy about a found family and their relationships set within the world of golf as it has never been shown before.

Hollywood actor and comedian Nora Lum (aka Awkwafina) is the descendant of restaurant royalty … but she can’t cook. Join the star on an inspiring culinary road trip as she learns the craft and attempts to revive her family’s beloved Chinese eatery.

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

They wouldn’t take Judy Heumann’s phone calls, so she took their building. In 1977, a young disabled woman (Ruth Madeley) and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way (Mark Ruffalo) takes action. Bringing rebellion in all its forms to the hallowed halls, a movement’s accidental leaders struggle to find their path forward where none has ever been paved for them. Directed by Academy Award winner Siân Heder (“CODA”) and based on true events, “Being Heumann” is the revolutionary, irreverent and deeply human story of the least likely people trying to pull off the impossible and change the lives of millions.

In the latest special under the acclaimed “Snoopy Presents” banner, the Peanuts kids are on their best behavior — but Snoopy has landed on Santa’s naughty list. With just 12 days until Christmas, he sets out to prove he’s not such a bad beagle after all, discovering along the way that the season is about more than gifts.

Middle school has been a nightmare for Marc (Jude Hill), a good kid who’s bullied by his classmates and feels like he’s behind in everything, from academics to P.E. to just making friends. That changes when his injured Uncle Jake (Chris Pratt), a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to spend the summer and recuperate with Marc and his mom, Sarah (Linda Cardellini). To help Marc defend himself, Jake devises an ambitious program he calls “Operation Warrior Kid” based on his SEAL training. Instead of teaching his nephew how to fight, Jake shows Marc what real courage is, facing down his own demons along the way. Based on the bestselling novel by former Navy SEAL Jocko Willink, “Way of the Warrior Kid” is directed by McG (“Charlie’s Angels,” “Terminator Salvation”) from a screenplay by Will Staples (“Without Remorse,” “The Right Stuff”).

#3440. 5 Big Challenges in Creating Criterion’s ‘The Complete Kubrick’: From Navigating HDR/4K to Preserving Stanley Kubrick’s Love of Mono Sound

In 2024, archivist Michael Chaiken was approached by the Criterion Collection about what was being described as a “big Kubrick project.” It would start with remastering the director’s last film, “Eyes Wide Shut,” but for months the scope of the ambitious project remained an open question: Was a complete Stanley Kubrick box set even possible?

Kubrick was a precise director, and his control over every aspect of his filmmaking process extended to its home video presentation. But home video technology has developed in ways (widescreen TVs, high dynamic range, 4K resolution, Dolby Atmos) that Kubrick could never have imagined before he died in 1999. As a result — from the image to sound to design of the box itself — there was the underlying question driving Chaiken and the team’s work: “What would Stanley do?” Related Stories Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night?

“I had to research the history of Stanley Kubrick on home video, and that’s a very specific thing,” said Chaiken. “It’s almost like for a biographer that would be [an important] footnote.”

In an interview with IndieWire, Chaiken broke down the challenges and key work behind “The Complete Kubrick,” which hit stores and mailboxes last week.

Home video fanatics are often completists. And if you are going to invest the time in a $599.95 box set (on sale for 30 percent off at most retailers), the motivation to make it comprehensive and definitive is obvious, but with a career spanning five decades, that isn’t always possible.

“You have to kick around the idea, ‘What does ‘complete’ mean? And how would we make that so?,” said Chaiken.

The heart of Kubrick’s feature film career has been well preserved. His final five films were made with Warner Bros., and the studio’s archive team has kept the original elements well preserved. Meanwhile, Criterion, back in its laser disc era, in the 1980s and ’90s, had a good working relationship with Kubrick himself (more about that later) and was already familiar with what was available (and already in-house) when it came to having to remaster his key films into the HDR/4K standards of today.

“It’s the early stuff that was tricky because he wasn’t working for a studio; he was an independent,” said Chaiken. “[A complete box set] almost didn’t happen; it was really at the 11th hour that it came together.”

In the case of “The Seafarers,” a 1953 30-minute documentary Kubrick was commissioned to make for the Seafarers International Union, the issue became untangling the project’s rights. “We thought we knew [who owned the rights], and then somebody said, ‘Hey, by the way, I’m actually the rights holder of that,’” Chaiken chuckled, retelling the story and imagining Kubrick himself groaning at the idea that Criterion had dug it up and restored it. “ I laugh because it’s a work for hire, but at the same time, it’s a very beautiful film, and it’s his first color film, and there’s elements in it that are so Kubrickian.”

The final missing piece was the original 12-minute version of the 1951 documentary “Day of the Fight,” which Kubrick shot and edited independently for Look magazine in 1949.

“There’s a version that [Kubrick] financed and made himself, and then there’s the version that exists,” said Chaiken. “He sold the film to RKO Pictures, and they re-edited the film; they added footage that he didn’t shoot, and they changed the narration and the soundtrack that Kubrick had commissioned Gerald Fried to make.”

Kubrick’s original version had never been presented in 4K, and locating the original elements was the final piece, in Chaiken’s mind, to the set being “complete.”

“Why do you need two cuts of Day of the Fight?” Chaiken rhetorically asked before answering the question: “They are different, and to reinforce that completeness, especially with [this being] Stanley’s very first film.  His cut is actually [four minutes] shorter than the one that RKO made [and] the very first film edited and produced and directed by him.”

Chaiken’s need to present both versions of a film also applied to “The Shining,” which, after it was released domestically in May 1980 — where it bombed with critics — Kubrick spent three months re-editing, making it 25 minutes shorter, for the international release in September 1980.

What’s fascinating is that both versions have been widely available for decades; they just didn’t cross the ocean. The shorter international version is Kubrick’s final cut, and what he considered his director’s cut, never made its way to the U.S.

“[Kubrick] never pulled the U.S. theatrical version, so that version is what has existed here on video. And if you’re doing complete Kubrick, the final edit of ‘The Shining’ has to be on there. It  just has to be,” said Chaiken, noting the significant differences. “The international version is a different experience. The tone of it does shift. It does leave open the possibility that none of this is happening, and it’s all happening in Jack’s head. You really don’t understand [Jack’s] relationship with Danny in the same way in the international version.”

As IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill fully explored, the significant differences between the versions are disorienting for those who grew up loving the longer U.S. version. Chaiken anticipated what “a headscratcher” the international version would be, which is why he commissioned a new commentary track. In the new box set, the U.S. version preserves steadicam operator and founder Garrett Brown’s original Criterion commentary track, but the international version features a newly recorded track by the great Pixar animation director Lee Unkrich, who co-authored a decades-in-the-making, 1,396-page, two-volume “Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining” book, which drew from rare documents, script notes, and storyboards in the Kubrick Archive, and is based on extensive interviews with the surviving cast and crew, to tell the definitive story of the legendary and misunderstood production.

“I imagine American audiences, who love the movie, saying, ‘Why would I want to watch a shorter version of ‘The Shining’? But I think having Lee Unkrich there walking you through it and talking about some of these decisions, and talking about the production of the movie, makes it a rewarding experience,” said Chaiken. “If you’re a skeptic, it’s at least worth watching once with Lee’s commentary because it is like a master-class in ‘The Shining.’”

Twenty years after Francis Ford Coppola and Walter Murch’s groundbreaking “Apocalypse Now” sound design and roadshow ushered in surround sound, and George Lucas used the box office power of his “Star Wars” franchise to leverage theaters into adapting the new technology he was pioneering at Skywalker, Kubrick was still avoiding even doing stereo mixes of his final films.

“He stuck with mono until the end,” said Chaiken. “He was obsessed with presentation, and he truly felt, ‘I would rather have good mono than bad stereo,’ and he didn’t trust that these theaters were set up in such a way that the stereo mix.”

For the box set, Criterion does offer 5.1 mixes of Kubrick’s films, but the default audio is Kubrick’s preferred mono mix. Chaiken and Criterion audio supervisor Ryan Hullings felt it important to go back to original mono mixes, which hadn’t been touched for home video in 30 years, to do new masters for the box set. In most cases, locating the original mono mix assets was not a problem, but there were exceptions, most notably “Full Metal Jacket.”

While Warner Archives had preserved all the original assets, identifying which was the final mono mix proved difficult, explained Chaiken, “ ‘Full Metal Jacket’ was a tricky one because they were trying to convince Stanley to do it in stereo. So there was the beginning of a stereo mix.” In going through what Hullings were the final mono mixes, they didn’t conform with the 35mm print he was using as a comparison. As they did throughout the process of making the box set, the Criterion team turned to Kubrick’s surviving collaborators, in this case “Full Metal Jacket” editor Martin Hunter and Nigel Galt, who would go on to edit “Eyes Wide Shut,” but had done Foley and sound work on “Full Metal Jacket.”

According to Chaiken, it was Galt who helped them solve the puzzle, telling Hullings, “You’ll know you have the right mono mix of ‘Full Metal Jacket’ because during the end credits, in the original mono theatrical mix, we screwed up.” The final song over credits is The Rolling Stones’ “Paint It Black,” but according to Galt, ‘When it went out originally theatrically, we had it at 25 frames per second, so it’s actually sped up. So if you have the mix that has ‘Paint It Black’ at 25 frames per second, that’s it.’”

And yes, on the new Criterion, the “Full Metal Jacket” mono mix preserved “Paint It Black” playing approximately four percent faster than The Rolling Stones recorded it.

“Stanley passed away in 1999, and that was the beginning of when the DVD revolution was starting to happen,” said Chaiken. “So, the idea of Blu-ray and then 4K, you’re in a realm that Kubrick could never have imagined.”

Chaiken confronted this head-on, starting the project with “Eyes Wide Shut”—which he described as one of Kubrick’s hardest films to bridge the gap between the filmmaker’s original intention and the latest in modern home video technology. In working with “Eyes Wide Shut” cinematographer Larry Smith, Chaiken came to understand how much of a “dreamy quality” is a product of the unique way Smith and Kubrick exposed and developed the celluloid.

“It’s never going to be a one-to-one correlation between film and video; you can get close, but video is getting sharper and sharper and sharper,” said Chaiken. “I saw it with ‘Eyes Wide Shut,’ that you could go very hardcore into the 4K, and you could see details in the shadows and things that Kubrick would never have wanted you to see.”

Chaiken and Criterion worked closely with the Warner Archives, Smith, and other collaborators, going back and forth with different passes to figure out how best to find a happy medium, which, with most films, meant sometimes dialing down the HDR and leaning into “more filmic, warmer curve” with the color grade.

The more Chaiken researched, the more he learned just how obsessive Kubrick was about the presentation of his films, and admitted he would get obsessive wondering if they had gotten the colors of a particular transfer right. He sought out advice from Maria Palazzola, long-time restoration supervisor, colorist, and former transfer expert at The Criterion Collection during 1980s and ‘90s, having overseen “director approved” versions of Kubrick’s Criterion laser discs.

“I had assumed that there was an intermediary, or Leon Vitali, Stanley’s longtime assistant, helping Maria,” said Chaiken.”But when I talked to her, she said, ‘No, no, Stanley was calling me directly.’”

Chaiken said he flooded Palazzola with questions trying to find out just how obsessive Kubrick was about his home video transfers and what, in particular, he obsessed about. Chaiken had heard the stories that Kubrick had made Palazzola re-transfer films countless times.

Chaiken explained his assumptions were wrong, “She said that was absolutely not the case. That  [Kubrick] understood the limitations of the technology at that time, and he wanted them to look as good as they could possibly look on home video.”

For example, according Palazzola told Chaiken with “2001: A Space Odyssey,” Kubrick only pressed hard on two key sections.

“He wanted to be sure that the Dawn of Man sequence — that was front projected: The backgrounds were projected when they were filming it — and so he wanted to make sure that you couldn’t see any reflection in the eyes of the apes from that front projection,” said Chaiken. “And she said the one reel that he made her re-transfer a few times was the last reel, in the French boudoir, because [Kubrick] didn’t want it to be too bright.”

Chaiken said the anecdotes of Kubrick’s collaboration with Palazzola changed his perspective on his own work: “Hearing that he was relatively easy to work with was a bit of a relief because he cared about this stuff immensely, but he understood that film is not video. It’s a completely different medium.”

Chaiken gives full credit to visual artist Drusilla Adeline (aka Sister Hyde) for the design of the Kubrick box set, and in this video, you can hear them discuss how the fonts, color, layout, and the box itself were built around the theme of “Kubrick at work,” and how, in going through his archive, you get a sense of him leaving his fingerprints (literally and figuratively) on the making of his films.

One of the things that is striking about the box set, loaded with 16 different films, extras, and supporting materials, is how — compared to most box sets — it is laid out in a way that it is very easy to find what you are looking for, but also clear explanations for each film (each separated by a tab and film poster) of what is versions, audio, and extras are available. Chaiken said that in going through Kubrick’s work, it was clear what an organized and clear archivist the filmmaker was himself.

“In my mind, I was thinking about the Library of America —  what would a Library of America compendium of Stanley Kubrick look like? That  was definitely a touchstone,” said Chaiken. “Library of America editions, where they’ll [be] a single compendium of a great American author and you have the major works, but then you also have these interesting tangential pieces, and they’re laid out so beautifully, they’re just so uniform. They have the little tab that marks a page.”

#3439. Stargate SG-1's Official New Release Confirms The Franchise Is Far From Finished

Stargate SG-1 has been off the air for nearly two decades after a solid ten-season run, but the franchise has never completely disappeared, largely thanks to the fans. Between its sprawling mythology, unforgettable cast of characters, and the sheer number of worlds left to explore, there's a reason fans have spent years hoping for another trip through the gate.

The fanbase took a major blow earlier this year when Amazon MGM scrapped its planned revival, seemingly shutting down one of the franchise's most promising opportunities for a comeback. Fortunately, Stargate fans finally caught a break in October, when reports emerged that a brand-new series was once again in development, this time with WandaVision creator Jac Schaeffer attached.

While it's still early, and there are plenty of questions about what the next chapter might look like, it's an encouraging sign that the franchise isn't going anywhere. And following another recent release, it's becoming increasingly clear that Stargate has a life well beyond its original television run, proving that this beloved sci-fi universe simply refuses to die.

Stargate SG-1 fans have even more to look forward to, as BlueBrixx has officially unveiled two new collectible building sets inspired by the franchise's most recognizable enemies. The German toy company has revealed its Goa'uld Symbiont and Jaffa Battlepack sets, bringing two iconic pieces of Stargate mythology to life.

The Goa'uld Symbiont is a 400-piece display model depicting one of the parasitic alien creatures responsible for controlling human hosts throughout the series. Featuring red eyes, an open mouth, and a segmented body, the set will retail for €19.95. Meanwhile, the 250-piece Jaffa Battlepack includes several Jaffa warriors, interchangeable helmets, staff weapons, and additional accessories for recreating battles from SG-1. That set is listed for €29.95. Both are currently marked as coming soon, with no confirmed release dates.

The Stargate series continues to thrive for fans to this day, and the Stargate SG-1: Serpent Replica is a great example of why that is.

These additions join BlueBrixx's growing collection of officially licensed Stargate sets, which includes recreations of the Stargate Command Gate Room, the F-302 fighter, the Goa'uld Al'kesh bomber, and the Asgard O'Neill-class spaceship. Other models explore the franchise's wider mythology, including the Zero Point Module from Stargate Atlantis and the iconic Destiny spacecraft from Stargate Universe.

For longtime fans, these releases offer an opportunity to recreate memorable scenes that helped define the franchise. With BlueBrixx continuing to expand its Stargate lineup, there's plenty of reason to believe even more fan-favorite designs could eventually receive the brick-building treatment.

For longtime Stargate fans, the arrival of these new BlueBrixx sets is just another sign that the franchise is entering an exciting new era. Although Stargate Universe ended in 2011, bringing the franchise's original television run to a close, the universe has continued expanding in unexpected ways, and momentum appears to be building toward a long-awaited return to television.

Beyond BlueBrixx's increasingly impressive collection, fans have also received new opportunities to explore the franchise through video games. Released in January 2024, Stargate: Timekeepers brought players back into the SG-1 universe through a real-time tactical strategy adventure, with a story set against the backdrop of the original series. Its additional campaign content, released later that year, offered even more opportunities to revisit this beloved sci-fi setting.

Of course, the biggest development is the newly reported Stargate television series from Jac Schaeffer. Although the project remains in its early stages, the announcement has renewed hopes that the franchise will finally return to screens after years of uncertainty, though fans are still reluctant to get too excited until more concrete details surface.

Between new collectibles, video games, and the possibility of an entirely new show, hype surrounding Stargate feels stronger than it has in years.
