#3438. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3437. Here’s what’s coming for the MacBook Pro next year, per report

Apple just unveiled a huge update to the Mac lineup last week, introducing the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

In a new report, Bloomberg has details on what’s next for the MacBook Pro, with multiple new models expected to come next year.

Apple’s current MacBook Pro lineup features multiple different tiers:

In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Mark Gurman says Apple will introduce a new version of the base MacBook Pro powered by the M7 chip next year. This machine will adopt the same design as the new high-end MacBook Pros introduced last week, which are thinner, lighter, and have slimmer bezels.

Yes! I hope “standard” MacBook Pro will have the new lighter and smaller design! Touch is not mandatory for me so I would prefer a cheaper version

The report also says Apple will introduce a second-generation touchscreen MacBook Pro next year, powered by M7 Pro and M7 Max chips.

Gurman previously reported on Apple’s plans to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, instead jumping all the way to the M7 family “as early as the first half of next year.” At the time, Gurman said the M7 line “is designed primarily around major advancements to on-device AI processing.”

Looking further into the future, Gurman eventually expects Apple to converge the MacBook Pro lineup:

With the first version, Apple is charging a $400 premium to add touch, OLED and the Dynamic Island interface. The M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros without touch are sticking around, but I’d be surprised if Apple continued developing non-touch versions of its high-end laptop models. There’s an added burden on its engineering, marketing and manufacturing teams to manage two sets of high-end MacBook Pros, and the prices are close enough for convergence to not be that far off.

#3436. Forget 'Memento,' Billy Bob Thornton's Noir Thriller Is the Perfect Replacement

The noir genre is present within the cinematic DNA of nearly every film by Joel and Ethan Coen, including their brilliant debut feature Blood Simple, the somber hardboiled mystery of Fargo, and even the The Big Lebowski's wacky sleuthing. Although it was evident that the Coens had deep admiration for the noir films of the 1940s, their 2001 film The Man Who Wasn’t There was a full-on throwback period piece, shot in black-and-white, that was heavily inspired by the thrillers of Alfred Hitchcock, most notably Shadow of a Doubt and Rope. It’s a film that contains the idiosyncrasies that are expected of the Coens, but also features one of their most transfixing and compelling protagonists ever in Ed Crane, a mild-mannered barber portrayed by Billy Bob Thornton. Thornton draws out the ambiguity within a character who is both completely vulnerable and entirely unreadable, and it's the different interpretations that can be spun out of The Man Who Wasn’t There that makes it one of the most underrated entries in the Coens’ entire body-of-work.

The Man Who Wasn’t There is set in 1949, where Ed works as a loyal employee at a business owned by his brother-in-law Frank (Michael Badalucco). Although Ed is a pragmatic investor, he is forced to come up with $10,000 to stake in dry cleaning technology that is proposed to him by his regular customer, Creighton Tolliver (Jon Polito). The Man Who Wasn’t There examines the ease with which an unassuming character can be drawn into conspiracy and murder when Ed, suspecting that his wife Doris (Frances McDormand) is having an affair with her boss, “Big Dave” (James Gandolfini), decides to blackmail him. It’s a murky, darkly comedic portrayal of the fractured state of the American psyche in the aftermath of World War II, and draws from both Hitchcock and other ‘40s classics to create a stirring thriller about the price of ambition.

A core tenant of many Hitchcock films is the notion of an “ordinary man in extraordinary circumstances,” and The Man Who Wasn’t There both adheres to and subverts these archetypes. It’s safe to assume that Ed served in the war and is dealing with some degree of post-traumatic stress disorder, but he is also clearly unprepared for a life of crime based on his clumsy self-defense against Dave. It’s similarly unclear if Ed’s drinking problem was the cause of his marital issues with Doris or if he developed his addiction as a result of it, and the loveless nature of their relationship makes his actions all the more fascinating. Ed is detached from reality in a way that is comparable to Meursault in Albert Camus's The Stranger, as he seems unaffected by violence and not particularly jealous as a result of Doris’ affair. Ed’s blackmailing of Dave is more of a strategic move than an act of vengeance, and so to see him suffer as a result of his bad call is all the more darkly ironic.

There’s no shortage of filmmakers who love Hitchcock, but the Coen brothers delivered an authentic throwback to 1949 thanks to their longstanding collaboration with the cinematographer Roger Deakins, who used shorter lenses and high contrast lighting to create the same sort of shadows that would appear in a classic noir. Setting the film at the tail end of the ‘40s, before the Cold War had sparked up, allowed the Coens to deal with a knotty period in American history when businesses were ramping up and ambitious investors were desperate to take advantage of new entrepreneurship opportunities, which may explain why Ed is so enthusiastic about the chance of escaping from the malaise of his empty life. This is where the title comes into play, because The Man Who Wasn’t There refers to more than just the unseen assailant in the crime who the police are seeking; it’s a reference to Ed himself, who has become so self-destructive that he’s nearly invisible to anyone around him.

The Man Who Wasn’t There features one of the Coens’ most underrated casts; Gandolfini in particular is excellent in a subversive role that asks him to be surprisingly vulnerable, despite still being an imposing physical presence. Although the film features an early performance from Scarlett Johansson which led to several other collaborations with the Coens, Thornton is downright brilliant as a tricky character who invites sympathy, despite the fact that his behavior is frequently destructive. Ed is in an sympathetic situation because he has been denied assistance for his alcoholism and cannot be blamed for his employment issues, and at first, his lack of passion would make him seem almost mild-mannered. It’s this transparency within his characterization that allows Thornton to truly shine, as it suggests that even those who have been emotionally deprived are capable of falling victim to human nature.

The Man Who Wasn’t There contains a number of fun Easter Eggs for cinephiles, but it is also a deeply strange film with one of the Coens’ most puzzling endings, which calls into question how much of the story should be taken seriously. In classic Hitchcock fashion, it’s a film that deals with suspenseful material while still being enormously entertaining. Although it didn’t get the attention that it deserved 25 years ago when it first debuted, The Man Who Wasn’t There is one of both the Coens’ and Thornton’s best films, as well as one that would make Hitchcock proud.

#3435. The Mad (Color) Science Behind Rian Johnson’s New Camera App

You shouldn’t ever take a photo of your midterm election ballot — it’s illegal in some states — but, thanks to Rian Johnson and his longtime DP Steve Yedlin, there is now a very cinematic way to take iPhone photos of everything else.

Yedlin has spent more than 20 years as a cinematographer, collaborating closely with Johnson on everything from “Brick” and “The Brothers Bloom” to “The Last Jedi” and the “Knives Out” films. But Yedlin has also spent 20 years delving into the science of color and how filmmakers can better craft imagery through the technical tools available. And now he and his friends are in the business of making new ones. Related Stories 5 Big Challenges in Creating Criterion’s ‘The Complete Kubrick’: From Navigating HDR/4K to Preserving Stanley Kubrick’s Love of Mono Sound Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

Yedlin, Johnson, and color science coder Eric Cameron have been in the process of creating new software for light controls to replace traditional dimmer boards, pixel mapping, and on-screen playback (ie., when actors are looking at phone or computer screens on camera) with something that embraces the world of color-tunable lights and LEDs. But as a side project, they’ve also just launched Chromagraph, an iPhone app that uses Yedlin’s deep, mathematical understanding of color to bypass the iPhone’s default photo processing settings for a more filmic look.

The app project started because Johnson wanted something on his phone that could capture photos the way that Yedlin captures film — using RAW images (ie., everything the sensor captures, not just what’s rendered on a screen) and bypassing the standard iPhone image processing protocols.

Surprisingly, it only took ten weeks to build, test, and refine the app Johnson wanted to a place the team was happy with it — although Yedlin admittedly told IndieWire the process to create Chromagraph was still pretty intense. The cinematographer had done the math to build an image processing look that works for cinema cameras like the Arri ALEXA, but even the newer, pro-level iPhone cameras have sensors so small they’re smol, and they also spread image information out in a different way from how film cameras work.

“ The code values themselves, like the actual numbers in the pixels, alone don’t tell you how bright something’s supposed to be. It’s the code values in the pixels plus this [metadata] evaluation,” Yedlin said of iPhone cameras, before worrying he was being way too technical for a 900-word article. “It’s not like we’re putting different parameters into existing processing math. It’s totally different math for the most part.”

To make a complicated story shorter, then, Yedlin and Cameron couldn’t reprogram the iPhone camera, but they could get it to behave differently in order to bring RAW images (everything the camera sensor captures) into Chromagraph and then do a bunch of different and complicated math to achieve the image processing for the cinematic look that Rian Johnson wanted to be able to pull up at the swipe of a screen.

The main thing that was important to the team to get right and reflect real color science, as opposed to “bullshit cinema color science,” according to Yedlin, was to work from the truth that images that look aesthetically pleasing are not clinical or technical reproductions. They are not photometrically or colorimetrically “correct.”

“What makes a good image is something that looks enough like what it’s representing to be recognizable and then to be beautiful,” Yedlin said. “Even when you have a very clinical-looking, like a broadcast look as opposed to a cinema look, it’s also not photometrically or colorimetrically correct. They’re just not correct in a different way, you know? It’s always a matter of taste.”

A lot of the very complicated math that went into how Chromagraph does image processing is based on Yedlin and Johnson’s taste for how to make an image look artful, but then the app has contrast and saturation tools for individual photographers to take the look of their work even further. The tools inside of Chromagraph are, in fact, meant to be exactly like the math of white balance in ISO on a film camera.

“It sort of gets repeated as giving photos the ‘Knives Out’ look, and that’s fine if people want to say that, but I don’t think of it that way. I think of it as generally artful rendering. Every single movie made with traditional film stocks was made with one of like three negatives and one of two print stocks, and they all have completely different looks based on the craftsmanship and the photography and what’s being photographed and lighting and everything,” Yedlin said. “This is just the image processing, so it’s one look for that part, but the image processing part isn’t the only thing that makes a photo.”

Where Chromagraph can really help photographers make their own photos, though, is in capturing color in a way that the iPhone default method can’t quite reach. “Vibrant colors is a place where I think Chromagraph really shows off. A lot of times, with garish colors, you can have that saturation clamped look where one of the three channels is slammed so the entire area kinda looks like it’s been just colored in like a coloring book,” Yedlin said. “So some people are posting photos [from the app] where the colors really stand out, but then somebody else is posting photos with the most subtle, nuanced colors. It’s only one look, but it’s for that last little bit of finesse for whatever kind of photo you take.”

For that reason, Yedlin, Johnson, and Cameron don’t necessarily want to support multiple looks inside of Chromagraph. They’re also not planning on building an Android version anytime soon, and while they’d like to support video, that’s still a long way from being worked out. But for photographers with an iPhone in their pocket, the app is a fun, easy shortcut past importing photos into professional post tools.

“It’s satisfying that every snapshot looks the way that we like it,” Yedlin said.

Chromagraph is now available in the Apple App Store.

#3433. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3432. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

Apple’s new HomeView product arrives in users’ homes next week, but today a report from The Information outlines what to expect from a larger, high-end ‘HomeView Ultra’ product coming next year.

Today Aaron Tilley at The Information published a report on a forthcoming HomeView product that could be dubbed ‘HomeView Ultra.’

Similar to Mark Gurman’s extensive reporting, Tilley classifies the new home product as a robotics project. He says, “Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots.”

Per the report, the HomeView Ultra product has “a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp.” Tilley writes:

Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it.

The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get oﬀ a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it.

Just get MagSafe going for iPads and create a base for it to attach to plus a HomeView like interface that turns on when attached.

Obviously though Apple wants an exclusive device because adding MagSafe to iPads would allow anyone to make such a base.

And if someone else comes up with an iPad solution it’ll likely get blocked from the App Store.

The report notes that much of the hardware for the product “has been finished for around two years.” Software, however, is keeping the device from shipping. This is due to a more ambitious slate of AI-powered features than was originally envisioned.

Pricing is expected to be “around $1,000” per the report, but it may cost more depending on market prices for components. Tilley spoke to several former employees who said they expect Apple to use ‘HomeView Ultra’ branding for the product. As we’ve seen this fall though, Apple has been hesitant to expand its slate of Ultra products.

As for release timing, Tilley says that “Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though.”

#3430. Dave Bautista’s Insane Kratos Transformation For God Of War Silences Skeptics

For years, Dave Bautista was widely fancast as God of War's Kratos. Surprisingly, when he finally landed the part in Prime Video's live-action God of War, many questioned whether he was the right fit. The skepticism came in the wake of Dave Bautista losing a lot of weight and deciding to move away from physically demanding roles like Drax in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

Dave Bautista was not the first choice to play Kratos in Prime Video's God of War. Before him, Ryan Hurst was cast for the role. He seemed almost perfect for the part because he had previously voiced Thor in God of War Ragnarök. Unfortunately, an injury forced Hurst to step back from the role, paving the way for Bautista to lead the show's roster.

While many defended Dave Bautista's casting and labeled him as the perfect choice for the part, others believed he had lost too much muscle over the years to accurately embody Kratos. Just a few months after his casting, Dave Bautista has already silenced all doubters with his impressive transformation.

Soon after his casting, Dave Bautista revealed he was training again and focusing on putting on muscle before the filming of Prime Video's God of War ensues. A few months into his training, Bautista has now revealed he has already gained 20 pounds of muscle for the part. He even posted a video to show his transformation, and it is hard not to notice how he already looks like Kratos from God of War's Norse saga:

This is the second update the former WWE star has given on his physique while preparing to play Kratos in God of War. The first update came just two weeks after he started training for the part (via Instagram), where he already seemed prepared for the role. After the 20-pound gain, Dave Bautista now closely resembles Kratos from the games' Norse Saga.

The actor's shaved head and overgrown beard further add to the resemblance, and it seems likely he will gain a few more pounds before the show's filming ensues. Now that his transformation has already silenced all skeptics, it is hard not to wait for the show's behind-the-scenes stills that will reveal him in Kratos' full Spartan armor.

Prime Video's God of War is cleverly skipping the games' Greek mythology arc and jumping ahead to the Norse Saga, which is more dense and poignant in terms of storytelling. It features Kratos as a transformed, grief-ridden man who works on his relationship with his son. Owing to the emotional heft of the source material, the Prime Video series needed someone with a good acting range to play Kratos.

At the same time, since the original game franchise's core appeal lies in its action and larger-than-life godly characters, someone with a towering frame had to be cast for the part. After his transformation, Bautista not only seems to perfectly convey Kratos' immense physical presence but also has the acting chops to capture the emotional weight of his story.

The live-action God of War adaptation has experienced a few early production setbacks, which have delayed its filming. However, Dave Bautista's casting as Kratos has seemingly turned out to be a blessing for the Prime Video series. If everything else falls into place for the upcoming video game adaptation, it will easily find its place among the greatest fantasy shows of our time.

#3429. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

#3428. Tolkien Had a Deeper Meaning Behind These 3 Classic Lord of the Rings Characters

There is no denying that, for J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings was always going to deeply reflect his religious convictions. He expressed as much in a 1953 letter to a fan, collected years later in The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, noting, “The Lord of the Rings is, of course, a fundamentally religious and Catholic work; unconsciously so at first, but consciously in the revision.”

Thus, it is not surprising that many of the themes, plot points, and characters expressed in his legendarium echo his Christian beliefs. But while the story of Middle-earth is expressly not allegory, some have pointed out that we see these ideas embodied best in the form of the epic's three most essential characters — Gandalf, Frodo, and Aragorn — who uniquely speak to different aspects of Jesus Christ.

Unlike how his longtime friend C. S. Lewis intended Aslan in The Chronicles of Narnia to literally be Christ manifested in another world, Tolkien actively avoided such direct religious ties. Instead of inserting direct parallels between his mythology and the Bible, Tolkien crafted Gandalf, Frodo, and Aragorn to embody different parts of Christ's role as the Messiah. Philosopher Peter J. Kreeft, author of The Philosophy of Tolkien: The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings, points out this very idea when writing for Ignatius Insight. Kreeft notes that all three characters experience a "death and resurrection" arc and are portrayed as saviors who sacrificially "save all of Middle-earth from the demonic sway of Sauron." As he concludes, "They exemplify the Old Testament threefold Messianic symbolism of prophet (Gandalf), priest (Frodo), and king (Aragorn)."

While the New Testament teaches that Jesus Christ fills each of these roles, Tolkien splits the offices individually. Beginning with the prophet, Gandalf plays the part quite well. The wandering wizard (who is technically akin to an angel) is famously a "servant of the Secret Fire." He calls Frodo out of his comfortable life in the Shire, convinces him to have mercy on Gollum, and performs miraculous feats reminiscent of the biblical prophets of old. Indeed, his wisdom and counsel often border on prophecy, offering comfort or conviction when needed. Gandalf also most perfectly embodies the Christian concept of resurrection. Though he dies to save his allies, he is reborn in white robes, evoking the image of Christ's return in the Book of Revelation.

On the other hand, Frodo represents Jesus' priestly nature. He takes away the evil from Middle-earth by delivering the One Ring to its doom, willing to suffer the burden as he intercedes for all creation. Along the way, he is betrayed, beaten, and even stabbed in the side (as Christ was on the cross), and yet he proceeds with his providential task. In the end, Frodo leaves the world for heavenly places upon the completion of his earthly work.

Finally, Aragorn clearly embodies Christ's messianic role as king. Just as Jesus comes from the line of King David, making him the rightful heir to the throne of Israel, Aragorn rightly takes his place as ruler of Gondor in the aptly named The Return of the King, centuries after the prophecies had foretold it. Of course, he comes only after he first conceals his true identity, unveiling his lineage when the time is right. His willingness to pick up this task, partnered with his ability to command the respect and loyalty of those around him, further embraces this idea. It's no coincidence that Aragorn leads an army of the dead against Sauron's vile forces (another nod to Revelation), and even heals the wounded by the laying on of hands.

Although The Lord of the Rings is not meant to be read as religious allegory, there's no denying that Tolkien's Christian faith was of chief inspiration (and importance) when crafting it. There's something to be said as well that there had to be three Christ figures in this story, not just to echo the three messianic roles, but also because of the Christian belief in a triune God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Indeed, Tolkien's writings did not entirely ignore the existence of a God in Middle-earth either. When unraveling the history of Arda (the name for "Earth" in Tolkien's work) in The Silmarillion, the author reveals that Eru Ilúvatar is the "One" behind the Sacred Fire that created all things. Many during the Second Age, dubbed "The Faithful," worshiped Ilúvatar.

Even behind the scenes, Tolkien could not entirely divorce the events of The Lord of the Rings from the hand of providence. In a 1956 letter likewise collected in The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, the author reveals that the climactic destruction of the One Ring was, itself, something of a miracle. After Samwise Gamgee defeats Gollum's repentance (an act that Tolkien once described as the book's most tragic), the creature returns after Frodo succumbs to the power of the ring.

Unlike Christ, Frodo is unable to resist the temptation, and thus, Tolkien writes, "The Other Power then took over: the Writer of the Story (by which I do not mean myself), 'that one ever-present Person who is never absent and never named' (as one critic has said)." The author implies that, while no one would have made it as far as Frodo did, it was Ilúvatar that caused Gollum to slip and the One Ring to meet its doom.

Time would fail us to make note of all the Christian illustrations Tolkien wove into The Lord of the Rings. Be it Galadriel's connection to the Catholic interpretation of the "Virgin Mary" or the Luciferian downfall of the villainous Morgoth, there are too many to make note of here. Yet, there is no denying that portions of Christ can be found in Middle-earth, largely in the form of a wandering wizard, an unlikely hobbit, and a warrior born to be king.

#3426. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3424. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3422. Superman's Most Dangerous Villain Unleashes Diabolical New Attack To Break DC's Greatest Hero

Everybody's reasonably come to expect nothing less than absolute benevolence from Kal-El in his most compelling major iteration. Absolute Superman has put its star through the emotional gauntlet, unearthing horrific trafficking, being constantly put up against twisted versions of classic foes who are otherwise peaceful, and on the other end of this is one of his most iconic nemeses, Brainiac. Absolute Brainiac's reign of terror has seen human beings twisted into unrecognizable killing machines, and while he's sent plenty of power to face Kal-El, he mostly wants to break his spirits. Even in their final showdown, this hasn't appeared to let up.

While full pages will surface soon, the preview for Absolute Superman #25 has set up the latest literal salvo of sadism put out by Brainiac, using "an endless supply of indentured clones of himself", he launches his horde head-on against Superman. It seemed as though the miniaturizing of Brainiac's ship was to hide from Superman, but instead, it appears to set up another twisted blow to his resolve, sending countless living clones to knowingly be slaughtered by crashing into Superman mid-flight. It's only the latest in a bold series of swings by this most deranged of Brainiacs from DC's modern era.

Generally speaking, aside from grittier turns for Superman such as in Man of Steel, Absolute Superman has stuck pretty consistently to the hero's no-kill rule. He's actively avoided taking such a direction many times now, with perhaps Toyman's offense being the closest readers have come to seeing Kal-El in an unchecked rage, but he's been able to avoid killing his antagonists as long as possible. While one may quibble about technicalities, Brainiac's clones being flung at him as a sort of countermeasure treated living beings as fodder, with the striking image of them splattering against Superman being no less grim. They may be more drone-like than him by comparison, but that might not be seen by Superman the same way.

As Superman noted, the combination of Brainiac's army of clones and miniaturization technology that are rather common in DC lore with a deeply sadistic "lead" Brainiac makes "a recipe for horror." It's the big showdown everybody's been waiting for, so the key villain of this saga is undoubtedly pulling out his dirtiest tricks ahead of a promised new status quo for Absolute Superman. After all, this final confrontation kicks off Superman's spacefaring quest that'll soon bring him into an encounter with the Phantom Zone. Brainiac, even if soundly defeated either temporarily or permanently in this universe, has had a profound effect on Superman, and has one more chance to leave lasting scars.

Jason Aaron and Rafa Sandoval have successfully crafted a gratifying, emotionally resonant story building up Superman, while breaking him down at just the right moment. There have been magnificently heartbreaking chapters like in issue #14, but much of the recent heartache has been engineered by Brainiac. Atomic Skull's story has been turned into much more of a tragedy, and Christopher Smith's turn as Metallo is so hauntingly dark in just how much the former drone-turned-mastermind broke his mind and altered his body. Perhaps most dark of all is Brainiac's massacre of Lex Luthor's family, which up to this point had yet to produce any meaningful results other than inducing enough trauma to, in his eyes, hopefully awaken the iconic Earthling menace.

Superman's most brilliant long-running adversary is moving up not just in power levels, but dark ambitions for the multiverse and all known futures.

The more people he's thrown in Superman's way, the more Absolute Brainiac has tested his enemy's resolve in inventive and unforgivable ways. Brainiac appears to have even pushed Superman past thresholds he never planned on crossing, like killing in this latest issue, and subjected him to immense psychological torture. He's already become an unforgettable menace, and even if he fails to awaken the villainous ego possibly dormant in Luthor, he still took the most extreme, brutal method to massacre an innocent family Superman could not save. Such a trail of blood and misery is hard to look past, even as the story moves on from this point soon.

#3420. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3417. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3415. 8 Books to Read if You Love Prime Video's ‘Reacher'

Ever since it premiered its first season back in 2022, Nick Santora’s Reacher has been a major streaming hit and pop culture phenomenon, becoming one of Prime Video’s flagship shows. Based on Lee Child’s Jack Reacher novels and starring Alan Ritchson in the lead role, the series has been a consistent success with both critics and audiences for years now, and the show has developed a massive fan following. And if you’re a Reacher fan hungry for more like it, it’s time to hit the bookstore.

The obvious choice for more Reacher is, of course, the Jack Reacher book series, the 31st of which was released in October 2026, written by Child’s brother Andrew Child. But beyond those, there are a lot of great books out there that feature characters similar to Reacher and/or explore comparable stories of crime, action, and mystery. Without further ado, here’s our handpicked selection of books to read if you love Reacher.

Arguably the most Reacher book that’s not a Reacher book, David Baldacci’s Zero Day is the first novel in the author’s John Puller series. Like Reacher, Puller is the perfect combination of brains and brawn — built like a mountain and the smartest guy in most rooms — and he applies those talents in service of his country as the best investigator in the US Army’s Criminal Investigations Division. The novel follows him on a shocking case in remote West Virginia that he soon suspects may be part of something much bigger than he initially anticipated.

Baldacci has built quite a reputation as an author of highly suspenseful thrillers, and Zero Day is fairly representative of his work. It’s a genre book, the kind you might pick up in an airport bookstore, and a masterfully executed one at that. With a charismatic protagonist and plenty of twists and turns to keep you on your toes, Zero Day and its three sequels are an excellent read for fans of Reacher.

Created by Robert Crais, Elvis Cole and Joe Pike are Los Angeles-based private investigators introduced in the 1987 novel The Monkey’s Raincoat. Since then, the series has expanded to include nineteen more books, all following Cole and Pike into L.A.’s sordid underbelly in various cases, some of which tie back to their own pasts. The latest book in the series, The Big Empty, was released in 2025.

Robert Crais may not be as internationally popular as Lee Child, but the author has been hailed by many as one of America’s best crime writers. His Elvis Cole and Joe Pike novels are easily among the most engaging detective books of all time, with decades' worth of stories to explore. Witty, surprisingly emotional, and anchored by a charismatic duo who are perfectly matched, the Elvis Cole and Joe Pike series is a delightful read for all fans of sharp crime fiction.

Vince Flynn’s Mitch Rapp is a modern literary action hero who has appeared in 20+ novels since his first appearance in 2010’s American Assassin. Capture or Kill isn’t one of Flynn’s books, but it is the first Mitch Rapp novel written by the franchise’s current author, Don Bentley. Set in 2011, the book revolves around the United States government’s efforts to capture or kill Osama bin Laden. A highly effective CIA assassin, Mitch Rapp is brought in to gather crucial intel and foil the plans of an Iranian foe bent on upending the power structures of the Middle East.

Though perhaps not as popular as the Reacher franchise, the Mitch Rapp series is a successful line of thriller novels, and Capture or Kill marks the beginning of an exciting new era for the series. Blending real-life facts with gripping spy fiction, the novel is an excellent read that stays true to the late Vince Flynn’s style while expanding the world in interesting ways. Since its publication in 2024, Capture or Kill has been followed by two sequels, 2025’s Denied Access and 2026’s Double Tap, both written by Bentley.

Four action series. One of them is built around exactly the way you handle pressure, people, and a room that has just gone very quiet. Here is where you would survive the trilogy, and probably headline it.

You are precision with a grudge. You don't posture, you don't escalate, and you don't warn anybody twice. That is exactly why the people who know you are so careful never to be the reason you start.

You understand the thing the whole franchise is secretly about: the cars are spectacular, but the crew is the point. You collect people, you keep them, and you'd drive through a building for any one of them.

You over-prepare and then take the dangerous part yourself anyway. It looks like control, but it's really responsibility. You have never worked out how to ask somebody else to carry the risk.

You are not the most trained person in the building, the best equipped, or the one anybody would have picked. You are simply the one still standing at the end, which turns out to be the only qualification that matters.

Written by Spanish author Juan Gómez-Jurado and translated into English by Nicholas Caistor, Red Queen is a mystery thriller novel that’s the first book in the Antonia Scott series. The story introduces Antonia Scott, the daughter of a British diplomat and a Spanish mother, who has a uniquely gifted mind that allows her to see connections others do not. After a personal tragedy, Antonia attempts to retreat from the world, but she’s brought out of her self-imposed retirement by a terrifying new case.

Often compared to Stieg Larsson’s Millennium trilogy (and its protagonist, Lisbeth Salander), Gómez-Jurado’s Antonia Scott novels are easily among the best thriller books of the past decade. An international bestseller that’s also earned high critical acclaim, Red Queen is a fast-paced crime read with the right balance of chills, thrills, humor, and emotion. The book was followed by two sequels, Black Wolf and White King, and a thriller series based on the novels, also titled Red Queen, premiered on Prime Video in 2024.

A classic political thriller novel written by Frederick Forsyth, The Day of the Jackal revolves around a professional assassin who is hired by French dissidents to kill Charles de Gaulle, the president of France. As the Jackal makes preparations for the kill, investigators uncover details of the plot and race against time to capture the assassin before he can finish the job. The book is inspired partly by true events — there was indeed an attempt to assassinate de Gaulle in 1962, which the book opens with — but the actual story is a work of fiction.

The Day of the Jackal was a big hit when it was first published in 1971, winning the Edgar Award for Best Novel in 1972. The novel has remained consistently popular ever since and has inspired multiple film and TV adaptations around the world, most recently the 2024 Sky-Peacock series starring Eddie Redmayne and Lashana Lynch. The Day of the Jackal is a thriller classic that’s highly suspenseful and thoroughly engrossing, and easily one of the most iconic novels in its genre.

Created by Robert Ludlum, the Bourne series is a collection of spy novels that started with 1980’s The Bourne Identity. The books follow Jason Bourne, whose story begins with him being found by fishermen in the Mediterranean Sea, with no idea who he is or how he got there. As he slowly recalls the pieces of his lost past, Bourne feels compelled to hunt down an international terrorist and finds unsettling evidence that he may be an assassin himself.

The Bourne novels and the movies they inspired are very different beasts entirely. Where the films focus on high-intensity action, the novels are gripping Cold War thrillers that are more about tradecraft and intrigue than just violence and explosions. Ludlum wrote three of the Bourne books, including 1986’s The Bourne Supremacy and 1990’s The Bourne Ultimatum. After his death, the series has been continued by authors Eric Van Lustbader and Brian Freeman, with the latest (and 22nd) novel, The Bourne Revenge, released in 2026.

Written by Gregg Hurwitz, Orphan X is a thriller novel that’s the first book in the series. The novel follows Evan Smoak, a former government assassin who helps people in need, going by the codename “The Nowhere Man." When a meeting with a client leads Evan into an ambush, he finds himself hunted by the program that created him.

A pulpy modern thriller hit that captures the gritty energy of genre classics like the Bourne series and the Jack Ryan novels, Orphan X is a thoroughly absorbing read from start to finish. Thrilling and suspenseful, with plenty of action, the book is an entertaining introduction to one of the best novel series of the 21st century. Today, the Orphan X series includes 12 books. There have been multiple attempts to adapt the novels for film or television, though none of them have panned out just yet.

Written by Tom Clancy, Patriot Games is the second published book in Clancy’s Jack Ryan series and the first chronologically. The novel follows Ryan, a former U.S. Marine lieutenant, who foils a kidnapping attempt on the Prince and Princess of Wales while holidaying in London. The incident makes him a target of the Irish terrorist group behind the failed kidnapping, putting his family in danger.

Jack Ryan and Reacher have been popularly compared and contrasted for practically as long as both have been around; especially these days, with Prime Video boasting hit adaptations of both. But though Reacher and Jack Ryan may share a first name and military connections, the two book series are vastly different, with the Jack Ryan books (Patriot Games, in particular) taking a more cerebral approach that reflects the geopolitics of their time. It may not be the actual first book of the series, but Patriot Games is an excellent introduction to Jack Ryan for new readers. The novel also inspired a film adaptation starring Harrison Ford in 1992.

#3414. Palm Beach Plane Crash: Investigators Share New Details in Day 2 Press Conference

The National Transportation Safety Board shared another update on the deadly Florida plane crash that killed nine people ... including just how far the debris ended up from the crash site.

The agency held another press conference Tuesday as investigators work to piece together what caused a private jet to plummet from the sky Sunday and crash into a Palm Beach County neighborhood.

A spokesperson for the NTSB said during the press conference that debris from the crash can be found up to 4 miles away from the crash site ... and they're asking members of the community to be vigilant -- while also imploring them not to move what they might find.

At least some important pieces of the aircraft separated before the impact, the NTSB agent added. He also noted the investigation into the pilots' certification as it relates to flying the Learjet 60.

He also made it clear there's no evidence to suggest this was an attack aimed at President Trump, whose club Mar-a-Lago is nearby.

As TMZ previously reported ... NTSB officials revealed Monday there were indications the Learjet 60 was breaking apart before it hit the ground. Investigators also said they were examining poor weather conditions, including ice and turbulence, but stressed it was still early in the investigation.

Chilling air traffic control audio captured the crew's frantic final moments ... including a mayday call as the jet rapidly lost altitude and a crew member warned they were about to crash.

All nine people aboard were killed ... including Texas entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, their two young children, three other passengers and two pilots.

As we first reported ... the group was headed from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas to celebrate Adam's birthday when tragedy struck.

The NTSB has not determined the cause of the crash.
